name: Mohrungen
place: Mohrungen (now Morąg), Ducal Prussia
commanders A: Swedish army of Gustavus Adolphus (field commander not named in the sources consulted)
Prussian force: About 1,800 Ducal Prussian troops sent by Elector George William, under pressure from Sigismund III of Poland to act against the Swedes; they went over to Swedish service and later formed the Swedish Yellow Regiment.
losses B: the whole force of about 1,800 taken into Swedish service
borderline: More a capitulation and change of sides than a battle: the source says the battle began and the Prussians quickly entered Swedish service; no date, commanders or casualties given.
doubts and flags: Borderline: More a capitulation and change of sides than a battle: the source says the battle began and the Prussians quickly entered Swedish service; no date, commanders or casualties given.
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: en.wikipedia Prussian campaign (1626–1629) (citing Essen, The Lion from the North (2020); Sundberg, Svenska krig 1521–1814 (1998); Geijer, The History of the Swedes (1845))
note: Placed in the source after Gustavus Adolphus's return to Pillau on 8 May 1627 and before his move against Koniecpolski at Dirschau (August 1627). George William otherwise kept the duchy neutral; the Polish army was not present.

name: Steinau (1632)
place: Steinau an der Oder (now Ścinawa), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Hans Georg von Arnim (Saxony); Jacob Duwall (Swedish troops)
Prussian force: Brandenburg regiments serving with Arnim's Saxon army and Duwall's Swedes in the 1632 Silesian campaign; their strength and commander are not given in the sources consulted.
borderline: Brandenburg participation and the result not verified online (pages could not be fetched); a series of combats rather than a single battle.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Brandenburg participation and the result not verified online (pages could not be fetched); a series of combats rather than a single battle. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: de.wikipedia Ścinawa (Steinau an der Oder), citing the study 'Die Gefechte bei Steinau an der Oder vom 29. August bis 4. September 1632'; Wilson, Europe's Tragedy (2009) (not checked online)
note: Calendar style of the dates in the cited study not stated. Saxon-led allied success opening the occupation of Lower Silesia; Imperial commander not confirmed.

name: Steinau (1633)
place: Steinau an der Oder (now Ścinawa), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Albrecht von Wallenstein
commanders B: Heinrich Matthias von Thurn (captured), Jacob Duwall
Prussian force: Brandenburg troops were among Wallenstein's opponents with the Swedes and Saxons (de.wikipedia); their strength and commander are not given in the sources consulted.
losses B: A Swedish corps of about 5,000 men and 60 guns captured
borderline: Size of the Brandenburg element unknown; the force captured was essentially Thurn's Swedish corps.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Size of the Brandenburg element unknown; the force captured was essentially Thurn's Swedish corps. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: de.wikipedia Ścinawa (Steinau an der Oder), citing 'Das Treffen bei Steinau an der Oder am 11. October 1633'; en.wikipedia Heinrich Matthias von Thurn
note: Wallenstein's surprise of Thurn's corps; Thurn was captured and released. Wallenstein then advanced into Brandenburg (Frankfurt (Oder), Landsberg).

name: Liegnitz (1634)
place: Liegnitz (now Legnica), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Hans Georg von Arnim (with Hans von der Pforte and Vitzthum)
Prussian force: A Brandenburg contingent is reported in Arnim's allied army in some accounts; de.wikipedia describes the army as Electoral Saxon and names no Brandenburg troops.
borderline: Brandenburg participation not confirmed in the sources consulted.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Brandenburg participation not confirmed in the sources consulted. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Liegnitz (1634); en.wikipedia Hans Georg von Arnim-Boitzenburg
note: The Imperials left the field after about three hours of fighting. The loss columns in de.wikipedia are unlabelled; the attribution above follows the context.

name: Kyritz
place: Kyritz, Prignitz, Brandenburg
commanders A: Johan Banér (army commander)
Prussian force: de.wikipedia 'Dreißigjähriger Krieg' says the Swedes beat 'ein brandenburgisches Heer' at Kyritz; no strength or commander given. Brandenburg had acceded to the Peace of Prague on 28 September 1635.
borderline: Sources conflict on who was beaten: a Brandenburg army (de.wikipedia Dreißigjähriger Krieg) or the remnants of the Saxon army after Dömitz (de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Dömitz). Role set to contingent until checked; it would be principal if the Brandenburg reading holds.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Sources conflict on who was beaten: a Brandenburg army (de.wikipedia Dreißigjähriger Krieg) or the remnants of the Saxon army after Dömitz (de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Dömitz). Role set to contingent until checked; it would be principal if the Brandenburg reading holds.
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: de.wikipedia Dreißigjähriger Krieg; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Dömitz; en.wikipedia Battle of Dömitz
note: de.wikipedia gives 7 December 1635, evidently Julian (it dates Dömitz to 22 October, i.e. 1 November New Style); converted here to 17 December.

name: Gartz (1638)
place: Gartz (Oder), Pomerania
commanders A: Hans Caspar von Klitzing
Prussian force: Brandenburg troops under Hans Caspar von Klitzing, general in command of the Elector's field troops and fortresses from late 1637 (his own regiment 850 men).
borderline: The source says only that Klitzing took the town; no fighting described, so it may have surrendered without a siege.
doubts and flags: Borderline: The source says only that Klitzing took the town; no fighting described, so it may have surrendered without a siege.
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: de.wikipedia Hans Caspar von Klitzing
note: 22 February 1638 Julian. Part of Brandenburg's attempt, allied with the Emperor, to win Pomerania from the Swedes after the death of Duke Bogislaw XIV.

name: Rathenow (siege, 1638)
place: Rathenow, Havelland, Brandenburg
commanders A: Hans Caspar von Klitzing
Prussian force: Brandenburg troops under Hans Caspar von Klitzing, who retook the town from its Swedish garrison.
borderline: Recapture ending in a capitulation (the garrison was given free passage); extent of the fighting not described.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Recapture ending in a capitulation (the garrison was given free passage); extent of the fighting not described.
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: de.wikipedia Hans Caspar von Klitzing
note: Calendar style of the date not stated. Not to be confused with Klitzing's siege of Rathenow in August–September 1636, made in Saxon service.

name: Warsaw (1656)
place: Right bank of the Vistula north of Praga, between Białołęka and Bródno, Warsaw
commanders A: Charles X Gustav of Sweden (wounded); Elector Frederick William, with Otto Christoph von Sparr second in command
commanders B: John II Casimir (with Wincenty Gosiewski and Aleksander Hilary Połubiński, who led the hussar charge)
Prussian force: Elector Frederick William in person with about 8,500 Brandenburgers (Otto Christoph von Sparr second in command), nearly half of the allied army led by Charles X Gustav; the first great battle of the Brandenburg army.
strength B: about 40,000 (36,000–39,000 Polish–Lithuanian, 2,000 Crimean Tatars); some sources up to 100,000
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Warsaw (1656); en.wikipedia Second Northern War (Frost 2000); de.wikipedia Zweiter Nordischer Krieg
note: Gregorian dates (18–20 July O.S.). Three-day battle; the allies took Warsaw but the Polish–Lithuanian army escaped largely intact.

name: Lubrze
place: Lubrze (Gmina Krzykosy), south-east of Środa Wielkopolska, about 47 km south-east of Poznań
commanders A: Andrzej Karol Grudziński, voivode of Kalisz
Prussian force: Brandenburg cavalry in a mixed Swedish-Brandenburg division marching to relieve Kalisz; Rudawski lists officers lost from the Brandenburg regiments of Pfuhl, Derfflinger and Wittgenstein and Colonel Kanneberg (acting major general).
losses B: 500–800 killed (the whole command of 800 according to des Noyers), many captured including a Prussian colonel
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lubrze (Rudawski 1855; Pierre des Noyers, Lettres 1859; Patrick Gordon, Diary)
note: A night surprise of a weakly guarded cavalry camp. Brandenburg's share of the division is not given; afterwards the Elector pulled Derfflinger's Brandenburg division back from the march on Kalisz to Toruń (Kalisz surrendered to the Poles on 8 November 1656).

name: Prostki
place: Prostken (now Prostki), on the Lyck (Ełk) river south of Lyck (Ełk), Ducal Prussia
commanders A: Wincenty Gosiewski; Subhan Ghazi Agha (Tatars)
commanders B: Georg Friedrich von Waldeck; Bogusław Radziwiłł (captured)
Prussian force: The Brandenburg general Georg Friedrich von Waldeck with a Brandenburg-Swedish force of about 3,500–4,000 and 9 guns, with Prince Bogusław Radziwiłł.
losses B: about 1,500 Swedes killed and captured, Brandenburg losses unknown; all 9 guns lost; only about 500 escaped
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Prostki; en.wikipedia Wincenty Korwin Gosiewski; de.wikipedia Zweiter Nordischer Krieg (Waldeck's defeat on the Lyck)
note: Followed by the Tatar raid that devastated south-eastern Ducal Prussia in 1656–57 (de.wikipedia: about 23,000 inhabitants killed, 3,400 enslaved); the raid is not a battle.

name: Filipów
place: Filipów, north-west of Suwałki
commanders A: Gustaf Otto Stenbock; Georg Friedrich von Waldeck
Prussian force: Waldeck's Brandenburgers fought with Gustaf Otto Stenbock's Swedes in a combined army of about 6,000; the Brandenburg share is not given.
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Filipów; en.wikipedia Wincenty Korwin Gosiewski
note: en.wikipedia's casualty table is unlabelled; the attribution of the losses above is the likely reading. The Lithuanians withdrew from Ducal Prussia; Radziwiłł escaped from captivity in the confusion.

name: Toruń (siege, 1658)
place: Thorn (now Toruń), Royal Prussia
commanders A: Jerzy Sebastian Lubomirski, Jan Fryderyk Sapieha, Krzysztof Grodzicki (Poland); Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches (Imperial); Bogusław Radziwiłł (Brandenburg-Prussian division)
Prussian force: A Brandenburg-Prussian division under Bogusław Radziwiłł, the Elector's governor in Ducal Prussia, cooperated with the Polish and Imperial besiegers; its size is not given.
strength A: about 18,700 Poles (including about 500 Tatars) and 4,600 Imperials, 40 guns, with the Brandenburg division
borderline: Brandenburg contingent of unknown size, mentioned only in passing
doubts and flags: Borderline: Brandenburg contingent of unknown size, mentioned only in passing.
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Toruń (1658); en.wikipedia Second Northern War
note: The Swedish garrison capitulated on 30 December 1658.

name: Als (1658)
place: Sonderburg (Sønderborg) and the island of Als (Alsen), Duchy of Schleswig
commanders A: Elector Frederick William; Admiral Peter Bredal (Danish ships, killed)
commanders B: Rutger von Ascheberg; Admiral Claes Uggla (relief squadron)
Prussian force: Elector Frederick William, commander of the allied army (about 16,000 Brandenburgers, 11,000 Imperials and 5,000 Poles), took Sønderborg and crossed to Als with about 4,000 men, Brandenburg and Polish cavalry landing first.
strength A: about 4,000 landed (first wave 700–800 Brandenburg and Polish cavalry), six Danish ships
losses B: two wounded during the evacuation (per en.wikipedia)
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: en.wikipedia Invasion of Als (1658); en.wikipedia Second Northern War
note: Gregorian dates (4–8 December O.S.). Ascheberg, driven into Sønderborg Castle after three skirmishes, broke out and was evacuated by Uggla's ships to Funen; the allies held Als and then Nordborg.

name: Ebeltoft
place: Ebeltoft Bay (Ebeltoft Vig), east Jutland
commanders A: Owen Coxe
Prussian force: No Brandenburg ships; Brandenburg is listed among the allies because the destroyed troop transport fleet for Funen was part of the Elector's landing plan.
strength B: 5 Danish and Dutch frigates escorting a troop transport fleet
losses B: 1 frigate blown up, 4 frigates captured, about 1,000 captured, transport fleet destroyed
borderline: Brandenburg role uncertain: listed as a belligerent, but no Brandenburg ships and the nationality of the embarked troops is not stated
doubts and flags: Borderline: Brandenburg role uncertain: listed as a belligerent, but no Brandenburg ships and the nationality of the embarked troops is not stated. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ebeltoft; en.wikipedia Siege of Stettin (1659) (the Elector's Funen plan 'thwarted at the Battle of Ebeltoft')
note: Date given as 23 July 1659 in Danish usage (Julian); converted here.

name: Greifswald (assault, 1659)
place: Greifswald, Swedish Pomerania
commanders A: Burchard Müller von der Lühnen
Prussian force: Elector Frederick William led an Austro-Brandenburg force of about 1,500 in the first assault on the so-called 'Fat Gate', his main army from Jutland arriving overnight; two storms failed.
strength A: about 400 soldiers (sortie of 250 cavalry and 150 infantry), with armed burghers
losses B: probably not over 500 killed, wounded and captured (older estimates 1,000 or more)
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: en.wikipedia Assault on Greifswald; ADB 'Müller von der Lühne, Burchard' (defence of Greifswald 23–30 September 1659); en.wikipedia Offensive into Swedish Pomerania (1659); en.wikipedia Second Northern War (Buchholz 1999)
note: Dates disputed: en.wikipedia's infobox has 22–28 September, its text 22–28 August; ADB gives 23–30 September. Calendar not stated (Pomerania still used the Julian calendar), so possibly early October N.S. The town was bombarded and set on fire; the Elector then turned to Demmin.

name: Stettin (siege, 1659)
place: Stettin (now Szczecin), Swedish Pomerania
commanders A: Paul Würtz (governor); Carl Gustaf Wrangel (relief)
commanders B: Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches (Imperial); Friedrich zu Dohna (Brandenburg)
Prussian force: Brandenburg reinforcements of 1,500–2,000 (two cavalry and three infantry regiments) under Friedrich zu Dohna, with the Brandenburg siege artillery, in the Imperial siege army under de Souches.
strength A: about 2,600 effectives, 36 guns, 4 mortars (later reinforced by Wrangel)
losses B: in the sortie of 31 October/1 November O.S. the Imperials lost 150–200 killed and 100–130 captured and most of the Brandenburg artillery was destroyed
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Stettin (1659) (von Essen 2023; Englund 2000); en.wikipedia Offensive into Swedish Pomerania (1659); de.wikipedia Zweiter Nordischer Krieg
note: en.wikipedia gives 19 September – 5 November, evidently Julian (de.wikipedia: the attack was abandoned on 16 November); converted here. The siege was lifted after Swedish sorties and raids on the allied depots; the Brandenburgers withdrew to Löcknitz.

name: Demmin (siege, 1659)
place: Demmin, on the Peene, Swedish Pomerania
commanders A: Elector Frederick William; Field Marshal Otto Christoph von Sparr
Prussian force: Brandenburg troops under Field Marshal Otto Christoph von Sparr, the Elector present; they ringed the town with redoubts, mined the outer ramparts and took the outworks. Strength not given.
losses B: garrison capitulated and marched off to Stralsund
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: de.wikipedia Demminer Stadtbefestigung (Festung Demmin); en.wikipedia Second Northern War (taken 9 November); en.wikipedia Siege of Stettin (1659)
note: A 28-day siege ending on 9 November 1659 (en.wikipedia, calendar not stated), so it began about mid-October. en.wikipedia Siege of Stettin (1659) dates the capture to 7 September, apparently a confusion with Damm (taken 7 September).

name: Nyborg
place: Nyborg, Funen
commanders A: Ernst Albrecht von Eberstein (Danish field marshal); Hans Schack; Michiel de Ruyter (Dutch fleet)
Prussian force: Brandenburg troops fought in Eberstein's army that crossed the Little Belt (ADB: Eberstein reported the battle to the Great Elector, 'whose troops fought in it'); their number is not given.
strength A: 9,000–11,200 (mostly Danish, with Brandenburg and Polish troops)
losses B: about 2,000 killed and 3,000 or more captured the next day
borderline: Brandenburg share unknown; may have been larger than a contingent
doubts and flags: Borderline: Brandenburg share unknown; may have been larger than a contingent.
period: The Thirty Years' War and the Northern War
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Nyborg; en.wikipedia Dano-Swedish War (1658–1660); ADB 'Eberstein, Ernst Albrecht von' (Henner 1877); en.wikipedia Second Northern War (24 November)
note: Danish and German sources give 14 November (Julian); en.wikipedia Second Northern War gives 24 November. The Swedes surrendered in Nyborg the next day and Funen was lost to Sweden.

name: Grave (siege, 1674)
place: Grave, on the Meuse, North Brabant
commanders A: William III of Orange; Carl von Rabenhaupt (Dutch); the Brandenburg commander is not named
Prussian force: Brandenburg troops reinforced Rabenhaupt's Dutch besieging force in August 1674, which made the full investment possible; units, commander and strength not given in the sources consulted.
strength A: about 30,000 (including 10,000 reinforcements that arrived on 9 October)
borderline: Brandenburg troops are mentioned only in general terms (en.wikipedia: Rabenhaupt 'supported by some Spanish and Brandenburgian forces'; 'Brandenburg troops reinforced him in August'); no unit, commander or strength given.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Brandenburg troops are mentioned only in general terms (en.wikipedia: Rabenhaupt 'supported by some Spanish and Brandenburgian forces'; 'Brandenburg troops reinforced him in August'); no unit, commander or strength given. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Grave (1674); en.wikipedia Carl von Rabenhaupt
note: The garrison capitulated on 27 October on favourable terms and left with the honours of war. The infobox gives casualties as about 2,000 and 7,000–8,000 without labelling the sides; the Rabenhaupt article says the garrison inflicted heavy casualties on the besiegers, so the larger figure is the besiegers'.

name: Turckheim
place: Between Colmar and Turckheim (Türkheim), Upper Alsace
commanders A: Vicomte de Turenne
commanders B: Alexander von Bournonville (Imperial army); Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg
Prussian force: The Brandenburg field army of about 20,000 under the Great Elector in person, which had joined Bournonville's Imperial army in its winter quarters around Colmar in October 1674.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Turckheim; en.wikipedia Battle of Mulhouse (1674) (Brandenburg reinforcement of about 20,000); de.wikipedia Nordischer Krieg (1674–1679)
note: 26 December 1674 in the Julian calendar (the date some German accounts give). The allies abandoned Alsace and recrossed the Rhine at Strasbourg; Brandenburg's absence on the Rhine led to the Swedish invasion of the Mark. Brandenburg was not at Entzheim (4 October 1674, before it arrived) and is not recorded at Mulhouse (29 December 1674).

name: Löcknitz
place: Löcknitz castle, west of Stettin (Szczecin)
Prussian force: A Brandenburg garrison of 180 men under Colonel Götz.
borderline: a castle that surrendered after one day's shelling; no named article
doubts and flags: Borderline: a castle that surrendered after one day's shelling; no named article.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: en.wikipedia Swedish invasion of Brandenburg (1674–1675)
note: 5 May Julian. Götz was court-martialled and executed on 24 March 1676 for the surrender. The Swedish attacks on the Rhin crossings (Oranienburg, Kremmen, Fehrbellin) and on Spandau in June 1675 are not entered: no named actions.

name: Rathenow
place: Rathenow, on the Havel
commanders A: Field Marshal Georg von Derfflinger, General Adolph von Goetze (under the Elector Frederick William)
Prussian force: About 1,000 men in the assault, from the Elector's column of about 5,000 cavalry, 600 dragoons, 1,350 musketeers and 14 guns that had marched from Magdeburg; Derfflinger led the surprise attack in person.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: de.wikipedia Schlacht um Rathenow; en.wikipedia Swedish invasion of Brandenburg (1674–1675); en.wikipedia Battle of Rathenow
note: 15 June 1675 Julian. A surprise attack with street fighting ('Überfall von Rathenow'); it split the Swedish army and opened the Fehrbellin campaign.

name: Nauen
place: Nauen, west of Berlin
commanders A: Lieutenant Colonel Sydow (vanguard), Field Marshal Georg von Derfflinger (under the Elector Frederick William)
Prussian force: The Brandenburg vanguard of about 1,200 cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel Sydow, with Derfflinger's detachment restoring the bridge.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Nauen; en.wikipedia Battle of Nauen; en.wikipedia Swedish invasion of Brandenburg (1674–1675)
note: 17 June 1675 Julian. A rearguard action: the Brandenburgers took the town and the Swedes retreated overnight towards Fehrbellin.

name: Fehrbellin
place: Near Hakenberg, south of Fehrbellin, northwest of Berlin
commanders A: Frederick William, the Great Elector; Georg von Derfflinger; Prince Frederick of Hesse-Homburg
Prussian force: The Elector's cavalry and dragoons, 6,000–7,000 men with 13 guns (the infantry had not come up), under Frederick William and Derfflinger; Hesse-Homburg opened the attack with the vanguard.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Fehrbellin; en.wikipedia Swedish invasion of Brandenburg (1674–1675); de.wikipedia Nordischer Krieg (1674–1679)
note: 18 June 1675 Julian. The first battle the Brandenburg army won on its own. Modern counts are small (en.wikipedia calls it almost a skirmish); older Prussian accounts give larger Swedish numbers and losses. The Swedes escaped over a repaired bridge at night; the pursuit ended after rearguard actions at Haberhof and near Wittstock (not entered: unnamed).

name: Carlsburg (siege, 1675)
place: Carlsburg fortress at Lehe, on the Weser estuary (now Bremerhaven)
commanders A: Lieutenant Colonel Sidon (relief force); the Carlsburg garrison
Prussian force: A seaborne Brandenburg landing force of about 534 soldiers (800–900 with the ship crews) under Admiral Simon de Bolfey, supported by a squadron of seven ships.
losses B: about 314, mostly captured (30 deserted during the siege)
borderline: a failed landing and short siege, known from the en.wikipedia campaign article only; no article of its own
doubts and flags: Borderline: a failed landing and short siege, known from the en.wikipedia campaign article only; no article of its own.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: en.wikipedia Bremen-Verden campaign
note: The garrison refused to surrender and repulsed the Brandenburgers; a Swedish sortie on 1 October was beaten off, but Sidon's relief force caught the Brandenburgers re-embarking on 2 October. The later siege of Carlsburg (late 1675 – 22 January 1676) was by Münster, Danish and Lüneburg troops (not entered). Other Brandenburg troops (Spaen, about 2,000–2,300) joined the allied advance into Bremen-Verden, but no specific engagement of theirs is recorded.

name: Wolgast (siege, 1675)
place: Wolgast, on the Peenestrom
commanders A: Frederick William, the Great Elector
Prussian force: A Brandenburg siege force of about 3,500 men and 8 guns under the Elector.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Wolgast; de.wikipedia Nordischer Krieg (1674–1679)
note: en.wikipedia gives 1–10 November 1675; de.wikipedia 31 October – 10 November (calendar not stated). The occupation of Wollin (10–13 October 1675) is not entered: no fighting recorded.

name: Wolgast (1676)
place: Wolgast, on the Peenestrom
commanders A: Colonel Heinrich Hallard, called Elliot
Prussian force: Six Brandenburg companies, about 300 men, under Colonel Heinrich Hallard (Elliot), holding the town.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: de.wikipedia Nordischer Krieg (1674–1679) (text and navbox 'Wolgast 1676', red link)
note: A failed Swedish storm on the Brandenburg-held town (de.wikipedia 'Sturmangriff auf Wolgast 1676'); calendar not stated.

name: Peenemünder Schanze
place: The Peenemünde redoubt at the mouth of the Peene, Usedom
Prussian force: The Brandenburg Leib-Dragoner regiment.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: de.wikipedia Nordischer Krieg (1674–1679) (text and navbox 'Peenemünder Schanze', red link 'Gefecht um die Peenemünder Schanze')
note: The capture opened the Peene mouth for the 1676 campaign against Anklam and Demmin; calendar not stated.

name: Anklam (siege, 1676)
place: Anklam, on the Peene
commanders A: Frederick William, the Great Elector
Prussian force: The Brandenburg field army under the Elector.
borderline: no article of its own; details of the siege not found
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article of its own; details of the siege not found.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: de.wikipedia Nordischer Krieg (1674–1679); en.wikipedia Siege of Stettin (1677) (background)
note: de.wikipedia: taken 29 August 1676; en.wikipedia: 17 August (probably Julian, = 27 August Gregorian).

name: Demmin (siege, 1676)
place: Demmin fortress, on the Peene
commanders A: Frederick William, the Great Elector
Prussian force: The Brandenburg field army under the Elector.
borderline: no article of its own; details of the siege not found
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article of its own; details of the siege not found.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: de.wikipedia Nordischer Krieg (1674–1679); en.wikipedia Siege of Stettin (1677) (background)
note: de.wikipedia: fortress taken 20 October 1676; en.wikipedia: 30 September 1676. Start date unknown (after Anklam).

name: Stettin (siege, 1676)
place: Stettin (now Szczecin), on the Oder
commanders A: Jacob Johann von Wulffen
Prussian force: The Brandenburg army under the Elector, which invested the city for about a month and then withdrew for the winter.
borderline: a first, abandoned investment; no fighting described; de.wikipedia treats the investment from late October 1676 to December 1677 as one siege
doubts and flags: Borderline: a first, abandoned investment; no fighting described; de.wikipedia treats the investment from late October 1676 to December 1677 as one siege.
period: The Great Elector: Swedes, Turks and Louis XIV
sources: en.wikipedia List of wars and battles involving Prussia; de.wikipedia Belagerung von Stettin (1677) (background); en.wikipedia Siege of Stettin (1677) (background)
note: Listed as a Brandenburg defeat (siege abandoned) in en.wikipedia's list. The dates conflict with the fall of Demmin (20 October per de.wikipedia).

name: Stettin (siege, 1677)
place: Stettin (now Szczecin), on the Oder
commanders A: Frederick William, the Great Elector
commanders B: Lieutenant General Jacob Johann von Wulffen
Prussian force: The main Brandenburg army under the Elector, about 18,000 Brandenburgers (16,226–26,000 in different counts) with 110 guns and 25 mortars, joined by 3,000 Lüneburgers and 1,200 Danes; the leased Brandenburg fleet (Raule) blockaded on the Oder.
losses A: about 10,000 dead, wounded and sick (de.wikipedia); en.wikipedia: about 4,000 Brandenburg dead plus 289 killed and 316 wounded in the Danish regiment
losses B: about 3,000 dead, wounded and sick (de.wikipedia; en.wikipedia 1,300–2,700 killed), and about 2,000–2,443 citizens killed

name: Chotusitz

name: Habelschwerdt (1745)
war: War of the Austrian Succession (Second Silesian War)

Prussian force: 14 battalions and two hussar regiments under Lehwaldt and Fouqué attacked in heavy snow.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Habelschwerdt (1745); en.wikipedia Hans von Lehwaldt; zinnfiguren-klio-sh.de 'Unter den schwarzen Fahnen, Teil 2'

The de.wikipedia infobox gives c. 8,000 and c. 12,000 as strengths and '52 dead' and '21 dead including 7 officers' as losses without clear side labels; Colonel von Gaudi of Infantry Regiment No. 2 was among the Prussian dead. Habelschwerdt also has an entry in 1779.

name: Zieten's Ride

note: German: Zietenritt. Disguised in fur caps like Austrian hussars, the column rode with an Austrian column, was discovered near Rosswald, and broke through a battalion and two free companies to reach Jägerndorf.

name: Landeshut (1745)
war: War of the Austrian Succession (Second Silesian War)
place: Reichhennersdorf (now Szarocin), just outside Landeshut (now Kamienna Góra)
commanders A: Hans Karl von Winterfeldt
Prussian force: Winterfeldt with about 2,400 men and 8 guns (grenadiers, hussars and dragoons called up from Hartmannsdorf); Rittmeister Seydlitz distinguished himself.
sources: kreislandeshut.de, 'Schlacht bei Reichhennersdorf 22.05.1745'; de.wikipedia Husarenregiment 'Hadik' ('Gefecht bei Reich-Hennersdorf')
note: Also called Reichhennersdorf. Austrian hussars, Croats and other columns attacked for some seven hours; Winterfeldt's bayonet charge and the arriving dragoons drove them back to Grüssau and Schömberg.

name: Hohenfriedberg
war: War of the Austrian Succession (Second Silesian War)
place: Hohenfriedberg (now Dobromierz) and Striegau (now Strzegom), south-west of Breslau (Wrocław)
commanders A: Frederick II
commanders B: Prince Charles of Lorraine, Duke Johann Adolf II of Saxe-Weissenfels
Prussian force: Frederick II with about 59,000–65,000 men and 192 guns; a dawn attack routed the Saxons, and the Bayreuth Dragoons' charge broke the Austrian infantry.
losses B: Saxons 2,029 killed and 915 wounded; Austrians 1,821 killed, 2,856 wounded and 5,655 captured
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Hohenfriedberg; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Hohenfriedberg; kulturstiftung.org Zeitstrahl 'Hohenfriedberg'
note: Also called Striegau. en.wikipedia gives Austro-Saxon losses of about 13,000 (some 5,500 captured) and 63 guns; the Kulturstiftung gives 13,600 Austro-Saxon and 4,700 Prussian losses.

name: Kosel (siege, 1745)
war: War of the Austrian Succession (Second Silesian War)
place: Cosel (now Koźle, part of Kędzierzyn-Koźle), on the Oder
commanders A: Count Christoph Ernst von Nassau
Prussian force: General Nassau's detachment sent to clear Upper Silesia after Hohenfriedberg, including the grenadier battalion Kleist.
sources: zinnfiguren-klio-sh.de, 'Unter den schwarzen Fahnen, Teil 2' ('im August 1745 an der Eroberung der Festung Cosel beteiligt'); Nassau's command from standard narratives, not checked online

name: Soor
war: War of the Austrian Succession (Second Silesian War)
place: Soor (now Hajnice), south of Trautenau (Trutnov)
commanders A: Frederick II
Prussian force: Frederick II with about 22,500 men, surprised in the camp of Staudenz, turned and stormed the Graner Koppe heights.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Soor; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Soor
note: Also called Sohr. Nádasdy's light troops plundered the abandoned Prussian camp during the battle and took the war chest (about 200,000 thalers) and the king's baggage.

name: Hennersdorf
war: War of the Austrian Succession (Second Silesian War)
place: Katholisch-Hennersdorf (now Henryków Lubański), north-west of Lauban (Lubań)
commanders A: Frederick II, Hans Joachim von Zieten, Friedrich Wilhelm von Rochow
Prussian force: The hussar regiments Ruesch and Zieten and the cuirassier regiments Rochow and Bornstedt under Zieten, followed by more cavalry, infantry and artillery of Frederick II's army.
strength A: 20 squadrons of hussars and 10 of cuirassiers
strength B: 6 squadrons of cuirassiers and 2 infantry battalions
losses B: 500 killed or wounded and 900 captured (en.wikipedia: 2,000 including 1,000 prisoners)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Hennersdorf; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Hennersdorf (and the austria-forum mirror with infobox labels); de.wikipedia 1. Leib-Husaren-Regiment Nr. 1
note: Also called Katholisch-Hennersdorf. The Saxon corps belonged to Prince Charles of Lorraine's Austro-Saxon army marching on Brandenburg through Lusatia; only Saxons were engaged. Prince Charles then retreated into Bohemia and the Prussians took the Saxon magazines at Görlitz.

war: War of the Austrian Succession (Second Silesian War)
place: Zittau, Upper Lusatia

name: Kesselsdorf
war: War of the Austrian Succession (Second Silesian War)
place: Kesselsdorf, west of Dresden
commanders A: Leopold I of Anhalt-Dessau, Prince Moritz of Anhalt-Dessau
commanders B: Count Friedrich August Rutowsky, Count Grünne (Austrians)
Prussian force: The Old Dessauer's army of about 30,000–32,000 with 33 field guns, joined by Lehwaldt's corps at Meissen; it stormed the Saxon battery at Kesselsdorf while Prince Moritz attacked the Saxon right.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kesselsdorf; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Kesselsdorf
note: Dresden capitulated on 17 December; the Peace of Dresden (25 December 1745) ended the war.

name: Pirna (siege)
place: The Saxon fortified camp between Pirna and Königstein (Struppen, Lilienstein), Saxony
commanders A: Frederick II
Prussian force: The main Prussian army that invaded Saxony (en.wikipedia gives 62,000 for the investing force) blockaded the Saxon camp while Frederick II took part of it to Lobositz.
losses B: the whole Saxon army surrendered (about 18,000; en.wikipedia infobox 15,000 captured)
borderline: Mainly a blockade; the fighting was limited to the failed Saxon breakout across the Elbe towards the Lilienstein (12–14 October).
doubts and flags: Borderline: Mainly a blockade; the fighting was limited to the failed Saxon breakout across the Elbe towards the Lilienstein (12–14 October).
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Pirna; de.wikipedia Siebenjähriger Krieg; Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: Capitulation 14 October (en.wikipedia) or 16 October (de.wikipedia, signed at Ebenheit). Browne's Austrian relief column (about 8,000) reached Lichtenhain/Schandau but failed to make contact; it is not counted as a belligerent here. The Saxon rank and file were forced into Prussian service and many deserted in 1757.

name: Lobositz
place: Lobositz (now Lovosice), on the Elbe, northern Bohemia
commanders A: Frederick II, Duke of Brunswick-Bevern
Prussian force: Frederick II with about 28,300 men and 98 guns; Bevern's infantry stormed the Lobosch hill after two cavalry charges (Kyau, Gessler) had failed.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lobositz; Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: Browne withdrew in good order and Frederick held the field, so it is scored a Prussian tactical victory; en.wikipedia stresses that Browne achieved his aim and calls it a strategic Austrian success.

Prussian force: The Prussian garrison of about 800 men, left behind when the other Rhenish garrisons (Wesel) were withdrawn.

note: en.wikipedia: the siege 'took three months to capture from its Prussian garrison of 800'. The capitulation is usually dated 24 August 1757 (not verified here); month and day left null.
