name: Prague (1757)
place: East of Prague, between Štěrboholy (Sterbohol) and the Žižkov (Ziska) and Tábor heights
commanders A: Frederick II, Field Marshal Kurt Christoph von Schwerin (killed), Hans Karl von Winterfeldt
commanders B: Prince Charles of Lorraine, Maximilian Ulysses Browne (mortally wounded)
Prussian force: Frederick II and Schwerin with about 64,000 men east of the city (Keith's 30,000 on the west bank were not engaged); Schwerin fell leading his regiment with a colour in his hands.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Prague (1757); Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: en.wikipedia also gives 115,000 for the Prussian total in Bohemia; 64,000 is the force engaged. The Austrians retired into Prague, which Frederick then besieged.

name: Prague (siege, 1757)
place: Prague, Bohemia
commanders A: Prince Charles of Lorraine
Prussian force: The Prussian army that won the battle of Prague, divided on both banks of the Moldau (Keith on the west bank); Frederick took part of it to meet Daun at Kolín.
borderline: A blockade and bombardment of the Austrian army shut up in Prague; en.wikipedia records no major sortie.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A blockade and bombardment of the Austrian army shut up in Prague; en.wikipedia records no major sortie.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Prague (1757) and Battle of Prague (1757); Almanach 'Schlachten und Belagerungen des Siebenjährigen Krieges' Nr. 5 (Deutsches Historisches Museum)
note: The siege was raised after the defeat at Kolín (18 June); scored as a defender's success, by the rule for sieges.

name: Kolín
place: West of Kolín, on the heights of Křečhoř (Krzeczhorz), about 55 km east of Prague
commanders A: Leopold Joseph von Daun, Franz Leopold von Nádasdy
commanders B: Frederick II, Hans Joachim von Zieten, Prince Moritz of Anhalt-Dessau, Johann Dietrich von Hülsen
Prussian force: Frederick II with about 33,000–34,000 men and 90 guns, detached from the siege of Prague; Frederick's first defeat in a pitched battle.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kolín; Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: Saxon chevauxleger regiments serving in the Austrian army took part in the decisive cavalry attacks (listed as allies). The defeat forced Frederick to raise the siege of Prague and evacuate Bohemia.

name: Memel (siege)
place: Memel (now Klaipėda), East Prussia
commanders A: William Fermor, Admiral Zakhar Mishukov (naval squadron), Stepan Apraksin (army commander)
Prussian force: A garrison of about 800 Landmiliz with 80 guns under Colonel von Rummel.
strength A: 16,000, 20 siege guns and a bombardment squadron of 6 vessels
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Memel (1757); Almanach 'Schlachten und Belagerungen des Siebenjährigen Krieges' Nr. 16
note: Julian dates 19–25 June 1757; the en.wikipedia infobox gives 16 July (N.S.) as the end, the text 6 July (N.S.), and most lists 5 July. Bombardment by land batteries and by ships and floating batteries on the Curonian Lagoon; the garrison marched out with the honours of war.

name: Gabel
place: Gabel (Deutsch Gabel, now Jablonné v Podještědí), northern Bohemia
commanders A: Johann Sigismund Maguire, Duke Charles of Arenberg
Prussian force: About 2,000 men under Puttkamer (two or three battalions, including Württemberg and Kalckreuth, with grenadiers and a squadron of Werner's hussars) guarding the supply route of Prince Augustus William's army.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Gabel (1757); Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: de.wikipedia dates the action 14–15 June 1757, which cannot be right: it followed Kolín (18 June) during the Prussian retreat from Bohemia, and standard accounts date the capitulation 15 July 1757. The Prussians repulsed an attack on the upper gate on 14 July and capitulated on the 15th when their ammunition ran out; some hussars broke out.

name: Zittau (1757)
place: Zittau, Upper Lusatia (Saxony)
commanders A: Prince Charles of Lorraine
commanders B: Prince Augustus William of Prussia (army commander)
Prussian force: The Prussian garrison and Schmettau's advanced detachment (with Seydlitz's squadrons, which escaped) holding the army's main magazine.
borderline: Chiefly a bombardment that burned the town; included because the Prussian garrison was attacked and driven out and the magazine lost.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Chiefly a bombardment that burned the town; included because the Prussian garrison was attacked and driven out and the magazine lost.
sources: miniatures.de Seven Years' War chronology ('Austrian Bombardment of Zittau'); en.wikipedia Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz and Prince Augustus William of Prussia; de.wikipedia Georg Reinhold von Thadden
note: Some chronologies date it 22 July; a Prussian flour convoy from Landeshut was intercepted on the night of 22–23 July. The 'fatal retreat of Zittau' led to Augustus William's disgrace.

name: Landeshut (1757)
place: Landeshut (now Kamienna Góra), Silesia
Prussian force: The Prussian post at Landeshut covering the Silesian border (details not found).
borderline: Listed as a combat only by the Kronoskaf project and derived chronologies; participants and result could not be verified.
doubts and flags: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored. Borderline: Listed as a combat only by the Kronoskaf project and derived chronologies; participants and result could not be verified.
sources: Kronoskaf, Project Seven Years War, '1757-08-13 – Combat of Landshut (1st)' (title only; page blocked); miniatures.de chronology

name: Gross-Jägersdorf
place: Gross-Jägersdorf (now Motornoye, Kaliningrad Oblast), near Norkitten, south-east of Wehlau (Znamensk)
commanders A: Stepan Apraksin, Pyotr Rumyantsev, Vasily Lopukhin (killed)
Prussian force: Lehwaldt's army of East Prussia, about 24,700–27,700 men, attacking Apraksin's army as it emerged from the Norkitten forest.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Gross-Jägersdorf and Hans von Lehwaldt
note: Julian date 19 August 1757. A Kalmyk contingent fought with the Russians. Apraksin did not follow up and soon left East Prussia.

name: Moys
place: The Holzberg (Jäckelsberg) at Moys (now Ujazd, part of Zgorzelec), east of Görlitz
commanders A: Franz Leopold von Nádasdy
Prussian force: Winterfeldt's detached corps of about 13,000 from the army of the Duke of Brunswick-Bevern, on the right bank of the Neisse.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Moys; de.wikipedia Schlacht von Moys
note: Winterfeldt, Frederick's closest military confidant, died the next day.

name: Peenemünde (siege, 1757)
place: The Peenemünde fort (Peenemünder Schanze), at the northern tip of Usedom, Prussian Pomerania
Prussian force: A Prussian detachment of about 200 men that had occupied and strengthened the fort in July 1757.
sources: de.wikipedia Peenemünder Schanze; en.wikipedia Peenemünde; miniatures.de chronology ('Swedish Siege of Fort Peenemünde, 13 to 23 September 1757')
note: Siege and bombardment by the Swedish army that had invaded Prussian Pomerania on 13 September. Some chronologies start it on 13 September.

name: Gotha
place: Gotha, Thuringia (Saxe-Gotha)
commanders A: Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz
commanders B: Prince de Soubise, Prince Joseph of Saxe-Hildburghausen
Prussian force: Seydlitz with a cavalry detachment of Frederick's army, who by a show of force drove the much larger Franco-Imperial advance guard out of Gotha.
borderline: A cavalry ruse with little bloodshed; no Wikipedia article.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A cavalry ruse with little bloodshed; no Wikipedia article.
sources: miniatures.de chronology ('Affair of Gotha, 19 September 1757'); Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: The allied commanders were surprised at dinner in the ducal palace and withdrew; the episode made Seydlitz's name before Rossbach.

name: Schweidnitz (siege, 1757)
place: Schweidnitz (now Świdnica), Silesia
commanders A: Franz Leopold von Nádasdy
Prussian force: The fortress garrison under the commandant von Seers.
sources: de.wikipedia Belagerungen von Schweidnitz im Siebenjährigen Krieg and Franz Ludwig von Thürheim; en.wikipedia Battle of Breslau (1757); Almanach 'Schlachten und Belagerungen des Siebenjährigen Krieges' Nr. 11
note: en.wikipedia (Battle of Breslau) says the Austrians invested the place on 14 October and received it on 13 November; de.wikipedia says trenches were opened at the end of October, two star redoubts and a lunette were stormed on 11 November (one column repulsed) and Seers capitulated on the morning of 12 November. Garrison size not verified (often given as about 6,000).

name: Berlin (raid, 1757)
place: Berlin, Brandenburg
commanders A: András Hadik
commanders B: Hans Friedrich von Rochow (governor of Berlin)
Prussian force: The Berlin garrison under the governor Rochow, who refused to surrender, was beaten at the gates and withdrew with the royal family to Spandau.
sources: en.wikipedia 1757 Berlin raid and András Hadik; de.wikipedia Siebenjähriger Krieg (Berliner Husarenstreich)
note: Hadik held the city for about a day and left with a ransom (200,000 thalers per en.wikipedia 1757 Berlin raid; 300,000 per the Hadik article) before Prince Moritz of Anhalt-Dessau's relief force arrived. Known in German as the 'Berliner Husarenstreich'.

name: Weißenfels
place: Weißenfels on the Saale, Saxony
commanders A: Frederick II, Johann von Mayr
Prussian force: Frederick's advance guard led by Colonel Johann von Mayr's Freibataillon surprised the town.
borderline: An advance-guard action of the Rossbach campaign, described in the Rossbach article rather than in its own.
doubts and flags: Borderline: An advance-guard action of the Rossbach campaign, described in the Rossbach article rather than in its own.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Rossbach and Johann von Mayr
note: The French burned the Saale bridge as they withdrew, trapping their rearguard.

name: Rossbach
place: Rossbach (now part of Braunsbedra) and Reichardtswerben, south-west of Merseburg
commanders A: Frederick II, Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz
commanders B: Prince de Soubise, Prince Joseph of Saxe-Hildburghausen
Prussian force: Frederick II with about 22,000 men and 79 guns; Seydlitz's 38 squadrons broke the allied columns and only seven Prussian battalions were seriously engaged.
losses B: 8,000–10,000 killed, wounded and captured (about 5,000 captured); 72 guns
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Rossbach; Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: Bodart gives Prussian losses as 169–170 dead and 430 wounded, allied losses as about 1,000 dead, 3,500 wounded and 5,000 missing or captured (French about 6,600, Imperials 3,552).

name: Breslau (1757)
place: Before Breslau (Wrocław), along the Lohe (Ślęza) between Kosel and Gräbschen
commanders A: Prince Charles of Lorraine, Leopold Joseph von Daun, Franz Leopold von Nádasdy
Prussian force: Bevern's Silesian army of about 28,000–28,400 in an entrenched line behind the Lohe; it retreated through Breslau towards Glogau and Bevern was captured on 24 November.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Breslau (1757); de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Breslau
note: The Prussians held most of their line on the day but withdrew in the night. The Breslau garrison (4,227 under Lestwitz) capitulated on 24/25 November without a siege; only 599 reached Glogau.

date: December 1757 (after Leuthen; capitulation late in the month)
name: Liegnitz (siege, 1757)
place: Liegnitz (now Legnica), Silesia
commanders A: Prince Moritz of Anhalt-Dessau
Prussian force: A Prussian siege corps under Prince Moritz of Anhalt-Dessau.
borderline: A short siege of the Austrian garrison left in Liegnitz; the extent of the fighting is not documented in the sources seen.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A short siege of the Austrian garrison left in Liegnitz; the extent of the fighting is not documented in the sources seen.
sources: de.wikipedia Georg Reinhold von Thadden
note: The Austrian garrison is said to have been allowed to march off to Bohemia; dates and numbers not verified.

name: Neumarkt
place: Neumarkt (now Środa Śląska), west of Breslau
commanders A: Frederick II
Prussian force: Frederick's advance guard (hussars with some infantry) on the march to Leuthen.
borderline: An advance-guard action on the eve of Leuthen; no Wikipedia article; details not verified online.
doubts and flags: Borderline: An advance-guard action on the eve of Leuthen; no Wikipedia article; details not verified online.
sources: Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985); Carlyle, History of Friedrich II of Prussia
note: Frederick's advance guard drove the Croat garrison out of Neumarkt and took the Austrian field bakery set up there.

name: Leuthen
place: Leuthen (now Lutynia), west of Breslau (Wrocław)
commanders A: Frederick II, Hans Joachim von Zieten, Prince Moritz of Anhalt-Dessau, Georg Wilhelm von Driesen
commanders B: Prince Charles of Lorraine, Leopold Joseph von Daun, Franz Leopold von Nádasdy
Prussian force: Frederick II with about 35,000–36,000 men and 167 guns; the oblique order against the Austrian left, with Driesen's cavalry deciding it at the end.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Leuthen; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Leuthen; Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: The Württemberg and Bavarian auxiliary contingents (subsidy troops, not the Reichsarmee) held the Austrian left that the Prussian attack struck first.

name: Breslau (siege, 1757)
place: Breslau (now Wrocław), Silesia
commanders A: Frederick II, Prince Ferdinand of Brunswick
Prussian force: Frederick's army after Leuthen (en.wikipedia gives 36,000 and 167 guns); Prince Ferdinand took the St Moritz suburb and General Wied the Polish suburb before the bombardment forced surrender.
losses B: 17,000 captured (including 13 generals per the text, 31 per the infobox), about 1,200 killed; 81 guns
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Breslau (1757); Almanach 'Schlachten und Belagerungen des Siebenjährigen Krieges' Nr. 14
note: Surrender agreed 19 December; the Prussians held the gates on the 20th and the garrison marched out on the 21st. en.wikipedia lists France among the defenders, but the garrison was Austrian.

name: Demmin (siege, 1757)
place: Demmin on the Peene, Prussian Pomerania (held by the Swedes)
commanders A: Hans von Lehwaldt (army commander)
Prussian force: Part of Lehwaldt's army, brought from East Prussia to clear the Swedes from Prussian Pomerania.
sources: de.wikipedia Wilhelm Carpelan; en.wikipedia Blockade of Stralsund; miniatures.de chronology ('Prussian Capture of Demmin, 29 December 1757')
note: The Swedish garrison withstood heavy artillery fire and an assault, then capitulated and was allowed free withdrawal on 1 January 1758. Some accounts date the fall of Demmin later in January 1758.

name: Kosel (siege, 1758)
place: Kosel (Cosel, now Kędzierzyn-Koźle), Upper Silesia
commanders A: Paul von Werner, von der Goltz (relief, sent by Fouqué)
Prussian force: The fortress garrison, relieved by troops under Werner and Goltz sent by Fouqué.
borderline: Dates, extent of fighting and numbers not found; possibly only a blockade.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Dates, extent of fighting and numbers not found; possibly only a blockade.
sources: en.wikipedia Heinrich August de la Motte Fouqué; en.wikipedia Paul von Werner
note: Besieged alongside Neisse in the autumn of 1758; the Austrians were driven off by the relief.

name: Peenemünde (siege, 1758)
place: Peenemünde fort (Peenemünder Schanze), at the mouth of the Peene on Usedom
commanders A: Heinrich von Manteuffel
Prussian force: A detachment of the Prussian army in Pomerania under Generalmajor Heinrich von Manteuffel blockaded the fort from January, built batteries from 9 March and opened fire on 12 March.
sources: de.wikipedia Peenemünder Schanze
note: On 13 March a shot blew up the powder magazine and the Swedes surrendered. On the night of 6 April 1758 a Swedish boat attack (200 men) on the fort was repulsed (16 dead, 60 captured); in July 1758 the Prussians gave the fort up without a fight (not listed).

name: Habelschwerdt (1758)
place: Habelschwerdt (now Bystrzyca Kłodzka), County of Glatz
commanders A: Heinrich August de la Motte Fouqué
Prussian force: Troops of Fouqué's corps from Glatz; numbers not given.
borderline: Known only from Fouqué's biography (en.wikipedia); no battle article; scale and name uncertain.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Known only from Fouqué's biography (en.wikipedia); no battle article; scale and name uncertain.
sources: en.wikipedia Heinrich August de la Motte Fouqué
note: Fouqué's men reached Habelschwerdt, overran an advancing Austrian force of about 6,000 within a few hours and returned to Glatz.

name: Schweidnitz (siege, 1758)
place: Schweidnitz (now Świdnica), Silesia
commanders A: Joachim Christian von Tresckow; Christian Friedrich von Diericke (storm of the Galgenfort); engineer Colonel Balbi
Prussian force: The siege corps under Lieutenant-General Tresckow (ready from 15 March; trenches opened 1 April); Diericke stormed the Galgenfort with grenadiers on the night of 16 April, taking its 156 defenders.
sources: de.wikipedia Belagerungen von Schweidnitz im Siebenjährigen Krieg; de.wikipedia Świdnica
note: Thürheim capitulated on 18 April 1758 (de.wikipedia Świdnica gives 16 April). The Austrians had taken the fortress in November 1757; Fouqué had blockaded it through the winter until 7 March.

name: Olmütz (siege)
place: Olmütz (now Olomouc), Moravia
commanders A: Ernst Dietrich von Marschall (commandant); Count Daun with the field army
Prussian force: Frederick II's main army invaded Moravia; the siege corps under Field Marshal Keith (about 11,000 in the siege) was covered by the king's army.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Olomouc; en.wikipedia Third Silesian War; de.wikipedia Siebenjähriger Krieg
note: English Wikipedia title: 'Siege of Olomouc'. Investment from 4 May; the siege proper from about 20 May. Raised on 2 July after the loss of the supply convoy at Domstadtl, so the defender wins.

name: Krefeld
place: Krefeld (the Hückelsmay in the Krefeld Forstwald), Lower Rhine
commanders A: Ferdinand of Brunswick (a Prussian field marshal commanding the allied army); the Hereditary Prince of Brunswick
Prussian force: Prussian cavalry (dragoons) serving in Ferdinand of Brunswick's allied army, a small part of its 32,000; de.wikipedia has the mounted Prussian troops breaking in from the north over the Landwehr against the French reserve.
doubts and flags: Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Krefeld; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Krefeld
note: Ferdinand's army was a Hanoverian-Hessian-Brunswick army in British pay; Prussian units were a small contingent. Higher loss figures are Bodart's.

name: Gundersdorf
place: Gundersdorf (now Guntramovice), on the convoy road from Troppau to Olmütz
commanders A: Friedrich Wilhelm von der Mosel
Prussian force: The escort of the great supply convoy to the siege of Olmütz under Colonel Mosel.
borderline: A preliminary clash, usually treated as part of the Domstadtl convoy fighting.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A preliminary clash, usually treated as part of the Domstadtl convoy fighting.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Domstadtl
note: Laudon's first attack on the convoy; he withdrew after a minor clash, though en.wikipedia says the Prussians lost more men than the Austrians.

name: Domstadtl
place: Domstadtl (now Domašov nad Bystřicí), north-east of Olmütz
commanders A: Ernst Gideon von Laudon, Josip Šišković
commanders B: Hans Joachim von Zieten, Friedrich Wilhelm von der Mosel
Prussian force: The escort of the great supply convoy under Mosel, reinforced by Zieten, about 7,000 men.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Domstadtl; de.wikipedia Siebenjähriger Krieg (Überfall bei Domstadtl)
note: The convoy was destroyed, forcing Frederick to raise the siege of Olmütz. German: 'Überfall bei Domstadtl'.

date: blockade from 5 August; siege 26 October – 6 November 1758
name: Neisse (siege, 1758)
place: Neisse (now Nysa), Upper Silesia
commanders A: Joachim Christian von Tresckow
Prussian force: The garrison of about 5,000 under Lieutenant-General Tresckow; a sortie of 600 infantry and 200 cavalry as the besiegers withdrew; relieved by Frederick II's approach after Hochkirch.
losses B: 8 officers and 800 men captured in the final sortie
sources: de.wikipedia Belagerung von Neisse (1758); en.wikipedia Battle of Hochkirch; en.wikipedia Third Silesian War
note: The blockade began on 5 August (de.wikipedia); an attack by about 12,000 from the Neustadt side failed; full investment from 26 October with about 100 guns and 40 mortars; the last besiegers left on 6 November (en.wikipedia: 5 or 7 November). en.wikipedia's Paul von Werner names Marquis de Ville as the besieger in October.

name: Küstrin (siege, 1758)
place: Küstrin (now Kostrzyn nad Odrą), on the Oder
commanders A: Schack von Wittenau (commandant)
Prussian force: The fortress garrison with 75 guns under its commandant; relieved by Frederick II's approach.
borderline: Mainly a bombardment that burned the town; no assault.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Mainly a bombardment that burned the town; no assault.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Küstrin; en.wikipedia Battle of Zorndorf; en.wikipedia Third Silesian War
note: Fermor lifted the siege to meet Frederick at Zorndorf. The en.wikipedia infobox loss entries (318 houses destroyed; 11 killed, 36 wounded) are not clearly assigned to sides.

name: Zorndorf
place: Zorndorf (now Sarbinowo), north-east of Küstrin (Kostrzyn)
commanders A: Frederick II; Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz, Christoph zu Dohna
Prussian force: Frederick II with 33,000–36,000 men and 167 guns; Seydlitz's cavalry saved the day twice.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Zorndorf; de.wikipedia Schlacht von Zorndorf; Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: Both sides claimed victory; en.wikipedia 'Inconclusive', de.wikipedia 'rather a draw'. The Russians withdrew two days later. de.wikipedia gives 36,800 and 44,300 men, 13,000 and 18,000 killed and wounded.

name: Sonnenstein (siege)
place: Sonnenstein fortress above Pirna, Saxony
commanders A: Duke Friedrich Michael of Zweibrücken
Prussian force: The Prussian garrison of the Sonnenstein under Colonel von Grape.
borderline: A short siege ending in capitulation; extent of the fighting not documented in the sources consulted.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A short siege ending in capitulation; extent of the fighting not documented in the sources consulted.
sources: de.wikipedia Schloss Sonnenstein
note: Grape capitulated on 5 September 1758; the fortress was then razed.

name: Tornow
place: Tornow, near Fürstenberg/Havel
Prussian force: Wedel's corps sent against the Swedish invasion of Brandenburg; Prussian hussars drove off the Swedish cavalry.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Tornow; en.wikipedia Pomeranian War; sv.wikipedia Pommerska kriget; en.wikipedia List of wars and battles involving Prussia
note: Sources disagree: en.wikipedia's article has a Swedish victory (the Swedish infantry held through six assaults and Wedel withdrew), while en.wikipedia Pomeranian War and sv.wikipedia call it a heavy defeat of a Swedish detachment and the en.wikipedia list a Prussian victory. The article's infobox gives 29 September, its text 26 September.

name: Fehrbellin (1758)
place: Fehrbellin, north-west of Berlin
commanders A: Carl Constantin De Carnall
Prussian force: Wedel with 5,000–6,000 men (6 battalions, 10 squadrons, 20 guns) attacked the town and broke in by the Mühlenthor before Swedish reinforcements arrived.
strength A: 800 men and 3 guns, reinforced by about 1,500
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Fehrbellin (1758); en.wikipedia Pomeranian War; sv.wikipedia Pommerska kriget
note: The Swedes held the town and the Prussians withdrew; Prussian losses were heavy (reportedly 15 wagons of dead and wounded) but are not given as a number.

name: Kolberg (siege, 1758)
place: Kolberg (now Kołobrzeg), Pomerania
commanders A: Heinrich Sigismund von der Heyde
Prussian force: About 700 regulars and militia under Major Heinrich Sigismund von der Heyde.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kolberg (Seven Years' War)
note: The Russians lifted the siege after several unsuccessful attacks. The en.wikipedia list of Prussian battles misdates this siege to 1759.

name: Hochkirch
place: Hochkirch, east of Bautzen, Upper Lusatia
commanders A: Count Daun, Franz Moritz von Lacy, Ernst Gideon von Laudon
commanders B: Frederick II, James Keith (killed), Hans Joachim von Zieten, Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz
Prussian force: Frederick II with 30,000–36,000 men, surprised in camp by a dawn attack; Field Marshal Keith was killed.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Hochkirch; de.wikipedia Siebenjähriger Krieg
note: The Prussians retreated in good order and Daun did not pursue.

name: Güstow
place: Güstow, north-west of Prenzlau, Uckermark
Prussian force: Prussian troops pursuing the Swedish army out of the Uckermark; commander and numbers not given in the sources consulted.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Güstow (after Säwe 1915 and von Schantz 1811)
note: en.wikipedia says it is also called the Battle of Tornow; not to be confused with Tornow (26 September 1758).

name: Demmin (siege, 1759)
place: Demmin, on the Peene, Swedish Pomerania
commanders A: Heinrich von Manteuffel
Prussian force: Manteuffel's Prussian corps from Stettin, which advanced on Demmin and Anklam in December 1758.
sources: de.wikipedia Demmin; en.wikipedia Pomeranian War; sv.wikipedia Pommerska kriget
note: The Swedish garrison capitulated on 18 January 1759; en and sv Wikipedia say Demmin, Anklam and Peenemünde were lost after resistance. Demmin changed hands many times in the war.

date: blockade early 1759; bombardment and surrender 9–10 April 1759
name: Peenemünde (siege, 1759)
place: Peenemünde fort (Peenemünder Schanze), at the mouth of the Peene on Usedom
Prussian force: Troops of Manteuffel's corps in Pomerania; the siege commander is not named in the source.
losses B: several killed, 60 wounded; 10 officers and 235 men captured with 33 guns
sources: de.wikipedia Peenemünder Schanze; en.wikipedia Pomeranian War
note: The bombardment of 9 April blew up the main powder magazine; the Swedes surrendered in the night of 9–10 April. Frederick II had the fort razed.

name: Peterswalde (1759)
place: Peterswalde (now Petrovice), northern Bohemia, and the passes of the Ore Mountains
commanders A: Prince Henry of Prussia, Johann Dietrich von Hülsen, Johann Jakob von Wunsch
commanders B: Ernst Gideon von Laudon, General Reinhard (captured), Johann Friedrich Karl von Ostein
Prussian force: Prince Henry's army from Saxony in two columns; Wunsch's vanguard took Peterswalde, Hülsen's column beat Reinhard at the Passberg.
losses B: about 3,000 captured, 3 guns; magazines and 200+ boats destroyed
borderline: A raid made up of several actions; one entry as in en.wikipedia.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A raid made up of several actions; one entry as in en.wikipedia.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Peterswalde; en.wikipedia Third Silesian War; en.wikipedia Johann Jakob von Wunsch
note: Includes Hülsen's action at the Passberg (Sebastiansberg), where General Reinhard and about 2,000 men were captured, and the destruction of magazines at Aussig, Lobositz, Leitmeritz and Budin. en.wikipedia's infobox gives the opponent as the 'Holy Roman Empire'.

name: Kay
place: Kay (now Kije) and Paltzig (now Pałck), near Züllichau (Sulechów)
commanders A: Pyotr Saltykov
commanders B: Carl Heinrich von Wedel; Moritz Franz Kasimir von Wobersnow (killed), Heinrich von Manteuffel (wounded)
Prussian force: Dohna's former army, 26,000–28,000 men under Carl Heinrich von Wedel, newly given command by Frederick II, attacking a strong Russian position.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kay; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Kay
note: Also called Paltzig. de.wikipedia gives 27,400 against 40,000–52,300 men and losses of 6,800 and 4,800.

name: Dresden (siege, 1759)
place: Dresden, Saxony
commanders A: Duke Friedrich Michael of Zweibrücken
Prussian force: A small Prussian garrison under the governor, Count Schmettau, with no hope of relief.
borderline: A siege ending in capitulation with free withdrawal; extent of fighting not documented in the sources consulted.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A siege ending in capitulation with free withdrawal; extent of fighting not documented in the sources consulted.
sources: en.wikipedia Third Silesian War; en.wikipedia Friedrich August von Finck; de.wikipedia Karl Christoph von Schmettau
note: Capitulation on 4 September 1759 (de.wikipedia's Schmettau article: 5 September); the garrison marched out with honours. Wunsch's relief came too late.

name: Minden
place: Minden, on the Weser (the plain north-west of the fortress, by Todtenhausen and Hahlen)
allies A: Great Britain; Hanover; Hesse-Kassel; Brunswick; Other German states
commanders A: Ferdinand of Brunswick; George Sackville, Friedrich von Spörcken, the Duke of Holstein-Gottorp
commanders B: Marquis de Contades, Duke de Broglie
Prussian force: Prussian dragoons with the cavalry of the Duke of Holstein-Gottorp on the allied left; with Hanoverian squadrons (19 in all) they charged the French infantry in the rear in the final phase.
doubts and flags: Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Minden; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Minden; britishbattles.com Battle of Minden
note: Allied army in British pay; Other German states = Schaumburg-Lippe (and Saxe-Gotha). en.wikipedia does not list Prussia as a belligerent, de.wikipedia does; contemporaries praised 'the Prussian dragoons'. de.wikipedia gives 40,000 against 55,000.

name: Kunersdorf
place: Kunersdorf (now Kunowice), east of Frankfurt (Oder)
commanders A: Pyotr Saltykov, Ernst Gideon von Laudon
commanders B: Frederick II; Friedrich August von Finck, Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz
Prussian force: Frederick II with 50,900 men and 230 guns, including Finck's corps; the army dissolved in the rout.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kunersdorf; de.wikipedia Siebenjähriger Krieg

name: Torgau (1759)
place: Torgau, on the Elbe, Saxony
commanders A: Johann Jakob von Wunsch
Prussian force: Wunsch's corps sent into Saxony after Kunersdorf (10,000–12,000 in all), with barely 8,000 engaged.
sources: de.wikipedia Johann Jakob von Wunsch; ADB (deutsche-biographie.de) Wunsch, Johann Jakob
note: Wunsch had retaken Wittenberg (28 August) and Torgau (31 August) from the Reichsarmee; on 8 September he beat the Austro-Imperial force sent to retake Torgau.

name: Frisches Haff
place: Stettin Lagoon (Stettiner Haff), between Neuwarp (Nowe Warpno) and Usedom
commanders A: Karl Rutensparre (Wilhelm von Carpelan)
Prussian force: The improvised Prussian flotilla built at Stettin: 4 galiots of 14 guns, 4 galleys of 10–11 guns and 4–5 gunboats under Ernst von Köller.
losses B: 30 killed and wounded, 490 captured (600+ in the article text); 2 galleys and 2 galiots captured, 2 galleys and 2 galiots sunk, 1 gunboat captured
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Frisches Haff
note: Despite the name used by en.wikipedia, the action was fought in the Stettin (Szczecin) Lagoon, not the Vistula Lagoon (Frisches Haff). Swedish losses in the article text: 13 killed, 14 wounded. The Prussians then lost Usedom and Wollin.

name: Korbitz
place: Korbitz, west of Meissen, Saxony
commanders A: Friedrich August von Finck, Johann Jakob von Wunsch
Prussian force: Finck's corps with Wunsch's detachment; Finck received the Black Eagle for the action.
sources: en.wikipedia Friedrich August von Finck; en.wikipedia Third Silesian War
note: Finck sharply defeated a larger force of Austrians and Imperial contingents. No battle article in en or de Wikipedia.

name: Hoyerswerda
place: Hoyerswerda, on the Black Elster (Schwarze Elster), Upper Lusatia
commanders A: Prince Henry of Prussia
Prussian force: The vanguard of Prince Henry's army on its march from Lusatia into Saxony, 3,000–4,000 engaged.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Hoyerswerda; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Hoyerswerda
note: en.wikipedia gives 3,000 for each side and Prussian losses as 'minimal'; de.wikipedia 4,000 and 3,000 and 100 Prussian losses.

name: Pretsch
place: Pretzsch (Elbe) and the Golmer Berg, between Torgau and Wittenberg
commanders A: Prince Henry of Prussia; Johann Jakob von Wunsch
commanders B: Duke of Arenberg; Joseph von Brentano
Prussian force: Detachments of Prince Henry's army under Wunsch, which surprised the Austrian corps sent to cut Henry's communications.
sources: de.wikipedia Heinrich von Preußen (1726–1802); de.wikipedia Johann Jakob von Wunsch; de.wikipedia Pretzsch (Elbe); Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: Spelled Pretsch in English works, Pretzsch in German. de.wikipedia's Wunsch article calls it a victory over General Brentano 'at Kemberg' on the same day; the Pretzsch town article speaks of a decisive Gefecht at the Golmer Berg in 1759. Arenberg as the defeated commander is from standard accounts (not verified online); losses not verified.

name: Maxen
place: Maxen, south of Dresden, Saxony
commanders A: Count Daun
commanders B: Friedrich August von Finck, Johann Jakob von Wunsch
Prussian force: Finck's corps of 14,000–15,000, sent by Frederick II into Daun's rear and surrounded on the Maxen plateau; it capitulated on 21 November (the 'Finckenfang').
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Maxen; de.wikipedia Gefecht von Maxen; en.wikipedia Friedrich August von Finck
note: German: 'Gefecht von Maxen'. Nine generals besides Finck were captured; Wunsch's cavalry breakout failed.

name: Meissen
place: Meissen (Meißen), on the Elbe, Saxony
commanders A: Philipp Levin von Beck
Prussian force: Diericke's detachment of 3,500 on the right bank of the Elbe opposite Meissen.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Meissen; en.wikipedia Third Silesian War
note: Some accounts date the action to 3–4 December 1759.

name: Anklam (1760)
place: Anklam, on the Peene, western Pomerania
Prussian force: The Prussian troops wintering at Anklam under Generalleutnant Heinrich von Manteuffel, with Belling's hussars nearby; strength not given in the sources consulted.
borderline: A winter raid known mainly from narrative accounts and regimental histories; no separate article; strengths and losses not found.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A winter raid known mainly from narrative accounts and regimental histories; no separate article; strengths and losses not found.
sources: en.wikipedia Pomeranian War; de.wikipedia Husaren-Regiment Nr. 5 (Überfall auf Anklam, 1760)
note: After a Prussian thrust into Swedish Pomerania was repulsed on 20 January 1760, Swedish troops crossed the frozen Peene and surprised Anklam on 28 January, capturing Manteuffel.

name: Koßdorf
place: Koßdorf, near Mühlberg an der Elbe
commanders A: Ernst Heinrich von Czettritz (captured); Levin August von Dingelstädt; Kurt Friedrich von Flanß
Prussian force: Czettritz's cavalry outposts: two squadrons of the Schmettau Cuirassiers (No. 4), the Puttkamer Hussars and Flanß's cuirassiers from Blumberg, who drove the raiders off.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Koßdorf
note: Beck's surprise raid captured Generalmajor Czettritz but was driven back by Flanß's cuirassiers; de.wikipedia counts it a repulse of the Austrians, though Prussian losses were the heavier.

name: Neustadt (1760)
place: Neustadt in Upper Silesia (now Prudnik)
commanders A: von der Goltz
Prussian force: The Prussian detachment (garrison) at Neustadt in Upper Silesia, commonly given as under General von der Goltz; strength not found.
borderline: Prussian commander, strengths and losses not verified.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian commander, strengths and losses not verified.
sources: en.wikipedia Third Silesian War
note: en.wikipedia calls it an inconclusive engagement between Laudon's Austrians and the Prussian garrison near Neustadt.

name: Glatz (siege, 1760)
place: Glatz (now Kłodzko), County of Glatz
commanders A: Ernst Gideon von Laudon
Prussian force: The fortress garrison of about 3,200 under Colonel Bartholomäus d'O.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Glatz; en.wikipedia Third Silesian War
note: Blockaded from June; the fortress was taken by storm on 26 July (en.wikipedia's Third Silesian War article gives 29 July).

name: Landeshut (1760)
place: Landeshut (now Kamienna Góra), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Ernst Gideon von Laudon
commanders B: Heinrich August de la Motte Fouqué (wounded and captured)
Prussian force: Fouqué's corps of about 12,000 with 68 guns, holding the entrenched heights round Landeshut; it was destroyed and Fouqué captured.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Landeshut (1760); de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Landeshut; Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: Named with the year because of other Landeshut actions (e.g. 1745).

name: Dresden (siege, 1760)
place: Dresden, Saxony
commanders A: John Sigismund Maguire (commandant); Count Daun and Lacy with the field armies
Prussian force: Frederick II's main army, which crossed the Elbe, overran the suburbs and bombarded the city with heavy guns.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Dresden; de.wikipedia Siebenjähriger Krieg
note: Frederick lifted the siege when Daun's army approached; the bombardment destroyed much of the inner city (Kreuzkirche). en.wikipedia lists the defenders as Austria and Saxony.

name: Breslau (siege, 1760)
place: Breslau (now Wrocław), Silesia
commanders A: Friedrich Bogislav von Tauentzien (governor); Prince Henry (relief army)
commanders B: Ernst Gideon von Laudon; General Draskovich
Prussian force: Tauentzien's garrison of only about 3,000 men; Prince Henry's relieving army forced Laudon to lift the siege.
sources: kronoskaf.com (Project Seven Years War) 1760 – Siege of Breslau; Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: Laudon invested the city on 31 July and bombarded it; he raised the siege on 3 August on news of Prince Henry's approach. Saltykov's Russians, marching to join him, halted short of Breslau.

name: Liegnitz
place: Pfaffendorf and Panten, north-east of Liegnitz (now Legnica)
commanders A: Frederick II; Hans Joachim von Zieten
commanders B: Ernst Gideon von Laudon (Daun's main army did not engage)
Prussian force: Frederick II with about 30,000 men; the Anhalt-Bernburg regiment led the decisive infantry counter-attack while Zieten held off Daun's approach.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Liegnitz (1760); Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: Frederick caught Laudon's corps alone at dawn before Daun's larger army could join it.

name: Strehla
place: Between Strehla and Oschatz (the Dürrenberg), Saxony
commanders A: Johann Dietrich von Hülsen
commanders B: Frederick Michael, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken; Prince Stolberg (reserve)
Prussian force: Hülsen's corps of about 12,000, left in Saxony after the siege of Dresden; its cavalry threw back the Imperial attack.
losses B: 1,800 killed, wounded and captured (de.wikipedia: about 2,000 killed and wounded; the Prussians took about 1,200 prisoners)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Strehla; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Oschatz
note: German Wikipedia calls it the Gefecht bei Oschatz. The Prussians held the field but withdrew towards Torgau as Zweibrücken's main army came up; the Imperials also claimed victory. en.wikipedia lists the opponent as Austria; it was the Reichsarmee with Austrian troops.

name: Kolberg (siege, 1760)
place: Kolberg (now Kołobrzeg), Farther Pomerania
commanders A: Heinrich Sigismund von der Heyde (commandant); Paul von Werner (relief)
Prussian force: Heyde's garrison held the fortress until Werner's relief force of 3,800, marched from Glogau, surprised and routed the besiegers on 18 September.
strength A: garrison (not given) plus 3,800 in Werner's relief force
strength B: about 8,000 troops; 21 ships of the line, 3 frigates and 3 bomb vessels, joined by 6 Swedish ships of the line and 3 frigates
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kolberg (Seven Years' War); en.wikipedia Paul von Werner
note: A combined Russian land and sea siege with Swedish naval support; the besiegers re-embarked and the fleets left on 20–23 September.

name: Hohen Giersdorf
place: Hohen Giersdorf (Hohgiersdorf, now Modliszów) and the Kreuzberg near Kunzendorf (now Mokrzeszów), between Freiburg (Świebodzice) and Schweidnitz (Świdnica)
commanders A: Frederick II; Count Wied (attack on the Kreuzberg)
commanders B: General d'Ayasassa; General Wilhelm O'Kelly (of Daun's army)
Prussian force: Frederick II's army: the grenadiers of regiments 23, 29, 31, 33, 42 and 46, Infantry Regiments 18, 35 (Prinz Heinrich) and 39, Cuirassier Regiment 2 and Hussar Regiments 2 and 3 (brigades Queis and Syburg); Count Wied took the Kreuzberg with Regiment Jung-Braunschweig and the 2nd battalion Kleist.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Hohen Giersdorf (after Taeglichsbeck, Das Fuesilier-Regiment Prinz Heinrich von Preussen (Nr. 35); Paalzow, Tagebuch des dritten Schlesischen Krieges; Finke, Geschichte des k. k. 36. Linien-Infanterie-Regiments); en.wikipedia Modliszów, Mokrzeszów
note: Also called the Gefecht bei Kunzendorf. The Prussians took the Kreuzberg and seven guns and threw back the Austrian grenadiers' counter-attack; the page states no formal result, and Frederick's advance on Waldenburg next day was given up because Daun held it. de.wikipedia gives the modern name as Gałązczyce, but that is a different village (Gmina Grodków); Hohgiersdorf is Modliszów and Kunzendorf is Mokrzeszów, both in Gmina Świdnica.

name: Wittenberg (siege, 1760)
place: Wittenberg, on the Elbe
commanders A: Frederick Michael, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken; Major Anton Grumbach (artillery); Count Wartensleben
Prussian force: A garrison of about 2,000 under Lieutenant-Colonel von Salenmon, which surrendered after the bombardment of 13 October.
losses B: the whole garrison captured, with 15 colours, 28 cannon and 6 mortars
sources: de.wikipedia Belagerung von Wittenberg (1760)
note: The bridgehead was stormed on 29 September, trenches opened on 11 October and a bombardment on 13 October set the town (and the Schlosskirche) on fire; the garrison capitulated on 14 October. The Reichsarmee included Saxon and Austrian units.

name: Berlin (raid, 1760)
place: Berlin (Cottbus and Halle gates, Lichtenberg, Mariendorf) and the surrounding Mark as far as Potsdam
commanders A: Gottlob Curt Heinrich von Tottleben; Zakhar Chernyshev; Franz Moritz von Lacy
commanders B: Hans Friedrich von Rochow (commandant); Friedrich Eugen of Württemberg; Johann Dietrich von Hülsen; Johann von Lehwaldt
Prussian force: The Berlin garrison under Rochow, reinforced by Württemberg's corps from Templin and Hülsen's from Beelitz, about 14,000 in all (other sources 18,000).
sources: de.wikipedia Russische Besetzung Berlins (1760); en.wikipedia Third Silesian War; en.wikipedia List of wars and battles involving Prussia (Raid on Berlin)
note: Tottleben's assault on the gates was repulsed on 3 October; on 7 October Chernyshev fought Württemberg at Lichtenberg and Lacy fought Hülsen at Mariendorf; the Prussian corps withdrew to Spandau and Rochow capitulated on 8/9 October. The allies (with Saxon and Croat troops) left on 11–13 October as Frederick approached. de.wikipedia gives 4,500 prisoners without making the side clear.

name: Pasewalk (1760)
place: Pasewalk, Uckermark–Pomerania border
commanders A: Augustin Ehrensvärd (wounded)
Prussian force: Werner's corps of about 4,200, fresh from the relief of Kolberg, which stormed the redoubts but withdrew at nightfall.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Pasewalk; en.wikipedia Paul von Werner; en.wikipedia Pomeranian War
note: Werner's attack on Ehrensvärd's detachment holding the town; Ehrensvärd was wounded and resigned his command. Named with the year because Pasewalk has other entries (the 1806 capitulation).

name: Kloster Kampen
place: Kloster Kamp (Kamp-Lintfort), near Rheinberg, Lower Rhine
side B: Hanover; Great Britain; Hesse-Kassel; Brunswick; Prussia
commanders A: Marquis de Castries
commanders B: Hereditary Prince Charles William Ferdinand of Brunswick
Prussian force: Two squadrons of Prussian hussars in Major-General George Augustus Eliott's vanguard of the allied army.
borderline: Prussian contingent of only two squadrons.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian contingent of only two squadrons.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kloster Kampen
note: Night attack of 15/16 October; en.wikipedia's infobox gives 15 October.

name: Torgau
place: Süptitz heights, west of Torgau, Saxony
commanders A: Frederick II (wounded); Hans Joachim von Zieten
commanders B: Leopold Joseph von Daun (wounded); Franz Moritz von Lacy
Prussian force: Frederick II with 48,500 men and 309 guns; the King attacked from the north while Zieten's corps stormed the Süptitz heights from the south at dusk and decided it.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Torgau; Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: A costly victory: the Prussians held the field and Daun retreated to Dresden, but it decided little strategically.

name: Langensalza (1761)
place: Langensalza (now Bad Langensalza) and Merxleben, on the Unstrut, Thuringia
commanders A: Friedrich von Spörcken (Hanoverians); Generalmajor Friedrich Wilhelm von Syburg (Prussians)
commanders B: Jacques Philippe de Choiseul-Stainville; the Saxon corps under Lieutenant-général Saint-Pern (en.wikipedia names Friedrich Christoph zu Solms-Wildenfels)
Prussian force: A Prussian corps of 5,000–7,000 under Generalmajor von Syburg, detached from Prince Henry's army in Saxony, which marched from Weißenfels and joined Spörcken's Hanoverians north of the town.
losses B: about 2,000 captured (mostly Saxons), 13 guns, 7 colours and standards
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Langensalza (1761); de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Langensalza
note: Part of Ferdinand of Brunswick's winter offensive of 1761; no single allied commander on the field. de.wikipedia spells the Prussian general both 'Syburg' and 'Sydow'. The Saxons were the Saxon contingent serving with the French. Named with the year because of Langensalza 1866.

name: Saalfeld (1761)
place: Saalfeld, on the Saale, Thuringia
Prussian force: A Prussian force described as greatly superior; its commander and strength were not found in the sources consulted.
losses B: baggage and many prisoners; the unit of Captain Ferdinand Caspar von Kleist (Wildenstein regiment) surrendered
borderline: Listed in de.wikipedia's Seven Years' War navigation box, but the article itself could not be read; commanders, strengths and the exact Prussian role not verified.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Listed in de.wikipedia's Seven Years' War navigation box, but the article itself could not be read; commanders, strengths and the exact Prussian role not verified.
sources: de.wikipedia navigation box (western theatre: 'Saalfeld'); de.wikipedia Ferdinand Caspar von Kleist; de.wikipedia Clemens August von Kleist
note: Imperial troops were forced to retreat or surrender and Ferdinand Caspar von Kleist was captured. Named with the year because of Saalfeld 1806.

name: Kolberg (siege, 1761)
place: Kolberg (now Kołobrzeg) and the entrenched camp before it, Farther Pomerania
commanders A: Pyotr Rumyantsev; Vice-Admiral Andrey Polyansky (fleet)
commanders B: Heinrich Sigismund von der Heyde (commandant); Friedrich Eugen of Württemberg (entrenched camp); Dubislav Friedrich von Platen
Prussian force: A garrison of about 4,000 under Heyde and Württemberg's entrenched corps of 12,000, reinforced by Platen on 30 September to nearly 20,000.
strength A: 22,000 with 70 guns (other figures 31,000–36,000 including detachments); 24 Russian ships and 9 Swedish ships
strength B: about 4,000 (garrison) plus 12,000 in Württemberg's camp; nearly 20,000 after Platen arrived
losses A: about 3,000 in the storm of 18 September alone
losses B: the garrison captured at the capitulation (about 2,900 men and 146 guns per en.wikipedia's table)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kolberg (Seven Years' War); en.wikipedia Third Silesian War
note: en.wikipedia's text dates the investment to 22 August, its infobox to 24 August. The Russian storm of Württemberg's lines on 18 September failed; Württemberg broke out in November and Kolberg capitulated on 16 December. Peter III later returned it. The relief actions at Treptow, Körlin, Gollnow and Spie are separate entries.

name: Treptow
place: Treptow an der Rega (now Trzebiatów), Farther Pomerania
Prussian force: Werner's detachment of about 2,000 men, sent to harass the Russians besieging Kolberg; after heavy losses Werner was captured.
sources: en.wikipedia Paul von Werner; en.wikipedia Siege of Kolberg (Seven Years' War)
note: en.wikipedia's Kolberg article records 59 officers and 1,840 men taken prisoner at Treptow without a date; this may refer to the later capitulation there of Major-General Knobloch's detachment (October 1761), which is not entered separately.

name: Gostyń
place: Gostyń (German Gostyn), near the monastery (Święta Góra), Greater Poland
commanders A: Dubislav Friedrich von Platen
Prussian force: Platen's raiding corps, sent from the Bunzelwitz camp, with battalions of the Rothenburg, Arnim, Görne and Wunsch regiments.
losses B: the wagon column and a large magazine captured
sources: en.wikipedia Dubislav Friedrich von Platen; Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: A raid on the Russian supply train on Polish (Commonwealth) territory; Platen went on to destroy the magazine at Posen on 17 September before marching to Kolberg.

name: Neuensund
place: Neuensund, near Strasburg (Uckermark), about 6 km west of Rothemühl
commanders A: Jacob Magnus Sprengtporten
Prussian force: Belling's corps of about 3,000 with 11 guns, which withdrew to Strasburg at sunset fearing encirclement.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Neuensund; en.wikipedia Wilhelm Sebastian von Belling
note: The article's text gives about 200 Prussians killed and about 300 captured; it does not say whether the date is Gregorian (Swedish sources of the period used the Gregorian calendar from 1753).

name: Körlin
place: Körlin (now Karlino), bridge over the Persante (Parsęta), south-east of Kolberg
commanders A: Dubislav Friedrich von Platen
Prussian force: Platen's corps on its march to relieve Kolberg; it took the bridge intact.
borderline: Minor action known from Platen's biography; no separate article.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Minor action known from Platen's biography; no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Dubislav Friedrich von Platen
note: It opened Platen's way to Württemberg's camp at Kolberg, which he joined the same day.

name: Schweidnitz (siege, 1761)
place: Schweidnitz (now Świdnica), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Ernst Gideon von Laudon; the assault columns under Amadei
Prussian force: The fortress garrison of about 3,800 under Zastrow, taken by a night escalade in four columns.
losses B: 3,776 captured (the whole garrison, including wounded), 211 guns and large stores
sources: de.wikipedia Belagerungen von Schweidnitz im Siebenjährigen Krieg (Erstürmung von Schweidnitz 1761); en.wikipedia Third Silesian War
note: A storming (Erstürmung) at 2 a.m. after a blockade, not a formal siege. en.wikipedia calls it an allied (Austro-Russian) storming and names Karl Christoph von der Goltz as Prussian commander; de.wikipedia names only Austrian troops and Zastrow as commandant. Russian participation is listed as allies but not confirmed in detail.

name: Gollnow
place: Gollnow (now Goleniów), bridge over the Ihna (Ina), north-east of Stettin
commanders A: William Fermor
Prussian force: Platen with 5,500 men, trying to break through to Gollnow to bring supplies to Kolberg.
borderline: Mostly an artillery duel at the bridge; known from Platen's biography.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Mostly an artillery duel at the bridge; known from Platen's biography.
sources: en.wikipedia Dubislav Friedrich von Platen
note: Fermor's Russians stopped Platen at the Ihna bridge.

name: Spie
place: Spie, about 8 km south-west of Kolberg (Kołobrzeg)
commanders A: Pyotr Rumyantsev
Prussian force: Württemberg's corps in its last attempt to relieve the fortress; about 8,000 remained to retreat to Stettin afterwards.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kolberg (Seven Years' War); en.wikipedia Dubislav Friedrich von Platen
note: A distinct named action within the siege of Kolberg; Württemberg retreated to Stettin and Kolberg capitulated four days later. Platen's biography describes a three-hour fight at Spie without a date, perhaps an earlier clash.

name: Malchin
place: Malchin, Mecklenburg
commanders A: Jacob Magnus Sprengtporten; Augustin Ehrensvärd
Prussian force: Prussian troops operating in Mecklenburg (probably Belling's corps); strength not given.
sources: en.wikipedia Pomeranian War
note: Sprengtporten defeated a Prussian force, was then surrounded at Malchin by superior Prussian forces and relieved by Ehrensvärd. The Prussian commander is not named in the source consulted.

name: Neukalen
place: Neukalen, Mecklenburg
commanders A: Carl Constantin De Carnall; Augustin Ehrensvärd
Prussian force: Belling with more than 2,000 men in 5 battalions, 2 companies and a hussar regiment of 10 squadrons, blocking the road to Malchin.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Neukalen; en.wikipedia Pomeranian War
note: The last battle between Swedes and Prussians; the Truce of Ribnitz followed on 7 April and the Peace of Hamburg on 22 May 1762.

name: Döbeln
place: Döbeln, on the Freiberger Mulde, Saxony
commanders A: Prince Henry; Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz; Quintus Icilius
commanders B: Johann Anton Franz von Zedtwitz (captured); Serbelloni (army)
Prussian force: Prince Henry with 8,000–9,000 men and 30–35 guns in four columns, surprising Serbelloni's outposts on the Mulde.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Döbeln; kronoskaf.com 1762 – Prussian campaign in Saxony
note: Opened Prince Henry's 1762 campaign in Saxony and kept the Reichsarmee from joining the Austrian main army.

name: Oederan
place: Oederan, between Chemnitz and Freiberg, Saxony
commanders A: General Luzinsky
Prussian force: Bandemer's detachment of 4 battalions and 5 squadrons, sent to observe the Reichsarmee.
borderline: Known from kronoskaf's campaign narrative; no Wikipedia article found.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Known from kronoskaf's campaign narrative; no Wikipedia article found.
sources: kronoskaf.com 1762 – Prussian campaign in Saxony
note: kronoskaf places Luzinsky on the Austrian/Reichsarmee side without making clear which army he belonged to.

name: Adelsbach
place: Adelsbach (now Struga), near Waldenburg (Wałbrzych), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Josef Brentano (corps covering the wing of Daun's army)
commanders B: Frederick II; General Karl von Wied (Prussian corps)
Prussian force: A Prussian-Russian force of about 20,000 under Frederick II, with General Wied's Prussian corps making the attack (Dragoon Regiment No. 1 among the Prussian units); it was repulsed by Brentano's corps of about 6,000.
sources: Golik and Kryska, Adelsbach 1762: zapomniana porażka Fryderyka Wielkiego (Kraków: Avalon, 2022; abstract in the Jagiellonian University repository); English edition Adelsbach 1762: The Forgotten Defeat of Frederick the Great (Helion, 2026); de.wikipedia Altpreußisches Dragonerregiment D I
note: Austrian defensive success: despite a superiority of more than three to one the Prussian-Russian attack failed and Frederick's force withdrew from Adelsbach (Struga) (Golik and Kryska, who call it Frederick's 'forgotten defeat'). Two weeks later Frederick dislodged Daun at Burkersdorf.

name: Burkersdorf (1762)
place: Burkersdorf (now Burkatów) and Leutmannsdorf (Lutomia), south-west of Schweidnitz (Świdnica)
commanders A: Frederick II; Zakhar Chernyshev (Russian corps, did not fight)
Prussian force: Frederick II's army, about 23,000 engaged, stormed the fortified heights of Burkersdorf and Leutmannsdorf; Chernyshev's 18,000 Russians, already recalled by Catherine II, stood by without fighting.
losses B: about 3,000 killed, wounded, captured or deserted
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Burkersdorf (1762); en.wikipedia Third Silesian War
note: Daun was cut off from Schweidnitz, which was then besieged. Russia is listed as an ally because its corps was present, though it did not engage. Named with the year because of Burkersdorf (Soor) 1866.

name: Teplitz
place: Teplitz (now Teplice), northern Bohemia
commanders A: Prince Christian Philipp of Löwenstein-Wertheim
Prussian force: A corps from Prince Henry's army under Seydlitz, raiding into Bohemia (Kleist's light troops had skirmished there the day before); it attacked Löwenstein's well-placed corps and was repulsed.
sources: kronoskaf.com 1762 – Prussian campaign in Saxony; de.wikipedia Christian Philipp von Löwenstein-Wertheim; de.wikipedia Husaren-Regiment Nr. 5 (Gefecht bei Teplitz)
note: The Prussians withdrew to Oberleutensdorf.

name: Schweidnitz (siege, 1762)
place: Schweidnitz (now Świdnica), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Frederick II; Friedrich Bogislav von Tauentzien (siege corps); Major Simon Lefebvre (mines)
commanders B: Franz Guasco (commandant); Jean-Baptiste Vaquette de Gribeauval (engineer)
Prussian force: Tauentzien's siege corps of 21 battalions and 25 squadrons (about 25,000 in all with the covering troops), with the mine war directed by Lefebvre.
losses B: about 3,000–3,550 killed and wounded and about 9,000 captured
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Schweidnitz (1762); de.wikipedia Belagerungen von Schweidnitz im Siebenjährigen Krieg; Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life (1985)
note: The fortress had been blockaded since 21 June; the formal siege began on 7 August and Guasco capitulated on 9 October after a long mine war (on 8 October the powder chamber of the Jauernick fort blew up, killing 200).

name: Reichenbach (1762)
place: Peilau (now Piława Górna) and the Fischerberg, south-west of Reichenbach (now Dzierżoniów), Silesia
commanders A: Duke of Brunswick-Bevern; Frederick II; Paul von Werner; Wichard von Möllendorff
commanders B: Leopold Joseph von Daun; Franz Moritz von Lacy; Philipp Levin von Beck; Ernst Gideon von Laudon; Brentano
Prussian force: Bevern's corps covering the siege of Schweidnitz held off Daun's relief attack until the King arrived; Werner's cavalry and horse artillery, supported by Möllendorff's battalions, decided it in the evening.
losses B: about 800 killed and wounded, 340 captured, 5 colours
sources: de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Reichenbach; en.wikipedia Paul von Werner
note: Also called the battle of the Fischerberg. Daun's attempt to relieve Schweidnitz failed. Named with the year because of Reichenbach 1813.

name: Erbisdorf
place: Erbisdorf (now Brand-Erbisdorf) and the Kuhberg, south of Freiberg, Saxony
commanders A: Campitelli; Prince Christian Karl of Stolberg-Gedern
commanders B: Friedrich Wilhelm von Syburg; Wilhelm Sebastian von Belling; Prince Henry (army)
Prussian force: Syburg's brigade and Belling's hussars on Prince Henry's left; the Salmuth Fusiliers and Kalckstein's grenadier battalion were largely captured.
borderline: Named only in kronoskaf's narrative (Erbisdorf / Kuhberg); German works may treat it as the first action at Freiberg; conventional name not verified.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Named only in kronoskaf's narrative (Erbisdorf / Kuhberg); German works may treat it as the first action at Freiberg; conventional name not verified.
sources: kronoskaf.com 1762 – Prussian campaign in Saxony
note: The defeat forced Prince Henry to give up Freiberg on 15–16 October; he retook it with the battle of 29 October.

name: Freiberg
place: Heights east and south of Freiberg, Saxony
commanders A: Prince Henry; Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz; Wilhelm Sebastian von Belling
commanders B: Prince Christian Karl of Stolberg-Gedern (Reichsarmee); John Sigismund Maguire; en.wikipedia also names András Hadik

sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Freiberg; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Freiberg; kronoskaf.com 1762 – Prussian campaign in Saxony
note: The last major battle of the Seven Years' War in Europe between Prussia and its enemies; an armistice with Austria followed on 24 November 1762 and the Peace of Hubertusburg on 15 February 1763.

name: Dittersbach
place: Dittersbach (linked by en.wikipedia to Ogorzelec, Kamienna Góra County), on the Silesian side of the Bohemian border
commanders A: Colonel Wilhelm Klebeck (Croat column), under Dagobert Sigmund von Wurmser
Prussian force: A Prussian post of the winter cordon; unit and commander not named in the sources consulted.
borderline: raid; exact date and site not established
doubts and flags: Borderline: raid; exact date and site not established.

name: Náchod (1778)
place: Náchod, north-eastern Bohemia

note: Nauendorf's hussars sallied from the Náchod garrison; after a brief skirmish Wunsch withdrew. Frederick II's army entered Bohemia on 5 July 1778.

name: Biebersdorf (1778)
place: Biebersdorf, a hamlet of Rückers (now Szczytna), County of Glatz

Prussian force: A Prussian supply convoy and its escort on the road from Glatz to the army in Bohemia; commander not named.

name: Zuckmantel
place: Zuckmantel (now Zlaté Hory), Austrian Silesia
commanders A: Colonel Franz Levenehr
Prussian force: Wunsch's Prussian force from Upper Silesia, given as 10,000 men, against the Austrian post at Zuckmantel.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Zuckmantel; War of the Bavarian Succession; de.wikipedia Warasdiner Grenz-Husaren-Regiment
note: Date 14 January 1779 in the en.wikipedia battle article; its war article gives 1 January 1779. A limited action, not a pitched battle; Austrian sources speak of the defence of Zuckmantel.

name: Habelschwerdt (1779)
place: Habelschwerdt (now Bystrzyca Kłodzka) and Oberschwedeldorf (now Szalejów Górny), County of Glatz

commanders B: Major General Prince Adolf of Hesse-Philippsthal-Barchfeld (captured)
Prussian force: About 3,000 Prussians holding Habelschwerdt and the 'Swedish blockhouse' at Oberschwedeldorf under the Prince of Hesse-Philippsthal.
losses B: about 400 killed and wounded, about 1,100 captured (with the Prince, 3 guns and 7-10 colours)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Zuckmantel; War of the Bavarian Succession; Dagobert Sigmund von Wurmser; Ludwig, Baron of Terzi
note: Night raid in five columns; Habelschwerdt and Oberschwedeldorf were burned. Prisoner counts vary (714 at Habelschwerdt plus 300 taken by Terzy; 'over 1,000' in total).

name: Biebersdorf (1779)
place: Biebersdorf, a hamlet of Rückers (now Szczytna), County of Glatz
commanders A: Friedrich Joseph, Count of Nauendorf
Prussian force: The Prussian garrison of the village; strength and commander not given.
strength A: a large force of infantry and hussars
borderline: raid

note: Spelled 'Berbersdorf' in en.wikipedia's Nauendorf and war articles; its Szczytna article places both 1778 and 1779 raids at the hamlet of Biebersdorf.

name: Hinderdam
place: Hinderdam redoubt on the Vecht, near Nederhorst den Berg, south-east of Amsterdam
Prussian force: Prussian troops of Brunswick's army advancing on Amsterdam from the east (Dragoon Regiment No. 1 among them).

name: Gorinchem (1787)
place: Gorinchem (Gorcum), on the Merwede, Holland
commanders A: Lieutenant General von Knobelsdorff (under the Duke of Brunswick)
Prussian force: Knobelsdorff's division of the Duke of Brunswick's 20,000-strong Prussian army.
strength B: Free Corps only (the States regiments had defected)

name: Amstelveen
place: Amstelveen and Sloten, south of Amsterdam
commanders A: Charles William Ferdinand, Duke of Brunswick
Prussian force: About 4,000 Prussians in a frontal attack and about 2,000 landed by boat from Aalsmeer at Sloten, part of Brunswick's army of about 20,000.
sources: en.wikipedia Prussian invasion of Holland; Charles William Ferdinand, Duke of Brunswick
note: Part of the attack of 1 October on Amsterdam's outer defences: attacked in the rear from Sloten, the defenders fell back towards Ouderkerk, opening the southern approach. The attacks at Ouderkerk and Duivendrecht were repulsed. A ceasefire followed on 2 October and Amsterdam capitulated on 10 October 1787 (not entered separately). The campaign cost the Prussians 211 dead (71 killed, 140 of disease).

name: Ouderkerk
place: Ouderkerk aan de Amstel, south of Amsterdam
commanders A: Colonel George Hendrik de Wilde (Amsterdam schutterij)
Prussian force: Prussian columns of Brunswick's army attacking the Amstel line; units not named in the sources consulted.
borderline: part of the attack of 1 October 1787 on Amsterdam's outer line
doubts and flags: Borderline: part of the attack of 1 October 1787 on Amsterdam's outer line.
sources: en.wikipedia Prussian invasion of Holland
note: De Wilde's guns repelled several attacks; the village was evacuated the next day after Amstelveen had fallen. A Prussian assault from Abcoude on Duivendrecht was also repulsed the same day (not entered separately).

name: Longwy (siege, 1792)
place: Longwy, Lorraine
commanders A: Duke of Brunswick; King Frederick William II present
Prussian force: Brunswick's Prussian invasion army, 'composed mostly of Prussian veterans', which crossed into France on 19 August.
borderline: bombardment and capitulation with little fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: bombardment and capitulation with little fighting.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Verdun (1792); Battle of Valmy; War of the First Coalition; de.wikipedia Erster Koalitionskrieg
note: Invested 20 August, bombarded, capitulated 23 August. The Prussians gave it up again on 22 October 1792.

name: Verdun (siege, 1792)
place: Verdun, on the Meuse, Lorraine
commanders A: Duke of Brunswick; King Frederick William II present
Prussian force: Brunswick's Prussian main army, 40,000 (en.wikipedia infobox; 60,000 with 40 guns in its text).
strength B: about 3,000-4,000 (92nd Line and six National Guard battalions)
borderline: a bombardment (night of 31 August - 1 September) and capitulation
doubts and flags: Borderline: a bombardment (night of 31 August - 1 September) and capitulation.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Verdun (1792); War of the First Coalition
note: Beaurepaire was found dead (shot or suicide) when the council voted to surrender on 2 September. The Prussians abandoned Verdun on 8 October 1792.

name: Valmy
place: Valmy, between Sainte-Menehould and Châlons, Champagne
commanders A: Charles François Dumouriez, François Christophe Kellermann
commanders B: Duke of Brunswick, Count Clerfayt; King Frederick William II present
Prussian force: Brunswick's Prussian army, about 34,000 with the allies present; a cannonade in which the Prussian infantry attack was called off.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Valmy; War of the First Coalition; de.wikipedia Kanonade von Valmy
note: Essentially a cannonade (de.wikipedia 'Kanonade von Valmy'); tactically indecisive, but standard works count it a French victory because it ended the invasion. Austrian and émigré troops were with the allied army but barely engaged.

name: Limburg
place: Limburg an der Lahn, Hesse
commanders A: Jean Nicolas Houchard (advance guard of Custine's army)
commanders B: Duke of Brunswick (army commander, per the infobox); Grenadier Battalion Kenitz
Prussian force: One grenadier battalion (Kenitz), 1,200 men, of the Duke of Brunswick's army, which had gone into quarters around Limburg after the retreat from France.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Limburg (1792) (citing Smith, The Napoleonic Wars Data Book (1998); Phipps, The Armies of the First French Republic, vol. II)
note: en.wikipedia also calls it the Battle of Friedberg. Houchard surprised the weakly posted Prussians; after about 90 minutes they were driven out of the town and fell back to Montabaur. French losses unknown.

name: Königstein (siege, 1792-93)
place: Königstein fortress, Taunus, north-west of Frankfurt
Prussian force: Prussian troops of Frederick William II's army (Dragoon Regiment No. 1 among them) besieging the French garrison left by Custine.
borderline: mainly a blockade; dates and details not verified in a battle article
doubts and flags: Borderline: mainly a blockade; dates and details not verified in a battle article.
sources: de.wikipedia Altpreußisches Dragonerregiment D I ('Belagerung von Königstein', 1793)
note: The French garrison held the fortress through the winter and capitulated in March 1793 (8 March in standard accounts; not verified here).

name: Frankfurt (1792)
place: Frankfurt am Main
commanders A: King Frederick William II (supreme command); Hesse-Kassel troops of Landgrave William IX
Prussian force: The Prussian army of Frederick William II in overall command; the storm of the city was carried mainly by Hesse-Kassel troops.
sources: en.wikipedia Army of the Rhine (1791-1795); Adam Philippe, Comte de Custine; de.wikipedia Erster Koalitionskrieg
note: Recaptured from Custine's garrison 'unter preußischem Oberkommando' by Hessian troops (de.wikipedia). If the Hessians did nearly all the fighting, Prussia's role is nearer 'major ally'.

name: Hochheim
place: Hochheim am Main, east of Mainz-Kastel
Prussian force: Prussian troops of Frederick William II's army closing on the Mainz bridgehead at Kastel; units not established.
borderline: date and result from standard accounts, not verified in the sources reached
doubts and flags: Borderline: date and result from standard accounts, not verified in the sources reached.
sources: standard accounts of the 1792-93 Rhine campaign (not verified in a battle article; de.wikipedia 'Gefecht bei Hochheim' is the 1813 action)
note: The Prussians drove the French out of Hochheim back towards Kastel during the winter investment of Mainz's right-bank bridgehead.

name: Stromberg
place: Stromberg and Waldalgesheim, Hunsrück, west of Bingen
Prussian force: Prussian troops that had crossed the Rhine at Bacharach (Dragoon Regiment No. 1 among them), turning Custine's position at Bingen.
borderline: date and Neuwinger's capture from standard accounts, not verified in a battle article
doubts and flags: Borderline: date and Neuwinger's capture from standard accounts, not verified in a battle article.
sources: de.wikipedia Altpreußisches Dragonerregiment D I ('Gefecht bei Waldalgesheim und Stromberg', 1793); standard accounts of Custine's retreat
note: Called 'Gefecht bei Waldalgesheim und Stromberg' in Prussian regimental records. The defeat forced Custine to abandon Bingen and fall back towards Landau, leaving Mainz isolated.

name: Mainz (siege, 1793)
place: Mainz and Kastel
allies A: Austria; Saxony; Hesse-Kassel; Hesse-Darmstadt; Other German states
commanders A: Field Marshal Friedrich Adolf von Kalckreuth (siege), Duke of Brunswick (covering army); King Frederick William II present
commanders B: François Ignace d'Oyré (garrison); Alexandre de Beauharnais (Army of the Rhine)
Prussian force: The Prussian main army of Frederick William II; Kalckreuth conducted the siege, the largest part of a coalition force of 36,000-43,000.
losses B: 4,000 killed and wounded; 18,000-19,000 marched out on parole
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Mainz (1793); Republic of Mainz; Friedrich Adolf von Kalckreuth
note: Other German states: the Palatinate and Saxe-Weimar. Bombardment from the night of 17 June; the garrison capitulated on 23 July (22 July in some accounts) and was paroled for a year.

name: Raismes
place: Raismes and the Forest of Vicoigne, north-west of Valenciennes
commanders A: Prince Josias of Saxe-Coburg (army), Count Clerfayt, Duke of York; Alexander von Knobelsdorff (Prussians)
commanders B: Auguste Picot de Dampierre (mortally wounded), François Lamarche
Prussian force: Knobelsdorff's Prussian contingent of about 8,000 holding Maulde, Lecelles and Saint-Amand on the Scarpe; pushed back on 8 May, it stormed the French entrenchments with Clerfayt on 9 May.
borderline: Prussians about an eighth of the allied army; counted as major ally because Knobelsdorff's division fought as a unit
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussians about an eighth of the allied army; counted as major ally because Knobelsdorff's division fought as a unit.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Raismes; Low Countries theatre of the War of the First Coalition; historyofwar.org Battle of Condé or St. Amand, 8 May 1793
note: Also called Condé or Saint-Amand; Dampierre's attempt to relieve Condé. The Prussian contingent left Flanders for the Rhine after Valenciennes fell in July 1793. A French attack on 1 May had driven the Prussians out of Saint-Amand (not entered separately).

name: Landau (siege, 1793)
place: Landau in der Pfalz
commanders A: Joseph Marie Tennet de Laubadère (garrison)
Prussian force: Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen's Prussian corps of 25 battalions with 40 six-pounder field guns, without siege artillery.
borderline: chiefly a blockade aimed at starving the garrison
doubts and flags: Borderline: chiefly a blockade aimed at starving the garrison.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Landau (1793); Battle of Haguenau (1793); de.wikipedia Altpreußisches Dragonerregiment D I
note: The siege was lifted on 23 December after the French victories at Froeschwiller and Wissembourg.

name: Pirmasens
place: Pirmasens, Palatinate Forest
commanders A: Duke of Brunswick; Ludwig Karl von Kalckstein (left), Prince Charles Louis of Baden (right)
commanders B: Jean René Moreaux; Guillaume, Freytag, Lequoy (columns)

sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Pirmasens; de.wikipedia Erster Koalitionskrieg

name: Bitche (1793)
place: Bitche citadel, northern Vosges
Prussian force: 1,200 picked troops of Brunswick's army in a night coup de main on the citadel.
losses A: a handful killed and wounded, 63 captured
sources: en.wikipedia Second Battle of Wissembourg (1793); de.wikipedia Altpreußisches Dragonerregiment D I and Karl Friedrich Ludwig Georg von Uttenhoven ('Sturm auf Bitsch')
note: German 'Sturm auf Bitsch'. A traitor led the Prussians into the outer works, but the garrison drove them out.

name: Biesingen
place: Biesingen (now part of Blieskastel), between Biesingen and Blieskastel
commanders A: Friedrich Adolf von Kalckreuth
Prussian force: Kalckreuth's Prussian corps of 7,000-13,000 blocking Hoche's Army of the Moselle.

sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Biesingen; Second Battle of Wissembourg (1793)
note: Hoche announced it as a victory, but Kalckreuth held and withdrew to Homburg next morning on orders.

name: Kaiserslautern (1793)
place: Kaiserslautern and the heights around Morlautern, Palatinate
commanders A: Duke of Brunswick; Kalckstein, Schönfeld, Kalckreuth (divisions)
Prussian force: Brunswick with three Prussian divisions (Kalckstein, Schönfeld, Kalckreuth), Szekely's advance guard and a Guards brigade, with a Saxon division: 26,000 in 35 battalions and 54 squadrons with 80 guns.

sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kaiserslautern; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Kaiserslautern; Erster Koalitionskrieg
note: Also called the battle of Morlautern (de.wikipedia). Brunswick repulsed Hoche's attacks over three days but did not pursue.

name: Second Wissembourg (1793)
place: The Geisberg heights south of Wissembourg, Alsace
commanders A: Lazare Hoche, Charles Pichegru
commanders B: Dagobert Sigmund von Wurmser (Austrians), Duke of Brunswick (Prussians)

borderline: size of the Prussian force at the Geisberg not established; role could be 'contingent'
doubts and flags: Borderline: size of the Prussian force at the Geisberg not established; role could be 'contingent'.
sources: en.wikipedia Second Battle of Wissembourg (1793); Battle of Haguenau (1793); Dagobert Sigmund von Wurmser
note: Also called the Geisberg. Other German states: Hessians. The defeat relieved Landau and drove the allies back across the Rhine; Austrians and Prussians blamed each other. The First Battle of Wissembourg (13 October 1793), Haguenau and Froeschwiller were Austrian actions and are not entered.

name: Kaiserslautern (May 1794)
place: Kaiserslautern, Palatinate
commanders A: Wichard von Möllendorf; Frederick Louis of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen (left wing); Kalckreuth, Knobelsdorff, Kleist, Romberg, Rüchel (divisions)
commanders B: Jean-Jacques Ambert (division), René Moreaux (wing of the Army of the Moselle)
Prussian force: Möllendorf's Prussian army in five infantry divisions and Württemberg's cavalry division, with a Saxon contingent: about 46,000 with the allies.
losses B: about 1,000 killed, wounded and missing, 17 guns, 2 colours
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kaiserslautern (1794); Army of the Rhine (1791-1795); de.wikipedia Erster Koalitionskrieg
note: Ambert's division escaped encirclement with heavy loss. The same day an Austrian-Bavarian attack on the Army of the Rhine at Schifferstadt was repulsed (not entered: no Prussian force established there). en.wikipedia's Low Countries article dates the action 24 May.

name: Szczekociny
place: Szczekociny, north-east of Zawiercie, Lesser Poland
commanders A: King Frederick William II with Francis Favrat (Prussians); Fyodor Denisov (Russians)
Prussian force: About 17,500 Prussians on the allied right, two-thirds of the Russo-Prussian army; Favrat's massed artillery was decisive.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Szczekociny; Kościuszko Uprising
note: en.wikipedia's infobox names Favrat and Denisov, its text Tormasov, as the allied commanders; Frederick William II was with the Prussian army. Kraków then fell to the Prussians without a fight on 15 June (not entered).

name: Raszyn
place: Raszyn, south-west of Warsaw

doubts and flags: Borderline: a delaying action before the siege; date and details not established.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Warsaw (1794); Kościuszko Uprising (campaign box, no article); pl.wikipedia Pierwsze oblężenie Warszawy (1794)
note: Kościuszko fought a delaying battle at Raszyn while preparing Warsaw's defences, then withdrew to the fortified line. Not to be confused with Raszyn 1809 (no Prussian force).

name: Gołków
place: Gołków, near Piaseczno, south of Warsaw
Prussian force: The Prussian army of Frederick William II advancing on Warsaw; the units engaged and any Russian share are not established.

note: One of the battles on the approaches to Warsaw (with Raszyn) in which Kościuszko, outnumbered about two to one, fell back to the city's fortified line.

name: Kolno
place: Kolno, northern Masovia near the East Prussian border
commanders A: General Heinrich Johann Günther
Prussian force: Günther with about 750 Prussians in a pre-dawn surprise attack.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kolno
note: Polish-Lithuanian infantry fire stopped the attack; Günther had the prisoners shot and withdrew towards Pisz, Kwaśniewski to Borkowo.

name: Rajgród
place: Rajgród, near the East Prussian border
Prussian force: Prussian troops holding Rajgród; units and commander not given in the sources consulted.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Rajgród (1794)
note: Outcome per the en.wikipedia stub: the Polish-Lithuanian insurgents, without heavy artillery, temporarily drove the Prussians out of the town. Not cross-checked with Polish sources (the pl.wikipedia article could not be read).

name: Błonie
place: Błonie, west of Warsaw
commanders A: Stanisław Mokronowski
Prussian force: Prussian troops advancing on Warsaw from the west; commander not identified.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Błonie (1794)

name: Schänzel

commanders B: Prince Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen (corps); Major General Theodor Philipp von Pfau (killed)

doubts and flags: Borderline: en.wikipedia treats it as part of the Battle of Trippstadt (13-17 July 1794).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Trippstadt; Army of the Rhine (1791-1795); de.wikipedia Karl Friedrich Ludwig Georg von Uttenhoven ('Gefecht am Schänzel')
