note: German 'Gefecht am Schänzel'. Dated 12-13 July in en.wikipedia's Army of the Rhine table.

name: Trippstadt
place: Trippstadt and Johanniskreuz, Palatinate Forest, south of Kaiserslautern
commanders A: Claude Michaud, René Moreaux, Alexandre Taponier, Laurent Gouvion Saint-Cyr
commanders B: Wichard von Möllendorf, Prince Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen; Hohenlohe-Kirchberg (Austrians)
Prussian force: Möllendorf's Prussian army; the camp at Trippstadt held for a day against Taponier's division and withdrew to Kaiserslautern, which was given up on 17 July.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Trippstadt
note: Also called the Battle of the Vosges, and Platzberg in some studies. The French gained the passes of the lower Vosges.

name: Warsaw (siege, 1794)
place: Warsaw (Wola, Szwedzkie Górki, Powązki, Marymont)
commanders A: Tadeusz Kościuszko; Józef Poniatowski, Jan Henryk Dąbrowski, Józef Zajączek (sectors)
commanders B: King Frederick William II; Johann Hermann von Fersen (Russians)
Prussian force: Frederick William II with 25,000-30,000 Prussians (40 battalions, 60 squadrons, 100-179 guns), the larger part of the besieging army.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Warsaw (1794); pl.wikipedia Pierwsze oblężenie Warszawy (1794)
note: Assaults on Wola (repulsed 27 July), Szwedzkie Górki (taken by the Prussians 26 August) and Powązki-Marymont (repulsed 28 August) are part of this entry. The siege was raised after the Greater Poland rising behind the Prussian lines.

name: Kaiserslautern (September 1794)
place: Kaiserslautern, Palatinate
commanders A: Prince Frederick Louis of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen (under Möllendorf)
Prussian force: Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen's corps of the Prussian army with Saxon troops.
sources: en.wikipedia Army of the Rhine (1791-1795); Frederick Louis, Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen; Battle of Trippstadt; de.wikipedia Erster Koalitionskrieg
note: The 'third' battle of Kaiserslautern; Hohenlohe's distinction 'in the Battle of Kaiserslautern on 20 September'. The Prussians retook Kaiserslautern but withdrew to the Rhine soon after.

name: Łabiszyn
place: Łabiszyn (Labischin), south of Bromberg (Bydgoszcz)
commanders A: Jan Henryk Dąbrowski
Prussian force: Székely's pacification force from Inowrocław: a fusilier battalion and three squadrons of hussars, about 1,000.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Łabiszyn
note: Night action; Székely withdrew across the Brda to Bromberg. Loss figures are marked 'citation needed' in en.wikipedia.

name: Bydgoszcz
place: Bromberg (now Bydgoszcz)
commanders A: Jan Henryk Dąbrowski
commanders B: Colonel Johann Friedrich Székely (mortally wounded and captured); Colonel Wittel and Major Wedelstadt (killed)
Prussian force: Székely's detachment, fewer than the Polish force, with three companies of townsmen holding the left bank.
strength A: about 4,000 with 16 guns, plus about 5,000 local insurgents
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bydgoszcz; Greater Poland uprising (1794)
note: Colonel Hinrichs escaped with part of the force and retook the town on 25 October 1794.

name: Saalburg
place: Saalburg, at the crossing of the upper Saale, Thuringia
commanders A: Joachim Murat (light cavalry ahead of Bernadotte's I Corps)
commanders B: Outposts of Bogislav von Tauentzien's division
Prussian force: Outposts of Tauentzien's Prussian-Saxon division holding the Saale crossing; no strength given in the sources consulted.
borderline: minor cavalry skirmish at a river crossing
doubts and flags: Borderline: minor cavalry skirmish at a river crossing.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia War of the Fourth Coalition; napoleon-empire.org list of battles 1805-1815 ('Fight of Saalbourg')
note: Dated 8 October by en.wikipedia and 9 October by napoleon-empire.org; the opening clash of the campaign.

name: Schleiz
place: Schleiz, Thuringia
commanders A: Joachim Murat, Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte, Jean-Baptiste Drouet
Prussian force: Tauentzien's Prussian-Saxon division, about 9,000 men and 12 guns, of whom about 2,600 with 8 guns were engaged.
losses B: 566 killed, wounded, captured and missing, 1 gun
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Schleiz; en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Fourth Coalition
note: Saxon units formed part of Tauentzien's division.

name: Saalfeld
place: Saalfeld (battlefield by Wöhlsdorf), Thuringia
commanders A: Jean Lannes (V Corps, Suchet's division)
Prussian force: Prince Louis Ferdinand's advance guard of Hohenlohe's army, 8,300-9,000 Prussians and Saxons with 44 guns; the prince was killed in a cavalry melee.
losses B: about 900 killed and wounded, 1,800 captured, 33 guns (15 Prussian, 18 Saxon)
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Saalfeld; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Saalfeld

name: Jena
place: Jena (the plateau west of the town, around Vierzehnheiligen), Thuringia
commanders A: Napoleon I, with Lannes, Soult, Ney, Augereau, Murat and Lefebvre
commanders B: Prince Friedrich Ludwig of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen; Ernst von Rüchel (wounded); Julius von Grawert; Bogislav von Tauentzien
Prussian force: Hohenlohe's army, about 40,000 Prussians and Saxons, joined late in the day by Rüchel's corps of about 15,000; Grawert's division bore the brunt before Vierzehnheiligen.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Jena-Auerstedt; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Jena und Auerstedt
note: Fought the same day as Auerstedt, 20 km to the north; listed separately as in most standard works. The Saxon contingent formed a large part of Hohenlohe's army.

name: Auerstedt
place: Auerstedt and Hassenhausen, near Bad Sulza (Thuringia / Saxony-Anhalt)
commanders A: Louis-Nicolas Davout (III Corps: Gudin, Friant, Morand)
commanders B: Duke Charles William Ferdinand of Brunswick (mortally wounded); Frederick William III; Friedrich Wilhelm von Schmettau (mortally wounded); Count Kalckreuth; Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher; Gerhard von Scharnhorst
Prussian force: The main Prussian army under the Duke of Brunswick, with the king present, about 64,000 men, committed piecemeal against Davout's single corps; Kalckreuth's reserve was never engaged.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Jena-Auerstedt; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Jena und Auerstedt

name: Erfurt (1806)
place: Erfurt, Thuringia
commanders A: Joachim Murat
commanders B: William, Prince of Orange (Prussian lieutenant-general); Field Marshal Wichard von Möllendorf (wounded)
Prussian force: Fugitives and wounded from Jena-Auerstedt gathered in the citadel and town, 10,000-12,000 men with 65 guns, under the Prince of Orange.
losses B: 10,000-12,000 prisoners and 65 guns (other estimates 9,000-14,000, including up to 8,000 wounded)
borderline: capitulation without a siege; the only fighting was a cavalry clash before the town on 15 October
doubts and flags: Borderline: capitulation without a siege; the only fighting was a cavalry clash before the town on 15 October.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Capitulation of Erfurt
note: On 15 October Murat's cavalry drove Jung-Larisch's Prussian cavalry back across the Gera and took a battery; the town surrendered next day.

name: Greussen
place: Greußen, north of Erfurt, Thuringia
commanders A: Nicolas Soult (IV Corps advance)
commanders B: Rear guard of Count Kalckreuth's retreating column
Prussian force: The rear guard of the main army's remnants retreating under Kalckreuth towards Nordhausen; no strength given in the sources consulted.
borderline: minor rearguard action; details thin in the sources consulted
doubts and flags: Borderline: minor rearguard action; details thin in the sources consulted.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-empire.org list of battles 1805-1815 ('Fight of Grenssen', 16 October 1806)
note: Recorded in French lists as a French success during the pursuit after Jena-Auerstedt.

name: Halle (1806)
place: Halle (Saale), Saxony-Anhalt
commanders A: Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte (I Corps)
Prussian force: The Prussian Reserve under Duke Eugen of Württemberg, 13,700-16,000 men with 58 guns, which had not fought at Jena-Auerstedt.
losses B: 5,000-5,200 killed, wounded and captured, 11 guns, 4 colours
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Halle

name: Magdeburg (siege, 1806)
place: Magdeburg, on the Elbe, Saxony-Anhalt
commanders A: Joachim Murat, then Michel Ney (VI Corps)
commanders B: General of Infantry Franz Kasimir von Kleist
Prussian force: The garrison of Magdeburg, the strongest Prussian fortress, 24,000-25,000 men (many of them fugitives from Jena-Auerstedt) and 700 guns under von Kleist.
losses B: the whole garrison captured, with 20 generals, 54 colours and 700 guns
borderline: little real fighting: skirmishes and one sortie (4 November); capitulated under threat of bombardment
doubts and flags: Borderline: little real fighting: skirmishes and one sortie (4 November); capitulated under threat of bombardment.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Magdeburg (1806)
note: Armistice 7 November, capitulation 8 November, garrison marched out 11 November.

name: Zehdenick
place: Zehdenick, on the Havel, Brandenburg
commanders A: Antoine Lasalle, Emmanuel de Grouchy (under Murat)
Prussian force: Schimmelpfennig's flank guard of Hohenlohe's retreating army, about 1,300 men, chiefly cavalry including the Queen's (Königin) Dragoons.
losses B: the Königin Dragoon Regiment almost destroyed
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Prenzlau (preliminary actions); napoleon-empire.org ('Fight of Zehdenick')
note: The survivors fled to Stettin.

name: Altenzaun
place: Altenzaun, near Hohenberg-Krusemark on the Elbe, Saxony-Anhalt
commanders A: Oberst Ludwig Yorck
commanders B: Advance guard of Nicolas Soult's IV Corps
Prussian force: Yorck's rear guard of the Duke of Saxe-Weimar's column: six Jäger companies, three fusilier battalions and two guns.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht von Altenzaun; en.wikipedia Battle of Lübeck (related actions)
note: Covered the crossing of the Elbe by Saxe-Weimar's troops; called the first Prussian success after Jena and Auerstedt.

name: Boitzenburg
place: Boitzenburg, Uckermark, Brandenburg
commanders A: Advance guard of Hohenlohe's army
Prussian force: Hohenlohe's advance guard on the march to Prenzlau; no strength given.
borderline: minor action
doubts and flags: Borderline: minor action.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Prenzlau (preliminary actions)
note: Milhaud's cavalry, caught pillaging the estate, took about three hours to drive out.

name: Wichmannsdorf
place: Wichmannsdorf, near Boitzenburg, Uckermark, Brandenburg
commanders A: Emmanuel de Grouchy (dragoons, under Murat)
Prussian force: Hohenlohe's right-flank guard, including the Gensdarmes (Cuirassier Regiment No. 10).
losses B: the Gensdarmes regiment driven into a marsh and captured
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Prenzlau (preliminary actions)

name: Prenzlau
place: Prenzlau, Uckermark, Brandenburg
commanders A: Joachim Murat
commanders B: Prince Friedrich Ludwig of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen; Christian von Massenbach (chief of staff)
Prussian force: Hohenlohe's corps, the remnant of his army after Jena, about 10,000-12,000 men with 64 guns; after a cavalry fight Hohenlohe surrendered to Murat's bluff.
losses B: 3,500 killed or captured in the fighting, about 10,000 surrendered, 64 guns (Petre: about 12,000 in all)
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Prenzlau

name: Pasewalk (1806)
place: Pasewalk, Western Pomerania
commanders A: Édouard Milhaud, Antoine Lasalle
Prussian force: Hagen's column of Hohenlohe's army, about 4,200 men and 8 guns, trapped between two French cavalry brigades.
borderline: capitulation of a field column without fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: capitulation of a field column without fighting.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Capitulation of Pasewalk
note: Stettin capitulated to Lasalle's bluff the same night without a siege (excluded).

name: Anklam (1806)
place: Anklam, on the Peene, Western Pomerania
commanders A: Nicolas Beker (dragoon brigade)
Prussian force: Bila's column of about 2,100 men, a fragment of Hohenlohe's army.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Prenzlau (later actions); napoleon-empire.org ('Fight of Anklam', 31 October 1806)
note: Beker forced Bila north of the Peene on 31 October; Bila capitulated next day. Höpfner's 600 men had surrendered at Boldekow on 30 October without a fight (excluded).

name: Waren-Nossentin
place: Waren (Müritz), Jabel and Nossentin, Mecklenburg
commanders A: August von Pletz, Ludwig Yorck (Blücher's rear guard)
Prussian force: The rear guard of Blücher's corps, 4,000-5,000 infantry, Jäger and hussars with 4 guns, under Pletz and Yorck.
losses B: over 46 at Waren; unknown at Nossentin
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Waren-Nossentin; en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Fourth Coalition
note: A successful rearguard action: Drouet's dragoons took Nossentin, but the Prussians got away intact to Alt Schwerin; en.wikipedia scores it a Prussian victory.

name: Crivitz
place: Crivitz, east of Schwerin, Mecklenburg
commanders A: General-Major Oswald (Blücher's rear guard)
commanders B: Advance guard of Bernadotte's I Corps
Prussian force: Oswald's rear guard of Blücher's corps, 2,500-3,000 infantry, 1,200-1,500 cavalry and 8 guns; the Rudorff Hussars counter-attacked and took a French colonel (Gérard) prisoner.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lübeck (related actions)
note: The 1st battalion of the Arnim Infantry Regiment was destroyed at Pinnow during the action; the French later took Meuss near Schwerin.

name: Lübeck
place: Lübeck (neutral Hanseatic city), Schleswig-Holstein
commanders A: Joachim Murat, Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte, Nicolas Soult
commanders B: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher; Gerhard von Scharnhorst (chief of staff); Duke Frederick William of Brunswick-Oels
Prussian force: Blücher's corps, about 16,000-17,000 men (21,000 on 1 November), with 17 battalions and 52 guns defending the city.
losses B: about 2,000 killed and wounded and 4,000 captured (Smith); French estimate 3,000 killed and wounded and 5,000-6,000 captured
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lübeck
note: Blücher surrendered the rest of his corps (8,000-9,000 men, 80 guns) at Ratekau on 7 November; a Swedish detachment caught at Lübeck was captured with it. The city was sacked.

name: Hamelin (siege)
place: Hamelin (Hameln), on the Weser, Lower Saxony
commanders A: Édouard Mortier (VIII Corps); Jean-Baptiste Dumonceau; Anne Jean Marie René Savary
commanders B: General Karl Ludwig von Lecoq; General-Major von Schöler
Prussian force: The garrison of Hameln, about 10,000 men and 175 guns, under Lecoq.
losses B: 600 captured; about 10,000 capitulated (most of them slipped away), 175 guns
borderline: a blockade without assault, sortie or bombardment, ended by capitulation
doubts and flags: Borderline: a blockade without assault, sortie or bombardment, ended by capitulation.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Hamelin; en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Fourth Coalition
note: Nienburg (2,911 men) capitulated on 26 November after a blockade without fighting (excluded).

name: Glogau (siege, 1806)
place: Glogau (now Głogów), on the Oder, Lower Silesia
commanders A: Dominique Vandamme (IX Corps under Jérôme Bonaparte)
commanders B: Prussian garrison (commandant not named in the sources consulted)
Prussian force: The garrison of the fortress of Glogau; no strength given in the sources consulted.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-online.de, Württemberg contingent 1806-07 (Kloeffler); napoleon-empire.org ('Capture of Glogau', 2 December 1806)
note: Start date from Württemberg accounts; the capitulation is dated 2 December by napoleon-empire.org, 7 December in the Württemberg study.

name: Breslau (siege, 1806-07)
place: Breslau (now Wrocław), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Dominique Vandamme, Jérôme Bonaparte (IX Corps)
commanders B: Prussian garrison (governor not named in the sources consulted)
Prussian force: The garrison of Breslau, the capital of Silesia; no strength given in the sources consulted.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-online.de, Württemberg contingent 1806-07 (Kloeffler); napoleon-empire.org ('Capture of Breslau', 7 January 1807); en.wikipedia Dominique Vandamme
note: Invested after the fall of Glogau (Württemberg cavalry reconnoitred the city from 16 November); relief attempts were beaten at Strehlen (24 December) and Ohlau (29/30 December). Vandamme had the fortifications levelled.

name: Gülzow
place: Gülzow (probably today's Golczewo), between Stettin and Kolberg, Pomerania
commanders A: Ferdinand von Schill
Prussian force: Schill's mounted party from the Kolberg garrison; no strength given.
borderline: minor skirmish
doubts and flags: Borderline: minor skirmish.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kolberg (1807)
note: Date as given by en.wikipedia; widely noted as Schill's first success and the start of his partisan war around Kolberg. Identification of the site is approximate.

name: Bieżuń
place: Bieżuń, on the Wkra, north-west Masovia (then New East Prussia)
commanders A: Jean-Baptiste Bessières (II Reserve Cavalry Corps)
commanders B: Antoine-Charles de La Roche-Aymon (detachment of L'Estocq's corps)
Prussian force: A detachment sent by L'Estocq to retake the town: two infantry regiments, a dragoon regiment, two hussar regiments and a horse battery; half the Towarczys Uhlan Regiment, the Schleiffen Grenadier Battalion and a horse battery bore the brunt.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Czarnowo (Prussian actions nearby); ADB L'Estocq (de.wikisource); napoleon-empire.org ('Fight of Bieżuń')

name: Strehlen
place: Strehlen (now Strzelin), south of Breslau, Lower Silesia
commanders A: Covering troops of Vandamme's siege corps
commanders B: Relief column from the Schweidnitz garrison (Prince Ferdinand of Anhalt-Pless's command)
Prussian force: A relief column drawn from the Schweidnitz garrison, sent to raise the siege of Breslau; no strength given.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-online.de, Württemberg contingent 1806-07 (Kloeffler)
note: The relief attempt was repulsed.

name: Soldau
place: Soldau (now Działdowo), southern East Prussia
commanders A: Michel Ney (VI Corps, Marchand's division)
Prussian force: L'Estocq's corps, trying to retake the town; the Rüchel (No. 2) and Schöning (No. 11) infantry regiments, about 3,000 men in four battalions with eight 12-pounders, are named.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Czarnowo (Prussian actions nearby); ADB L'Estocq (de.wikisource)
note: Marchand drove the Prussian garrison out; L'Estocq's counter-attack failed and he withdrew to Neidenburg. Fighting also at Mława the same day.

name: Ohlau
place: Ohlau (now Oława), south-east of Breslau, Lower Silesia
commanders A: Covering troops of Vandamme's siege corps
commanders B: Prince Ferdinand of Anhalt-Pless (relief of Breslau)
Prussian force: Troops of the Silesian fortresses collected by the Prince of Anhalt-Pless to relieve Breslau; no strength given.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-empire.org ('Fight of Ohlau', 30 December 1806); napoleon-online.de, Württemberg contingent 1806-07 (Kloeffler)
note: Dated 29 December in the Württemberg study. The second relief attempt failed and Breslau capitulated on 5 January (French entry 7 January). Some accounts also name a fight at Canth (Kąty Wrocławskie) in the same operation.

name: Schweidnitz (siege, 1807)
place: Schweidnitz (now Świdnica), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Dominique Vandamme (IX Corps)
commanders B: Prussian garrison (commandant not named in the sources consulted)
Prussian force: The garrison of the fortress of Schweidnitz; no strength given in the sources consulted.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-empire.org ('Capture of Schweidnitz', 16 February 1807); en.wikipedia Siege of Danzig (1807) (siege guns from Schweidnitz)
note: Start of the siege not dated in the sources consulted (after the fall of Brieg); the heavy guns taken here were sent on to the siege of Danzig.

name: Brieg (siege, 1807)
place: Brieg (now Brzeg), on the Oder, Silesia
commanders A: Troops of Jérôme Bonaparte's IX Corps (Vandamme)
commanders B: Prussian garrison (commandant not named in the sources consulted)
Prussian force: The garrison of the fortress of Brieg; no strength given in the sources consulted.
borderline: short siege; scale of the fighting not documented in the sources consulted
doubts and flags: Borderline: short siege; scale of the fighting not documented in the sources consulted.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-empire.org ('Capture of Brieg', 17 January 1807); napoleon-online.de, Württemberg contingent 1806-07 (Kloeffler)

name: Cosel (siege, 1807)
place: Cosel (Kosel; now Koźle, part of Kędzierzyn-Koźle), on the Oder, Upper Silesia
commanders A: Oberst David von Neumann (died during the siege)
commanders B: Troops of Jérôme Bonaparte's IX Corps
Prussian force: The garrison of the fortress of Cosel; no strength given in the sources consulted.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: de.wikipedia Schlesischer Feldzug (Glatz, Silberberg and Cosel held until Tilsit); Belagerungsgeschichte der Vestung Cosel (bibliotekacyfrowa.pl)
note: Blockaded and besieged from January 1807; still Prussian when the Peace of Tilsit ended the war.

name: Arnswalde
place: Arnswalde (now Choszczno), Pomerania
commanders A: A party of Ferdinand von Schill's Freikorps
Prussian force: A raiding party of Schill's Freikorps from Kolberg.
losses B: General Victor and his escort captured
borderline: a raid that captured a general on the road, not a battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: a raid that captured a general on the road, not a battle.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kolberg (1807)
note: Victor, designated to command before Kolberg, was later exchanged for Blücher.

name: Graudenz (siege)
place: Graudenz (now Grudziądz), on the Vistula, West Prussia
commanders A: Wilhelm René de l'Homme de Courbière
commanders B: Marie-François Rouyer, Claude Victor-Perrin, Johann Georg Schäffer von Bernstein, Georg Friedrich August von Polenz
Prussian force: The garrison of Graudenz, 4,500-5,709 men, under the aged General Courbière.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Graudenz; en.wikipedia Greater Poland uprising (1806) (Zajączek's Kalisz division)
note: Blockade and siege; the place never fell, and the besiegers withdrew after Tilsit once the Prussian-Warsaw border was settled.

name: Allenstein
place: Bergfried (now Barkweda), on the Alle north of Allenstein (Olsztyn), East Prussia
commanders A: Napoleon I, Nicolas Soult
Prussian force: Three Prussian batteries supporting Kamensky's Russian division at the Bergfried bridge.
borderline: Prussian share only three batteries
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian share only three batteries. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Eylau (preliminaries); en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Fourth Coalition; napoleon-empire.org ('Fight of Bergfried')
note: Also called Bergfried.

name: Waltersdorf
place: Waltersdorf (now Włodowo), near Liebstadt (Miłakowo), East Prussia
commanders A: Michel Ney (VI Corps)
Prussian force: Part of L'Estocq's corps (about 9,000 men at the start of its march) caught by Ney while marching to join Bennigsen.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-empire.org ('Fight of Waltersdorf', 5 February 1807); en.wikipedia Battle of Eylau
note: Ney's pursuit (of which this was the main clash) cost L'Estocq about a third of his strength before Eylau.

name: Eylau
place: Preussisch Eylau (now Bagrationovsk), south of Königsberg, East Prussia
commanders A: Napoleon I, with Murat, Davout, Soult, Augereau (wounded), Ney
commanders B: Levin August von Bennigsen (Russian commander-in-chief); Anton Wilhelm von L'Estocq, with Gerhard von Scharnhorst (Prussian corps)
Prussian force: L'Estocq's corps, 8 battalions, 28 squadrons and 2 horse batteries (7,000-9,000 men; ADB 5,000-6,000), with Scharnhorst as chief of staff; arriving about 16:00 on 8 February it struck Davout's flank at Kutschitten and saved the Russian left.
strength A: about 75,000 (49,000 at first, rising to about 74,000 with Davout and Ney)
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Eylau; en.wikipedia Anton Wilhelm von L'Estocq; ADB L'Estocq (de.wikisource)
note: Julian 26-27 January. The French held the field after the Russians withdrew on the night of 8 February, but the battle was strategically inconclusive; scored as a draw. The Prussian corps was about a tenth of the allied army but fought as a distinct corps at the decisive point.

name: Stolp
war: War of the Fourth Coalition (Greater Poland uprising)
place: Stolp (now Słupsk), Further Pomerania
commanders A: Polish troops (Michał Sokolnicki's command, per Polish accounts)
Prussian force: The Prussian troops holding Stolp; no strength given.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Fourth Coalition; en.wikipedia Greater Poland uprising (1806)
note: en.wikipedia lists the victors as Duchy of Warsaw and Polish rebels (the Duchy was created only in July 1807).

name: Neisse (siege, 1807)
place: Neisse (now Nysa), Upper Silesia
commanders A: Dominique Vandamme and Jérôme Bonaparte; Württemberg division under Seckendorf, then Camrer
Prussian force: The garrison of Neisse, reduced by desertion to about 4,000 by late May.
strength A: about 8,000 Württemberg troops at the investment
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-online.de, Württemberg contingent 1806-07 (Kloeffler)
note: Investment 22 February, formal siege from 1 March, the blockhouse redoubt stormed on 1 May; capitulation dated 14 or 16 June. A relief from Glatz under Count Götzen came too late.

name: Dirschau
war: War of the Fourth Coalition (Greater Poland uprising)
place: Dirschau (now Tczew), on the Vistula south of Danzig
commanders A: Jan Henryk Dąbrowski (wounded), then Amilkar Kosiński
Prussian force: A strong Prussian garrison covering the approaches to Danzig; no strength given.
strength A: the Poznań division (6 battalions, 3 squadrons) and 2,000 levy (pospolite ruszenie)
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Greater Poland uprising (1806)
note: Taken after about seven hours of fighting; earlier Polish attacks on the town (January and 15 February) had been driven back. French support for the assault is reported in some accounts.

name: Braunsberg
place: Braunsberg (now Braniewo), on the Passarge, East Prussia
commanders A: Pierre Dupont (division of Bernadotte's I Corps)
Prussian force: A detachment of L'Estocq's corps holding the Passarge crossing at Braunsberg; no strength given in the sources consulted.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-empire.org ('Fight of Braunsberg', 26 February 1807)
note: Dupont drove the Prussians out of the town and across the Passarge.

name: Danzig (siege, 1807)
place: Danzig (now Gdańsk), at the mouth of the Vistula
allies A: Polish insurgents; Saxony; Baden; Kingdom of Italy
commanders A: François Joseph Lefebvre; Jan Henryk Dąbrowski (Polish troops); Édouard Mortier (at the end)
commanders B: Field Marshal Friedrich Adolf von Kalckreuth; Nikolay Kamensky (Russian relief force)
Prussian force: The Danzig garrison of about 14,400-16,000 men under Field Marshal Count Kalckreuth; it marched out with the honours of war.
strength B: garrison about 14,400 (16,000 in some counts); Russian relief force about 7,000-8,000
losses B: garrison about 3,000 (10,000 in counts that include the capitulated men); Russian relief force about 1,500
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Danzig (1807); en.wikipedia Greater Poland uprising (1806)
note: Kamensky's Russian relief force landed at Weichselmünde and was beaten back on 15 May (napoleon-empire.org 'Fight of Danzig'); a British attempt to run powder in by river failed. Capitulation 24 May, French entry 27 May; Weichselmünde surrendered soon after.

name: Kolberg (siege, 1807)
place: Kolberg (now Kołobrzeg), Pomerania
allies B: Württemberg; Kingdom of Italy; Kingdom of Holland; Polish insurgents; Saxony
commanders A: Louis Maurice de Lucadou, then August Neidhardt von Gneisenau (from 29 April); Joachim Nettelbeck (citizens); Ferdinand von Schill (Freikorps)
commanders B: Pietro Teulié (mortally wounded), Louis Henri Loison; Édouard Mortier (briefly in April)
Prussian force: The garrison of Kolberg, about 6,000 after Schill's departure, with 230 guns, under Gneisenau, with Nettelbeck's citizens and Schill's Freikorps; British guns and a Swedish frigate supported from the sea.
strength B: about 8,000 in May, rising to about 14,000
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kolberg (1807); en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Fourth Coalition
note: The place never fell: fighting ended at noon on 2 July with news of the armistice. The Wolfsberg sconce was fought over on 7 and 17/18 May and surrendered on 11 June. en.wikipedia's list calls the result indecisive; scored as a defensive success by the siege rule.

name: Silberberg (siege)
place: Silberberg fortress (now Srebrna Góra), Owl Mountains, Silesia
commanders A: Prussian garrison (Count Götzen's Silesian command)
commanders B: Troops of Jérôme Bonaparte's IX Corps
Prussian force: The garrison of the mountain fortress of Silberberg; no strength given.
borderline: blockade only; no assault or named fighting found in the sources consulted
doubts and flags: Borderline: blockade only; no assault or named fighting found in the sources consulted.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: de.wikipedia Schlesischer Feldzug
note: One of the three Silesian fortresses (with Glatz and Cosel) still held when the Peace of Tilsit ended the war.

name: Spanden
place: Spanden (now Spędy), bridgehead on the Passarge, East Prussia
commanders A: Eugène-Casimir Villatte (Frère's brigade); Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte (wounded)
commanders B: Anton Wilhelm von L'Estocq; Michael Szabszinski von Rembow (division commander)
Prussian force: Rembow's division of L'Estocq's corps: 15 squadrons of the Ziethen (No. 6) and Baczko (No. 7) dragoons and 29 guns and 2 howitzers, with the Russian Sievsk and Perm infantry regiments (three battalions each).
strength B: about 3,000 infantry and 1,500 cavalry, up to 6,000 in some estimates
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Guttstadt-Deppen; napoleon-empire.org ('Fight of Spanden')
note: A diversion in support of Bennigsen's offensive (Guttstadt-Deppen) that became a failed assault on the French bridgehead. L'Estocq's corps then numbered about 20,000, 15,000 of them Prussians.

name: Heilsberg
place: Heilsberg (now Lidzbark Warmiński), on the Alle, East Prussia
commanders A: Napoleon I, Joachim Murat, Nicolas Soult, Jean Lannes
commanders B: Levin August von Bennigsen, then Andrei Gorchakov
Prussian force: About 3,000 Prussian cavalry and other reinforcements sent by L'Estocq, with the 21st Fusiliers under Ludwig August von Stutterheim holding the castle.
strength B: 90,000-95,000 around Heilsberg (about 53,000 engaged), including about 3,000 Prussian cavalry
losses B: 2,000-3,000 killed and 5,000-6,000 wounded (Smith, Russians and Prussians)
doubts and flags: Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Heilsberg; en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Fourth Coalition
note: Julian 29 May. A tactical draw; Bennigsen withdrew next day towards Friedland. L'Estocq himself was not present (ADB).

name: Königsberg
place: Königsberg (now Kaliningrad), East Prussia
commanders A: Nicolas Soult (IV Corps)
commanders B: Anton Wilhelm von L'Estocq; Nikolay Kamensky (Russian division)
Prussian force: L'Estocq's corps (about 15,000 Prussians a week earlier) with Kamensky's Russian division, defending the entrenched city.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-empire.org ('Capture of Königsberg', 16 June 1807); en.wikipedia Battle of Guttstadt-Deppen (L'Estocq's corps)
note: Fought the day of Friedland. The defenders held the entrenchments on 14 June but evacuated the city on 15 June on news of Friedland, and the French entered on 16 June; some accounts treat the 14 June fighting as a repulse of Soult. Scored for France because the place fell.

name: Glatz (1807)
place: Glatz (now Kłodzko), entrenched camp before the fortress, County of Glatz
commanders A: Troops of Jérôme Bonaparte's IX Corps (Vandamme)
commanders B: Count Friedrich Wilhelm von Götzen (governor-general of Silesia)
Prussian force: The troops of Götzen's Silesian command in the entrenched camp before the fortress of Glatz; no strength given.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: napoleon-online.de, Württemberg contingent 1806-07 (Kloeffler); de.wikipedia Schlesischer Feldzug
note: The entrenched camp was stormed; the fortress itself was not taken before the armistice, and the siege was abandoned on 14 July 1807.

name: Dömitz
war: War of the Fifth Coalition (Schill's rising)
place: Dömitz fortress, on the Elbe, Mecklenburg
commanders A: Westphalian troops pursuing Schill
commanders B: Detachment left by Ferdinand von Schill
Prussian force: A small detachment of Schill's corps left to hold the captured Mecklenburg fortress; no strength given.
borderline: The fortress was seized by surprise in mid-May and lost again later in May, and the details of the fighting were not verified in the sources consulted.
doubts and flags: Major Ferdinand von Schill took his hussar regiment to war against Napoleon and his German allies in April 1809 without orders, hoping to raise a rising; King Frederick William III disowned him. Prussian troops under a Prussian officer, so the battle is counted, and scored. Borderline: The fortress was seized by surprise in mid-May and lost again later in May, and the details of the fighting were not verified in the sources consulted.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: general histories of Schill's raid (not verified online)
note: One of the battles of Schill's raid; its date, opponents and outcome rest on general histories of the raid.

name: Dodendorf
war: War of the Fifth Coalition (Schill's rising)
place: Dodendorf (now part of Sülzetal), south of Magdeburg, Saxony-Anhalt
commanders A: Ferdinand von Schill; Ludwig Adolf Wilhelm von Lützow (badly wounded)
commanders B: Colonel Vautier (killed); General von Uslar (Magdeburg garrison under General Michaud)
Prussian force: Schill's 2nd Brandenburg Hussars, who had left Berlin without orders on 28 April; no total given (outnumbered by the Magdeburg sortie).
strength B: about 1,100 sent out from Magdeburg, joined by the 1st Westphalian Line Regiment (with two French companies of the 22nd Line)
losses A: 6 officers and 83 men killed or badly wounded (the monument names 21 Prussian dead)
losses B: heavier than Schill's (not quantified); Vautier killed
doubts and flags: Major Ferdinand von Schill took his hussar regiment to war against Napoleon and his German allies in April 1809 without orders, hoping to raise a rising; King Frederick William III disowned him. Prussian troops under a Prussian officer, so the battle is counted, and scored.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Dodendorf; en.wikipedia Battle of Dodendorf; en.wikipedia Ferdinand von Schill
note: Opponents: the Kingdom of Westphalia, with French companies from Magdeburg. de.wikipedia judges it militarily indecisive (Schill withdrew in the evening); en.wikipedia calls it a small Schill victory.

name: Damgarten
war: War of the Fifth Coalition (Schill's rising)
place: Damgarten (now part of Ribnitz-Damgarten), on the Recknitz between Mecklenburg and Pomerania
commanders A: Ferdinand von Schill
commanders B: Companies of the Mecklenburg contingent (under French command)
Prussian force: Schill's corps on its march to Stralsund; its hussars pursued the beaten Mecklenburgers.
doubts and flags: Major Ferdinand von Schill took his hussar regiment to war against Napoleon and his German allies in April 1809 without orders, hoping to raise a rising; King Frederick William III disowned him. Prussian troops under a Prussian officer, so the battle is counted, and scored.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: de.wikipedia Großherzoglich Mecklenburgisches Grenadier-Regiment Nr. 89
note: The Mecklenburgers ran out of ammunition and fell back, pursued by Schill's hussars.

name: Stralsund (1809)
war: War of the Fifth Coalition (Schill's rising)
place: Stralsund, Swedish Pomerania
commanders A: Pierre Guillaume Gratien (Dutch division); Johann von Ewald (Danish troops)
commanders B: Ferdinand von Schill (killed); Friedrich Gustav von Petersson (captured and executed)
Prussian force: Schill's corps, about 990 Prussians with about 500 Swedish volunteers and Rügen militia, holding the town it had seized on 25 May.
doubts and flags: Major Ferdinand von Schill took his hussar regiment to war against Napoleon and his German allies in April 1809 without orders, hoping to raise a rising; King Frederick William III disowned him. Prussian troops under a Prussian officer, so the battle is counted, and scored.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Stralsund (1809); en.wikipedia Ferdinand von Schill; de.wikipedia Schillsche Jäger
note: A street battle in which Schill was killed; eleven of his officers were later shot at Wesel. The Dutch and Danish troops acted under French orders (Gratien was a French general).

name: Ekau
place: Eckau (Ekau; now Iecava), Courland
commanders A: Julius von Grawert; Friedrich Kleist
Prussian force: Grawert's Prussian auxiliary corps of Macdonald's X Corps (the 27th Division), about 7,000 men and 32 guns engaged; Kleist's column struck the Russian position from the east in the evening.
doubts and flags: The Prussian auxiliary corps (Grawert, then Yorck) fought for Napoleon, as his ally under the treaty of 24 February 1812, in Macdonald's X Corps; the battle is counted and scored as Prussian. Yorck took the corps out of the war at Tauroggen on 30 December 1812.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ekau; en.wikipedia Siege of Riga (1812); en.wikipedia List of battles of the French invasion of Russia
note: Julian 7 July. German name Eckau. Prussia fought as Napoleon's ally under the treaty of 24 February 1812.

name: Riga (siege)
place: Riga and the left bank of the Daugava (Dvina) before it, Livonia
allies B: France; Duchy of Warsaw; Bavaria; Other German states
commanders A: Magnus Gustav von Essen, then Filippo Paulucci (from 26 October); Ivan Emme (commandant); Fabian Steinheil (Finland corps); Thomas Byam Martin (British naval forces)
commanders B: Jacques Macdonald (X Corps); Julius von Grawert, then Ludwig Yorck (Prussian corps)
Prussian force: The Prussian auxiliary corps of Macdonald's X Corps (the 20,000 men required by the treaty of February 1812), under Grawert and from August under Yorck; it formed the investing force before Riga.
strength A: about 27,000 (garrison about 14,000, plus about 10,000 of Steinheil's corps)
borderline: no formal siege was opened (the siege train never crossed the Daugava); the entry covers the blockade and the fighting around it
doubts and flags: The Prussian auxiliary corps (Grawert, then Yorck) fought for Napoleon, as his ally under the treaty of 24 February 1812, in Macdonald's X Corps; the battle is counted and scored as Prussian. Yorck took the corps out of the war at Tauroggen on 30 December 1812. Borderline: no formal siege was opened (the siege train never crossed the Daugava); the entry covers the blockade and the fighting around it.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Riga (1812); en.wikipedia List of battles of the French invasion of Russia
note: Named actions within it are separate entries (Dahlenkirchen, Mesoten). The Prussians began their retreat on 20 December (8 December O.S.), which ended in the Convention of Tauroggen (30 December). Grandjean's division (Polish, Bavarian and Westphalian units) was the non-Prussian part of X Corps.

name: Dahlenkirchen
place: Dahlenkirchen (near Ķekava), on the left bank of the Daugava south-east of Riga
commanders A: Magnus Gustav von Essen
commanders B: Julius von Grawert (Colonel Horn's wing), under Jacques Macdonald
Prussian force: The Prussian right wing under Colonel Horn, about 1,500 men and 8 guns, surprised and driven back.
doubts and flags: The Prussian auxiliary corps (Grawert, then Yorck) fought for Napoleon, as his ally under the treaty of 24 February 1812, in Macdonald's X Corps; the battle is counted and scored as Prussian. Yorck took the corps out of the war at Tauroggen on 30 December 1812.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Dahlenkirchen; en.wikipedia Siege of Riga (1812)
note: Julian 10 August. A sortie from Riga after feints towards Schlock and Olai; the Prussians recovered the ground in a counter-attack on 7 September (26 August O.S.).

name: Mesoten
place: Mesoten (now Mežotne), on the Lielupe south of Mitau (Jelgava), Courland
commanders A: Ludwig Yorck, with Friedrich Kleist and Colonel Horn
commanders B: Fabian Steinheil (Finland corps), with Magnus Gustav von Essen's Riga garrison
Prussian force: Yorck's Prussian auxiliary corps, about 16,000 men; after Horn's group was driven back, Yorck's counter-attacks (Kleist's night attack across the Lielupe on 29 September) forced Steinheil back to Riga.
doubts and flags: The Prussian auxiliary corps (Grawert, then Yorck) fought for Napoleon, as his ally under the treaty of 24 February 1812, in Macdonald's X Corps; the battle is counted and scored as Prussian. Yorck took the corps out of the war at Tauroggen on 30 December 1812.
period: Jena, Schill and the march on Russia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Mesoten; en.wikipedia Siege of Riga (1812); en.wikipedia List of battles of the French invasion of Russia
note: Julian 14-19 September. A series of combats around Mitau, Bauske and Mesoten, entered as one battle as in en.wikipedia; German accounts split it into several named combats, which were not verified separately here.

name: Magdeburg (siege, 1813–1814)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Magdeburg, on the Elbe
commanders A: Bogislav von Tauentzien (from 1814)
Prussian force: Prussian and Russian blockading troops; Tauentzien's IV Corps took over in 1814 after Torgau and Wittenberg fell.
borderline: A blockade rather than a formal siege; its start date (after Leipzig, month unknown, so placed last) and any sorties or fighting could not be verified. Magdeburg had already been watched by Allied troops since the spring of 1813.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A blockade rather than a formal siege; its start date (after Leipzig, month unknown, so placed last) and any sorties or fighting could not be verified. Magdeburg had already been watched by Allied troops since the spring of 1813.
sources: de.wikipedia Festung Magdeburg; en.wikipedia Bogislav Friedrich Emanuel von Tauentzien; en.wikipedia Siege of Magdeburg (disambiguation)
note: de.wikipedia: Magdeburg withstood the sieges by Prussian-Russian troops in 1813–14; Prussian troops entered on 24 May 1814 after Napoleon's abdication. Outcome given to the besiegers because the place was handed over to them.

name: Danzig (siege, 1813)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Danzig (now Gdańsk)
allies B: Duchy of Warsaw; Bavaria; Saxony; Other German states
commanders A: Matvei Platov, Fyodor Lewis (Löwis), Duke Alexander of Württemberg (from 1 May 1813)
commanders B: Jean Rapp, Étienne Heudelet, Charles Grandjean
Prussian force: Prussian (East Prussian) Landwehr joined the Russian siege army from 9 March 1813 and served to the end; the siege army grew from about 13,000 (May) to 35,000–40,000. Separate Prussian strength not found.
strength B: about 36,000 (20 January 1813, some 20,000 of them unfit); about 12,000 fit men on 1 May
losses A: Russians about 1,300 killed, 3,000 wounded, 500 captured; Prussians 460 killed
losses B: over 19,000 (about 2,000 killed, about 16,000 dead of disease, 1,000 deserted); 14 generals and about 15,000 men surrendered
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Danzig (1813); de.wikipedia Festungskrieg (1813)
note: Russian-led siege (Cossacks under Platov encircled the city by 21 January); British warships joined in March. Many sorties and assaults (e.g. 5 March, 28–29 August, 2 September, 10–11 October, 1 and 3 November). Garrison also included Westphalian and Neapolitan troops. The entry covers the whole siege.

date: 22 January – 15 April 1813 (Gregorian; garrison marched out 18 April)
name: Thorn (siege, 1813)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Thorn (now Toruń)
commanders A: Michael Barclay de Tolly (Langeron's corps conducted the siege)
Prussian force: No Prussian troops identified; Prussia supplied 32 heavy siege guns from Graudenz to the Russian besiegers.
strength B: 4,146 Bavarian infantry, about 100 Polish gunners and 50 guns, plus about 1,500 French (some 300 fit)
losses B: about 50 Bavarians killed and wounded in action, about 920 dead of typhus; the garrison capitulated
borderline: Russian siege; the Prussian share was the loan of siege artillery from Graudenz, not a troop contingent
doubts and flags: Borderline: Russian siege; the Prussian share was the loan of siege artillery from Graudenz, not a troop contingent.
sources: de.wikipedia Festungskrieg (1813)
note: Russian sources date it 10 January – 3 April 1813 (Julian). Bombardment from late February; no assault recorded. Kept as a named joint Russian-Prussian operation; the Prussian part was siege artillery, so it is not scored.

name: Küstrin (siege, 1813–14)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Küstrin (now Kostrzyn nad Odrą), on the Oder
Prussian force: Prussian blockade troops took over from the Russians who had invested and bombarded the fortress in March 1813; commanders and strength not found.
borderline: mainly a blockade: a Russian bombardment in March 1813 and the burning of the suburbs by the garrison, no assault recorded
doubts and flags: Borderline: mainly a blockade: a Russian bombardment in March 1813 and the burning of the suburbs by the garrison, no assault recorded.
sources: de.wikipedia Festung Küstrin
note: First Russian, later Prussian blockade; the fortress could not be stormed and capitulated in March 1814. The entry covers the whole blockade.

name: Glogau (siege, 1813)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Glogau (now Głogów), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Jean Grégoire Barthélemy Rouger de Laplane (governor)
commanders B: Guillaume de Saint-Priest (Russian blockade); Prussian General Scholler (spelling of historyofwar.org)
Prussian force: A Prussian siege force under General Scholler took over the siege from Saint-Priest's Russians by the end of March 1813, with 16 heavy guns; strength not given.
strength B: Saint-Priest's Russians: 8,000 infantry, 2,000 cavalry, 20 guns (initially); Prussian strength not given
sources: historyofwar.org Siege of Glogau
note: Real fighting: sorties of 31 March, 7 May and 21 May (a Prussian battery destroyed), and a failed Prussian night attack with fire ships on the bridgehead on 1 May. Lifted on the night of 27–28 May as Victor's II Corps approached after Bautzen. The second siege (September 1813 – surrender 10 April 1814) is a separate entry.

name: Stettin (siege, 1813)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Stettin (now Szczecin), on the Oder
commanders A: Bogislav Friedrich Emanuel von Tauentzien (to 18 May 1813), then von Plötz
Prussian force: Tauentzien's Prussian blockade corps, initially 13 battalions and 4 squadrons, with a Cossack regiment and 4 Swedish gunboats.
strength A: initially 13 battalions, 4 squadrons, a Cossack pulk and 4 gunboats
losses A: Prussians about 130 (7 April), about 200 (15 April) and 80 (12 May)
losses B: about 300 on 12 May; 7 generals, 533 officers and 7,100 men capitulated
sources: de.wikipedia Festungskrieg (1813)
note: Sortie to Finkenwalde (7 April), failed Prussian attack on the Oder bridge (15 April), further sorties (17 April, 1 and 10 May) and a repulsed sortie on Grabow (12 May). The entry covers the whole siege.

name: Spandau (siege, 1813)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Spandau citadel and town, west of Berlin
allies B: Duchy of Warsaw; Other German states
commanders A: Heinrich Ludwig August von Thümen
Prussian force: About 1,800 Prussians and two 6-pounder batteries under General von Thümen, with some 400 Russian cavalry.
strength A: about 1,800 Prussians, 400 Russian cavalry (80 Cossacks), two 6-pounder batteries
strength B: about 3,100 (530 French, 500 Dutch and Rheinbund troops, 1,800 Poles, 260 gunners), 115 guns
losses A: 10 killed in the failed assault (others not given)
losses B: fortress and guns surrendered; 244 officers and 2,985 men marched out, 500 sick and wounded left behind
sources: de.wikipedia Festungskrieg (1813)
note: Bombardment 16–20 April; on 18 April a powder magazine exploded and breached the Bastion Königin; a night assault through the breach failed; the capitulation was agreed on 21 April (some accounts give 24 April).

name: Lüneburg
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Lüneburg, Lower Saxony
commanders A: Wilhelm von Dörnberg; Major Karl von Borcke (Prussians)
Prussian force: An infantry battalion (fusiliers under Major Karl von Borcke) and half a battery from Borstell's brigade in Dörnberg's Russian-Prussian flying corps; the fusiliers stormed a city gate.
losses A: 300 killed and wounded (46 of them Prussian)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lüneburg; de.wikipedia Sechster Koalitionskrieg
note: First Allied success of the campaign; armed citizens joined in, and Johanna Stegen carried ammunition to the Prussian fusiliers. Davout's advance forced the Allies out the next day.

name: Möckern
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Möckern, Dannigkow, Vehlitz and Zehdenick, east of Magdeburg
commanders A: Peter Wittgenstein (in command), Ludwig Yorck, Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow, Karl Ludwig von Borstell, Friedrich von Hünerbein; Berg (Russian)
Prussian force: Yorck's corps (Hünerbein's brigade at Dannigkow; Borstell, with the Russian Berg, at Vehlitz) and Bülow's troops at Zehdenick formed most of Wittgenstein's force.
losses B: 900–2,200 killed and wounded, up to 1,000 captured
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Möckern; de.wikipedia Sechster Koalitionskrieg
note: Wittgenstein in overall command, but the fighting was mainly Prussian; first battle of the War of Liberation. Eugène fell back behind the Elbe to Magdeburg. Not to be confused with Möckern near Leipzig (16 October 1813).

date: April 1813 (assault 17 April; lifted 20 April; blockade under Bülow in May until the armistice)
name: Wittenberg (siege, 1813)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Wittenberg (Lutherstadt Wittenberg), on the Elbe
commanders A: Jean François Cornu de La Poype (governor)
commanders B: Peter Wittgenstein, Friedrich von Kleist, Hans Karl von Diebitsch; Lt-Col. von Steinmetz (Prussian column)
Prussian force: Kleist commanded the investing force of Russian light troops, Jäger and Cossacks with Prussian units; the third assault column, under Lt-Col. von Steinmetz, was stopped at the Eichbusch.
losses B: more than the garrison (figure not given)
sources: de.wikipedia Belagerung von Wittenberg (1813/14); de.wikipedia Festungskrieg (1813)
note: Russian observation from 26 March; Kleist took over in early April. Wittgenstein's assault of 17 April took the outer suburbs only; the bombardment of 18–19 April and attacks on the bridgehead failed, and most troops left on 20 April. Dated by the assault, as the start of the investment is not exact. The renewed siege (September 1813 – storm of 13 January 1814, Tauentzien) is a separate entry.

name: Halle (1813)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Halle (Saale)
commanders A: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow
commanders B: Donatien de Rochambeau (19th Division, Lauriston's V Corps)
Prussian force: Bülow with about 4,500–5,000 men and 24 guns: 4½ East Prussian battalions (3rd East Prussian Regiment), a Jäger company, 9 squadrons (West Prussian Dragoons, hussars), with a grenadier battalion and the Queen's Dragoons in reserve.
strength B: about 5,000 (four battalions of the 135th Line, 6 guns)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Halle (1813); de.wikipedia Gefecht um Halle
note: Fought the morning of Lützen; the French were driven out by 9 a.m. but the defeat at Großgörschen made the gain worthless. Background (part of the same German article): on 28 April Kleist's 5,000 repulsed Lauriston's 10,000 at Halle, then gave it up when the French took Merseburg; the French entered on 30 April.

name: Lützen
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Großgörschen, Kleingörschen, Rahna and Kaja, south of Lützen, south-west of Leipzig
commanders A: Napoleon I, Michel Ney, Auguste de Marmont, Henri Gatien Bertrand, Jacques MacDonald, Eugène de Beauharnais
commanders B: Peter Wittgenstein (in command), Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, Ludwig Yorck, Gerhard von Scharnhorst (mortally wounded); Alexander I and Frederick William III present
Prussian force: Blücher's corps (18,500 infantry and 5,500 cavalry) opened the battle at Großgörschen, followed by Yorck's corps; Scharnhorst was mortally wounded.
losses B: at least 12,000 (8,500 Prussian, 3,500 Russian); estimates to 30,000
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lützen (1813); de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Großgörschen
note: German name Großgörschen. A French victory 'on points': the Prussians held part of the field overnight, then the Allies withdrew towards Dresden. Napoleon's army also had Italian and Rheinbund troops. Kleist's detachment fought at Leipzig (Lindenau) the same day.

name: Colditz
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Gersdorf (now part of Hartha), east of Colditz, Saxony
commanders A: Mikhail Miloradovich; Lt-Col. von Steinmetz (Prussian brigade)
commanders B: Eugène de Beauharnais (MacDonald ordering; divisions of Charpentier, Gérard, Fressinet; Latour-Maubourg's cavalry)
Prussian force: Steinmetz's brigade (Hünerbein's, of Yorck's corps; Hünerbein wounded) and the 2nd Leib-Hussars under Major von Kall, with Miloradovich's Russians as rear guard after Lützen.
losses A: 587 killed (250 Prussian, 337 Russian) and about 400 wounded
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Gersdorf; historyofwar.org Battle of Bautzen (Combat of Colditz)
note: German name Gefecht bei Gersdorf. Rear-guard action: no clear winner; Eugène failed to cut off Steinmetz or stop the retreat over Waldheim and broke off at 18:30.

name: Königswartha
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Königswartha, north of Bautzen, Upper Lusatia
commanders A: Michael Barclay de Tolly
Prussian force: Yorck's Prussian corps (5,673) belonged to Barclay's flanking force but fought the simultaneous action at Weißig (separate entry); the blow at Königswartha itself was Russian.
losses B: Peyri's Italian division largely destroyed; Generals Peyri, St Andrea, Martelli and Balathier captured
borderline: Prussian troops not engaged at Königswartha itself; listed because the operation was a joint Russian-Prussian one
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian troops not engaged at Königswartha itself; listed because the operation was a joint Russian-Prussian one. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: de.wikipedia Königswartha, Weißig (Lohsa), Schlacht bei Bautzen; historyofwar.org Battle of Bautzen
note: Peyri's division belonged to Bertrand's IV Corps (Kingdom of Italy troops). Ney's advance then forced Barclay and Yorck back behind the Spree.

name: Weißig
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Weißig (now part of Lohsa) and the Eichberg, north of Bautzen
commanders A: Jacques Lauriston (V Corps, of Ney's wing)
Prussian force: Yorck's corps of 5,673 men, part of Barclay's flanking force, fought at the Eichberg from about 14:00 to 21:00.
losses B: 13 officers and 246 men killed, 62 officers and 1,411 men wounded
sources: de.wikipedia Weißig (Lohsa) (Schlacht am Eichberg); de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Bautzen
note: Yorck met Lauriston's much larger force and withdrew at night to the Kreckwitz heights; the French advance on Bautzen was delayed by about seven hours. Often described together with Königswartha.

name: Bautzen
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Bautzen, Kreckwitz and Wurschen, Upper Lusatia
commanders A: Napoleon I, Michel Ney, Nicolas Oudinot, Jacques MacDonald, Auguste de Marmont, Jean-de-Dieu Soult, Édouard Mortier
commanders B: Peter Wittgenstein (in command, with Alexander I), Michael Barclay de Tolly, Mikhail Miloradovich, Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, Ludwig Yorck, Friedrich von Kleist; Frederick William III present
Prussian force: Three Prussian corps (Blücher, Yorck, Kleist) beside four Russian corps; Blücher held the Kreckwitz heights. Separate Prussian strength not found.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bautzen (1813); de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Bautzen; historyofwar.org Battle of Bautzen
note: Also called Wurschen. A costly French victory: the Allies retreated in good order and lost no trophies. Napoleon's army included Rheinbund and Italian contingents.

name: Haynau
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Haynau (now Chojnów), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher; Col. Florens von Bockum-Dolffs (killed)
Prussian force: Blücher's rear guard laid an ambush; about twenty squadrons of cavalry under Colonel Bockum-Dolffs (killed leading the charge) surprised and almost destroyed Maison's division.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Haynau; en.wikipedia German campaign of 1813
note: The en.wikipedia campaign article calls the attacking horse Landwehr cavalry. The victory raised the morale of the Prussian cavalry; it helped bring Napoleon to the armistice.

name: Hoyerswerda (1813)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Hoyerswerda, on the Black Elster, Upper Lusatia
commanders A: Nicolas Oudinot
Prussian force: Bülow's Prussian-Russian corps (about 30,000, of whom some 9,000 had been left before Wittenberg) attacked on both banks of the Black Elster and was repulsed.
sources: historyofwar.org Combat of Hoyerswerda; en.wikipedia Battle of Luckau
note: Some accounts date it 27 May. Bülow fell back towards Cottbus and then Luckau. Oudinot's XII Corps included Bavarian troops.

name: Nettelnburg
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Nettelnburg sluice on the Dove Elbe, by Bergedorf (now part of Hamburg)
commanders A: Lieutenant Colonel Karl August Ferdinand von Borcke (under Friedrich Karl von Tettenborn)
Prussian force: The fusilier battalion of the 1st Pomeranian Infantry Regiment (later Grenadier Regiment No. 2), brought up from Lüneburg under Borcke; its concealed rearguard broke the French attack with a bayonet charge and covered the retreat of Tettenborn's Russian-Prussian force.
borderline: A small rearguard action; named in the de.wikipedia navigation box for 1813 (between Reichenbach and Haynau).
doubts and flags: Borderline: A small rearguard action; named in the de.wikipedia navigation box for 1813 (between Reichenbach and Haynau).
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht an der Nettelnburger Schleuse (citing von Mach, Geschichte des Königlich Preußischen Zweiten Infanterie- genannt Königs-Regiments); de.wikipedia navigation box of the battles of the Wars of Liberation (spring campaign 1813)
note: The French moved out of Wilhelmsburg on 28 May to outflank Tettenborn at Bergedorf while he was negotiating his withdrawal from Hamburg; the fight came on 30 May as the Allies fell back towards Lauenburg. No strengths are given.

name: Luckau
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Luckau, Lower Lusatia
commanders A: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow; Prince Ludwig of Hesse-Homburg (Prussian brigade); Harpe (Russian brigade)
Prussian force: Bülow's corps (his own force 15,800), with a Prussian brigade under Prince Ludwig of Hesse-Homburg and a Russian brigade under Harpe and a Cossack regiment.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Luckau; historyofwar.org Combat of Luckau; de.wikipedia Sechster Koalitionskrieg
note: Fought on the day the Armistice of Pläswitz was signed. historyofwar.org dates it 6 June. Oudinot's XII Corps had Bavarian, Hesse-Darmstadt and Neapolitan units; it fell back towards Dresden.

name: Kitzen
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), during the Armistice of Pläswitz
place: near Kitzen (now part of Pegau), south-west of Leipzig
commanders A: François Fournier-Sarlovèze; Karl von Normann-Ehrenfels (Württembergers)
Prussian force: The Lützow Free Corps (Royal Prussian Free Corps), mainly its cavalry of about 400 under Major von Lützow, returning from a raid behind French lines; Theodor Körner was wounded.
strength A: Fournier: about 1,100 infantry, 420 horse, 3 guns; Normann: 2 squadrons, 2 companies, 3 guns
losses B: about 30 killed, 12 officers and about 70 men captured (Fournier); 10 officers and about 100 men captured (Normann); local account 105 killed, 90 captured
borderline: attack during the armistice
doubts and flags: Borderline: attack during the armistice.
sources: de.wikipedia Brigade Normann; de.wikipedia Lützowsches Freikorps; de.wikipedia Kitzen (Pegau)
note: Each side blamed the other for the first shot; Germans saw it as a breach of the armistice. The corps was scattered and most of the infantry escaped. Many of its volunteers were not Prussian, but it was a Prussian royal corps.

name: Löwenberg
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Löwenberg (now Lwówek Śląski), on the Bober (Bóbr), Lower Silesia
commanders A: Napoleon I; Michel Ney, Jacques Macdonald, Jacques Lauriston
commanders B: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher; Ludwig Yorck, Fabian von der Osten-Sacken
Prussian force: Blücher's Russo-Prussian Army of Silesia, with Yorck's Prussian I Corps and Sacken's Russians on the line of the Bober; Yorck was pushed back towards Goldberg.
sources: historyofwar.org, Combat of the Bobr or Lowenberg, 21 August 1813; en.wikipedia Combat of Goldberg
note: Also called the combat of the Bober. Napoleon forced the Bober crossings at Löwenberg and Bunzlau; Blücher's retreat was deliberate under the Trachenberg Plan (no battle with Napoleon in person), and Napoleon turned back towards Dresden.

name: Goldberg
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Goldberg (now Złotoryja) and the Wolfsberg heights, Lower Silesia
commanders A: Jacques Lauriston (Jacques Macdonald in command of the army)
commanders B: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher; Prince Karl of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, Alexandre de Langeron
Prussian force: The brigade of Prince Karl of Mecklenburg-Strelitz from Yorck's I Corps at Niederau, with Langeron's Russian corps on the Wolfsberg; Blücher in command of the Army of Silesia.
sources: en.wikipedia Combat of Goldberg; historyofwar.org, Combat of Goldberg, 23 August 1813
note: Lauriston's V Corps drove the Allies from Goldberg and the Wolfsberg; Blücher fell back behind the Katzbach, where he won three days later.

name: Großbeeren
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Großbeeren, south of Berlin
commanders A: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow (Charles John, Crown Prince of Sweden, commanding the Army of the North)
Prussian force: Bülow's Prussian III Corps (about 38,000 with its Swedish support, per en.wikipedia) attacked Reynier's mostly Saxon VII Corps on its own initiative; Tauentzien's IV Corps held off Bertrand at Blankenfelde the same day.
strength A: 32,000 and 82 guns engaged (en.wikipedia); about 100,000 in the Army of the North (de.wikipedia)
strength B: 18,000 and 68 guns engaged (en.wikipedia); about 75,000 in Oudinot's army (de.wikipedia)
losses A: about 1,100 killed, wounded and missing (de.wikipedia); en.wikipedia: 500 killed, 1,000 wounded, 300 missing or captured, 6 guns
losses B: about 3,000, including about 1,500 prisoners, and 14 guns
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Großbeeren; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Großbeeren
note: Fought within Bernadotte's Army of the North but by Bülow's Prussians, against Bernadotte's wishes; de.wikipedia calls it a Prussian victory. Blankenfelde (Tauentzien against Bertrand, same day) is treated by en.wikipedia as part of the battle, so it has no entry of its own.

name: Katzbach
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: On the Katzbach (Kaczawa) and the Wütende Neiße (Nysa Szalona) between Liegnitz (Legnica) and Jauer (Jawor), near Wahlstatt (Legnickie Pole)
commanders A: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher; Ludwig Yorck, Fabian von der Osten-Sacken, Alexandre de Langeron
Prussian force: Blücher commanded the Russo-Prussian Army of Silesia; Yorck's Prussian I Corps and Sacken's Russians fought on the plateau, where Hünerbein's brigade counter-attacked at about 3 p.m. and the Prussian and Russian cavalry broke the French.
losses A: 4,000 killed and wounded (de.wikipedia); about 1,000 in the battle itself (en.wikipedia)
losses B: 30,000 killed, wounded and captured and 103 guns, including the pursuit to 1 September
sources: de.wikipedia Schlacht an der Katzbach; en.wikipedia Battle of Katzbach
note: The strengths are those of the two armies; far fewer were engaged in the rain-soaked battle. Most French losses came in the pursuit, including Puthod's division forced to surrender at Plagwitz near Löwenberg on 29 August (to Langeron's Russians; no entry of its own). Blücher was made Prince of Wahlstatt.

name: Dresden (1813)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Dresden, Saxony
commanders A: Napoleon I; Joachim Murat, Auguste de Marmont, Michel Ney, Laurent de Gouvion Saint-Cyr
commanders B: Karl von Schwarzenberg; Michael Barclay de Tolly, Peter Wittgenstein, Friedrich von Kleist (Alexander I and Frederick William III present)
Prussian force: Kleist's Prussian II Corps, with Wittgenstein's Russians on the allied right; on 26 August it attacked the southern suburbs and was driven back by artillery and musketry. The Prussian Guard was in the reserve.
losses B: 38,000–40,000 (about 15,000 killed and wounded, 25,000 captured or missing), 40 guns, 15 colours
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Dresden; de.wikipedia Schlacht um Dresden
note: Napoleon's last great victory in Germany; Schwarzenberg's Army of Bohemia (Austrians, Russians and Prussians) retreated into Bohemia.

name: Gadebusch
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), campaign on the Lower Elbe 1813
place: Forest of Rosenow near Gadebusch, Mecklenburg
commanders A: Ludwig Adolf Wilhelm von Lützow
Prussian force: The Lützow Free Corps (a Prussian volunteer corps of about 3,000 infantry, 600 horse and eight guns in August 1813, under Wallmoden's command) fighting on its own; its poet-adjutant Theodor Körner was killed pursuing the enemy.
borderline: A small raid-sized action, notable for Körner's death; ADB names it 'das Gefecht bei Gadebusch am 26. August'.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A small raid-sized action, notable for Körner's death; ADB names it 'das Gefecht bei Gadebusch am 26. August'.
sources: Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie and Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Lützow, Adolf Freiherr von' (deutsche-biographie.de); en.wikipedia Theodor Körner (author); en.wikipedia Ludwig Adolf Wilhelm von Lützow
note: An attack on a French detachment (a supply convoy and its escort) in the Rosenow forest; Lützow's men 'distinguished themselves' (en.wikipedia, after the 1911 Britannica), but the sources found give no figures. Körner is buried at Wöbbelin.

name: Hagelberg
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Hagelberg, near Belzig (Bad Belzig), in the Fläming
commanders A: Karl Friedrich von Hirschfeld; Alexander Chernyshev (Cossacks)
Prussian force: Hirschfeld's division, mostly Kurmark Landwehr (about 10,000 infantry and fewer than 1,000 cavalry), with Chernyshev's Cossacks intervening.
sources: de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Hagelberg; en.wikipedia Battle of Hagelberg
note: Also called the Gefecht bei Lübnitz; the classic 'Landwehr battle'. Girard's column had marched out of Magdeburg against Berlin; Saxon units in it went over during the fighting.

name: Kulm
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Kulm (now Chlumec) near Teplitz (Teplice), northern Bohemia; Kleist came down from Nollendorf (Nakléřov)
commanders A: Alexander Ostermann-Tolstoy (wounded), Michael Barclay de Tolly, Hieronymus von Colloredo-Mansfeld, Friedrich von Kleist
Prussian force: Kleist's Prussian II Corps, descending from Nollendorf into Vandamme's rear on 30 August while Russians and Austrians attacked in front, completed the destruction of the French I Corps; Kleist was later styled 'Kleist von Nollendorf'.
strength A: 15,000–16,000 on 29 August; 103,000 in all on 30 August (en.wikipedia)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kulm; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Kulm; historyofwar.org, Battle of Kulm
note: On 29 August the Russian Guard under Ostermann-Tolstoy held Vandamme alone; the Prussian part was decisive on the second day (Nollendorf).

name: Zahna
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Zahna (now Zahna-Elster), north-east of Wittenberg
commanders A: Nicolas Oudinot (XII Corps), under Michel Ney
Prussian force: The advance guard of Tauentzien's IV Corps (largely Landwehr), which after a hard fight fell back towards Jüterbog.
sources: historyofwar.org, Combat of Zahna, 5 September 1813; historyofwar.org, Battle of Dennewitz
note: The prelude to Dennewitz the next day.

name: Dennewitz
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Dennewitz, near Jüterbog, south of Berlin
commanders A: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow, Bogislav von Tauentzien (Charles John, Crown Prince of Sweden, arrived late)
commanders B: Michel Ney; Nicolas Oudinot, Henri Bertrand, Jean Reynier
Prussian force: Bülow's III Corps and Tauentzien's IV Corps (much of it Landwehr); Tauentzien held the first attack and Bülow took command of both corps and stormed the Denkmalsberg; Russian and Swedish troops came up late and were lightly engaged.
strength A: 50,000 and 150 guns in battle (80,000–85,000 in the area)
strength B: 45,000–60,000 and 200 guns in battle (70,000 in the area)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Dennewitz; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Dennewitz
note: Fought within Bernadotte's Army of the North but essentially by the two Prussian corps; Bülow was made 'Graf Bülow von Dennewitz'.

name: Dahme
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Dahme (Dahme/Mark), Lower Lusatia
commanders A: General von Wobeser
Prussian force: A Prussian cavalry force under General von Wobeser, pursuing Ney's army the day after Dennewitz.
losses B: 3,200 prisoners (2,800 at Dahme, 400 in the pursuit of Bertrand)
borderline: A pursuit action; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A pursuit action; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
sources: historyofwar.org, Combat of Dahme, 7 September 1813
note: Raglovich's Bavarian division of Oudinot's XII Corps was also at Dahme; the source does not say whether it fought.

name: Wittenberg (siege, 1813–1814)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Wittenberg (Lutherstadt Wittenberg), on the Elbe
commanders A: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow (September–October 1813), Bogislav von Tauentzien, Leopold Wilhelm von Dobschütz (the storm)
commanders B: Jean François Cornu de La Poype
Prussian force: Bülow's III Corps reinforced by Hirschfeld's division (a besieging force of about 35,000) in September; from 23 October Dobschütz's force from Tauentzien's IV Corps, which stormed the fortress on the night of 12–13 January 1814.
losses A: 500–600 killed and wounded in the storm
losses B: remaining garrison (75 officers and 1,200 men) captured; 96 guns and 2 eagles taken
borderline: de.wikipedia treats it as one siege with the spring 1813 blockade (March–May 1813, entered separately).
doubts and flags: Borderline: de.wikipedia treats it as one siege with the spring 1813 blockade (March–May 1813, entered separately).
sources: de.wikipedia Belagerung von Wittenberg (1813/14); en.wikipedia Bogislav Friedrich Emanuel von Tauentzien
note: Chernyshev's light troops invested Wittenberg on 9 September; Bülow opened trenches on the night of 24–25 September; the siege was lifted in early October after Wartenburg (the French relieved the place on 11 October) and renewed on 23 October. Tauentzien was made 'Graf Tauentzien von Wittenberg'. de.wikipedia's infobox ends it on 14 January 1814.

name: Nollendorf
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Nollendorf (now Nakléřov), on the road from Dresden into Bohemia, and on to Berggießhübel
commanders A: Peter Wittgenstein
commanders B: Georges Mouton, comte de Lobau; François Dumonceau
Prussian force: The Russian and Prussian part of the Army of Bohemia under Wittgenstein (with Kleist's II Corps); the units engaged are not named in the source.
borderline: Prussian share not confirmed unit by unit; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian share not confirmed unit by unit; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
sources: historyofwar.org, Combat of Nollendorf, 14 September 1813
note: Wittgenstein drove Dumonceau's division, the advance guard of Lobau's I Corps, out of Nollendorf and pushed Lobau back from Berggießhübel; Napoleon's counter-attack followed on 15–17 September.

name: Berggießhübel
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Berggießhübel (now Bad Gottleuba-Berggießhübel), south of Pirna, Saxony
commanders A: Napoleon I; Georges Mouton, comte de Lobau, Gabriel Mouton-Duvernet
Prussian force: The Russian and Prussian part of the Army of Bohemia under Wittgenstein (with Kleist's II Corps); the units engaged are not named in the source.
borderline: Prussian share not confirmed unit by unit; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian share not confirmed unit by unit; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
sources: historyofwar.org, Combat of Berggiesshübel, 15 September 1813
note: Lobau's I Corps, Mouton-Duvernet's division and the Guard under Napoleon forced Wittgenstein back to Peterswalde.

name: Göhrde
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), campaign on the Lower Elbe 1813
place: Göhrde forest, near Dahlenburg, east of Lüneburg
commanders A: Ludwig von Wallmoden-Gimborn; Ludwig Adolf Wilhelm von Lützow (wounded)
Prussian force: The Lützow Free Corps (Prussian), part of Wallmoden's mixed corps; Lützow was badly wounded leading his cavalry against a French square, and Eleonore Prochaska, serving disguised in its ranks, was mortally wounded.
borderline: Role uncertain: the Lützow Free Corps numbered about 3,600 in August 1813 (NDB); if most of it fought, the Prussian share approaches a quarter of Wallmoden's 12,300 and the role would be 'major ally'.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Role uncertain: the Lützow Free Corps numbered about 3,600 in August 1813 (NDB); if most of it fought, the Prussian share approaches a quarter of Wallmoden's 12,300 and the role would be 'major ally'. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of the Göhrde; de.wikipedia Schlacht an der Göhrde; Neue Deutsche Biographie and ADB, 'Lützow, Adolf Freiherr von'
note: Wallmoden's corps (Russian-German Legion, Hanoverians, King's German Legion, Mecklenburgers, the Hanseatic Legion of Hamburg and Lübeck, Swedes and the Lützowers) belonged to Bernadotte's Army of the North; 'Other German states' = the Hanseatic Legion.

name: Peterswalde (1813)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Peterswalde (now Petrovice), on the road from Dresden into Bohemia
commanders A: Napoleon I
Prussian force: The Russian and Prussian part of the Army of Bohemia under Wittgenstein (with Kleist's II Corps); the units engaged are not named in the source.
borderline: Prussian share not confirmed unit by unit; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian share not confirmed unit by unit; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
sources: historyofwar.org, Combat of Peterswalde, 16 September 1813
note: The Guard cavalry and the Polish light horse of the Guard drove Wittgenstein from the heights north of Peterswalde down onto the Bohemian plain.

name: Dolnitz
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Dolnitz and Arbesau (now Varvažov), east of Kulm (Chlumec), northern Bohemia
commanders A: Karl von Schwarzenberg
Prussian force: Part of the Army of Bohemia, whose Prussian (Kleist's II Corps), Russian and Austrian troops faced Napoleon's thrust on the Kulm plain; the units engaged are not named in the source, apart from an Austrian battery.
borderline: Prussian share not confirmed; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked. Also called the action at Arbesau or the second battle of Kulm.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian share not confirmed; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked. Also called the action at Arbesau or the second battle of Kulm.
sources: historyofwar.org, Combat of Dolnitz, 17 September 1813
note: Mouton-Duvernet took Arbesau and the Guard's Red Lancers overran an Austrian battery, but allied counter-attacks on the French left made Napoleon recall his troops; he left Bohemia the next day. Outcome judged as an allied success because the French withdrew.

name: Bischofswerda
