war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Bischofswerda, between Dresden and Bautzen
commanders A: Napoleon I; Jean-Baptiste Girard (advance guard)
Prussian force: The advance guards of Blücher's Russo-Prussian Army of Silesia; the units engaged are not named in the source.
borderline: Whether Prussian or Russian troops of Blücher's advance guard fought is not stated; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Whether Prussian or Russian troops of Blücher's advance guard fought is not stated; named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
sources: historyofwar.org, Combat of Bischofswerda, 22 September 1813
note: A minor French success: Napoleon with II and XI Corps took Bischofswerda and pushed Blücher's advance guards back; Blücher withdrew next day and Napoleon soon gave up the east bank of the Elbe.

name: Altenburg
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
theatre: Saxony and Thuringia (raids behind the French lines)
place: Altenburg, Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg (Thuringia)
commanders A: Johann von Thielmann (in Russian service), Emmanuel von Mensdorff-Pouilly, Matvei Platov
Prussian force: Prussian raiding detachments (Streifkorps) under Majors Peter von Colomb and Count Hermann von Pückler-Muskau rode with Thielmann's, Mensdorff's and Platov's Cossack, Saxon and Austrian light horse.
losses B: 600 killed and wounded and 1,000–1,400 prisoners (en.wikipedia); about 1,500 prisoners, 3 standards and 5 guns (de.wikipedia)
borderline: The Prussian share was a small raiding detachment; Thielmann's Streifkorps itself was mostly Cossacks.
doubts and flags: Borderline: The Prussian share was a small raiding detachment; Thielmann's Streifkorps itself was mostly Cossacks. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Altenburg; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Altenburg
note: Thielmann was a Saxon general who had gone over to the Allies; Lefebvre-Desnouettes's cavalry division was routed.

name: Torgau (siege, 1813–1814)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Torgau, on the Elbe
commanders A: Bogislav von Tauentzien
Prussian force: Tauentzien's IV Corps, about 20,000.
losses B: about 4,200 went into captivity on 10 January 1814, with about 3,000 more in the hospitals
borderline: Start date not verified (the investment followed the Battle of Leipzig); the garrison was ruined more by typhus than by the siege.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Start date not verified (the investment followed the Battle of Leipzig); the garrison was ruined more by typhus than by the siege.
sources: de.wikipedia Belagerung von Torgau; en.wikipedia Bogislav Friedrich Emanuel von Tauentzien
note: The garrison capitulated on 23 December 1813 (de.wikipedia; en.wikipedia says Tauentzien accepted the capitulation on 26 December) and marched out on 10 January 1814.

name: Wartenburg
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Wartenburg (now part of Kemberg) and Bleddin, on the Elbe south-east of Wittenberg
commanders A: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, Ludwig Yorck
Prussian force: Yorck's I Corps (about 16,000) crossed the Elbe on pontoon bridges; after Steinmetz's frontal attack failed, Prince Karl of Mecklenburg took Bleddin and Horn's brigades rolled up Bertrand's line.
losses A: 2,100 (en.wikipedia); 1,548 men and 67 officers killed and wounded (de.wikipedia)
losses B: 1,900–2,000 and 13 guns (en.wikipedia); 1,000–1,200 killed and wounded and 1,000 prisoners (de.wikipedia)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Wartenburg; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Wartenburg
note: Bertrand's IV Corps included Franquemont's Württemberg division (which held Bleddin) and an Italian division of the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy. Yorck became 'Graf Yorck von Wartenburg'.

name: Dessau
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Dessau, on the Mulde just south of the Elbe
commanders A: Michel Ney; Antoine Guillaume Delmas
Prussian force: An isolated Prussian division of Tauentzien's IV Corps (Army of the North), which defended the town stubbornly before giving way.
borderline: Named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Named only in the historyofwar.org series among the sources checked.
sources: historyofwar.org, Combat of Dessau, 12 October 1813; historyofwar.org, Leipzig campaign
note: Delmas's 9th Division of Ney's III Corps beat the Prussians; Tauentzien and Thümen then fell back north towards Berlin and missed Leipzig, while Reynier briefly relieved Wittenberg.

name: Liebertwolkwitz
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Liebertwolkwitz, Wachau and Güldengossa, south-east of Leipzig
commanders A: Peter Wittgenstein; Friedrich von Kleist
Prussian force: Kleist's II Corps with Röder's Prussian reserve cavalry; several Prussian cavalry regiments charged south of Güldengossa and at Wachau and Markkleeberg.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Liebertwolkwitz; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Liebertwolkwitz; historyofwar.org, Battle of Liebertwolkwitz
note: A reconnaissance in force by Wittgenstein's advance guard (with Austrian troops) against Murat two days before Leipzig, famous for its great cavalry fight; indecisive, listed separately from Leipzig by de.wikipedia's campaign box.

name: Leipzig
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Leipzig and its surroundings (Wachau, Markkleeberg, Möckern, Lindenau, Probstheida, Paunsdorf, Schönefeld), Saxony
allies B: Duchy of Warsaw; Saxony; Württemberg; Baden; Hesse-Darmstadt; Other German states
commanders A: Karl von Schwarzenberg; Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, Michael Barclay de Tolly, Levin von Bennigsen, Charles John (Crown Prince of Sweden); Alexander I, Francis I and Frederick William III present
commanders B: Napoleon I; Joachim Murat, Michel Ney, Auguste de Marmont, Jacques Macdonald, Józef Poniatowski (killed)
Prussian force: Three Prussian corps in three allied armies: Kleist's II Corps (with the Bohemian Army at Markkleeberg, Wachau and Probstheida), Yorck's I Corps (Blücher's Army of Silesia, at Möckern on 16 October) and Bülow's III Corps (Army of the North, at Paunsdorf and in the storm of the city on 18–19 October); Blücher commanded the Army of Silesia.
strength A: 205,000 and 918 guns on 16 October, 365,000 and 1,500 guns on 19 October (de.wikipedia); en.wikipedia: 257,000 (16–17 October), 359,000 (18–19 October)
losses A: 54,000 killed and wounded (official allied figure 53,804), of them about 16,600 Prussians (de.wikipedia; en.wikipedia gives 54,000–80,000)
losses B: 72,000: 38,000 killed and wounded, 30,000 prisoners, 5,000 deserters, and 300 guns (de.wikipedia)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Leipzig; de.wikipedia Völkerschlacht bei Leipzig; historyofwar.org, Battle of Leipzig
note: The Battle of the Nations; one entry for all four days. The Saxon and Württemberg troops went over to the Allies on 18 October. 'Other German states' = Napoleon's remaining Confederation of the Rhine contingents. Liebertwolkwitz (14 October) has its own entry. Yorck's storm of Möckern on 16 October (the northern sector against Marmont; about 7,000-8,000 Prussian losses; 2,000 prisoners, 40 guns and an eagle taken) is counted within this entry, like Wachau and Lindenau.

name: Freyburg
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Freyburg (Unstrut), at the crossing of the Unstrut
commanders A: Napoleon I (rearguard of the retreating army)
Prussian force: Yorck's I Corps of the Army of Silesia, pursuing after Leipzig, attacked the French rearguard covering the Unstrut crossing.
borderline: A rearguard action that historyofwar.org calls a 'minor affair'.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A rearguard action that historyofwar.org calls a 'minor affair'.
sources: historyofwar.org, Combat of Kosen, 21 October 1813; historyofwar.org, War of Liberation 1813
note: The French fought off Yorck's attack and completed the crossing intact; the same day Bertrand held off Gyulai's Austrians at Kösen on the Saale (no Prussians, no entry).

name: Erfurt (siege, 1813–1814)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), autumn campaign 1813
place: Erfurt, with the citadels of the Petersberg and the Cyriaksburg
commanders A: Friedrich von Kleist
Prussian force: Kleist's II Corps, with Austrian and Russian troops under his command, blockaded and bombarded Erfurt from late October 1813 until Kleist marched into France in early 1814.
borderline: Mainly a blockade and bombardment (the Petersberg was shelled on 6 November 1813).
doubts and flags: Borderline: Mainly a blockade and bombardment (the Petersberg was shelled on 6 November 1813).
sources: en.wikipedia Principality of Erfurt; en.wikipedia Friedrich Graf Kleist von Nollendorf
note: D'Alton signed a capitulation for the town on 20 December 1813 and withdrew to the Petersberg and the Cyriaksburg; the Allies entered the town on 6 January 1814, and the citadels capitulated in May 1814 (en.wikipedia gives 5 May 1814 as the end).

date: 21 November 1813 – April 1814 (handed over after the armistice of 23 April 1814)
name: Delfzijl (siege)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), campaign in the Netherlands 1813–1814
place: Delfzijl, on the Ems estuary (Dollart), with the besiegers in Appingedam, Termunterzijl and the surrounding villages, Groningen
commanders A: Major Karl Friedrich Friccius (Prussian, sent by Bülow); Colonel Marcus Busch and later Lieutenant Colonel Falkenberg (Dutch national guards)
Prussian force: Major Friccius's detachment of 400 men and 50 horses from Bülow's III Corps, which raised the East Frisian Landsturm (30 companies of about 80, armed with pikes), with Captain von Sydow's musketeers and Rittmeister von Blanckenburg's cavalry (from 12 December); Bülow withdrew the regulars on 1 January 1814 and the remaining Prussians on 6 February.
strength A: Friccius's 400 men and 50 horses, the Landsturm, Groningen national guards and Cossacks of Wintzingerode's army; besieger totals not given
strength B: about 1,500 and 270 guns at first; about 800 by the end of 1813
borderline: Prussian share uncertain and limited to the first half: the Prussians left on 6 February 1814 and the Dutch kept up the blockade until the handover; could be rated 'contingent'. Mostly a blockade, but with sorties repulsed while the Prussians were present.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian share uncertain and limited to the first half: the Prussians left on 6 February 1814 and the Dutch kept up the blockade until the handover; could be rated 'contingent'. Mostly a blockade, but with sorties repulsed while the Prussians were present.
sources: de.wikipedia Belagerung von Delfzijl (1813–1814); en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Sixth Coalition
note: Friccius and Busch set up a joint headquarters at Appingedam on 17 December; French sorties were repulsed on 17 and 25 December; further sorties on 16 January, 5 February and 3 March 1814 (the last destroyed several siege guns). British frigates blockaded the port from 6 December. en.wikipedia's list dates the siege 13 November 1813 – 23 May 1814 and calls it a Coalition victory; outcome given to the besiegers because the place was handed over, though only after the armistice. 'Netherlands' = the Sovereign Principality of the United Netherlands (as in the Breda 1813 entry).

name: Doesburg
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), campaign in the Netherlands 1813–1814
place: Doesburg, on the IJssel, Gelderland
commanders A: Adolf Friedrich von Oppen
Prussian force: Oppen's advance guard of Bülow's III Corps, 3,000 men, stormed the town 'without much trouble'.
borderline: A small storm described within the en.wikipedia Arnhem article rather than as a battle of its own.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A small storm described within the en.wikipedia Arnhem article rather than as a battle of its own.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Arnhem (1813)
note: Cossacks had seized Doesburg and Amey's 2,000-man French task force had retaken it before Oppen's attack; Zutphen surrendered to Bülow the next day without a fight (no entry).

name: Arnhem
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), campaign in the Netherlands 1813–1814
place: Arnhem, Gelderland
commanders A: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow; Adolf Friedrich von Oppen
Prussian force: About 10,000 of Bülow's III Corps (Oppen's advance guard reinforced by Krafft's and Thümen's brigades) stormed the entrenched town.
losses B: 1,500 killed, wounded and captured, and 14–15 guns
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Arnhem (1813)
note: A Prussian assault on 29 November had failed; the storm of 30 November opened the Netherlands to the Allies. Bülow's whole corps then numbered about 30,000 with 96 guns.

name: Gorinchem (siege, 1813–1814)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), campaign in the Netherlands 1813–1814
place: Gorinchem (Gorkum), on the Merwede, South Holland
commanders A: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow (III Corps)
Prussian force: Troops of Bülow's Prussian III Corps besieged and bombarded the fortress.
borderline: Start date not verified: a Dutch source speaks of a three-month siege with bombardment in the winter of 1813–14; Dutch forces may also have taken part.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Start date not verified: a Dutch source speaks of a three-month siege with bombardment in the winter of 1813–14; Dutch forces may also have taken part.
sources: en.wikipedia Antoine-Guillaume Rampon; en.wikipedia Siege of Breda (1813); coehoorn.nl, Gorinchem en Sleeuwijk (2025)
note: Rampon held Gorinchem until 7 February 1814, when he surrendered to the Prussians (en.wikipedia).

name: Breda (siege, 1813)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation), campaign in the Netherlands 1813–1814
place: Breda, North Brabant
commanders A: Van der Plaat, Stahl, Alexander Chechensky, Major von Colomb
Prussian force: A Prussian raiding detachment (Streifkorps) under Major von Colomb that entered the town during the siege; Bülow's corps arrived afterwards.
strength A: about 1,200 infantry (including Phaff's regiment and 500 Breda militia), 170 hussars, 4 guns (9 from 20 December)
borderline: Prussian share a small Streifkorps; the defence was mainly Russian and Dutch.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian share a small Streifkorps; the defence was mainly Russian and Dutch. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Breda (1813)
note: Cossacks had taken Breda unopposed on 10 December; the French attempt to retake it from Antwerp failed. 'United Netherlands' is the Sovereign Principality proclaimed in December 1813 (new entity name).

name: Hoogstraten
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Hoogstraten, north-east of Antwerp (Antwerpen)
commanders A: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow, Thomas Graham (covering the flank), Ferdinand von Wintzingerode (detached Russian division)
commanders B: François Roguet, Jean-Jacques Ambert, Charles Lefebvre-Desnouettes
Prussian force: Bülow's III Corps; Borstell's brigade led the attack and took most of the Prussian losses, with Thümen's and Krafft's brigades and Oppen's cavalry in support. Hoogstraten fell to the Prussians about 2 p.m.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Hoogstraten; en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Sixth Coalition
note: Graham's British Expeditionary Corps covered the Prussian right flank; the fighting was essentially Prussian.

name: Metz (siege, 1814)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Metz and its outskirts (Lorry-lès-Metz, Woippy, Moulins-lès-Metz), Moselle
commanders A: Pierre François Durutte
commanders B: Prince Wilhelm of Prussia (January), Nikolay Borozdin, Dmitri Yuzefovich, Moritz von Müller (Kurhessian brigade)
Prussian force: Prussian cavalry of Yorck's I Corps invested Metz by 13 January, then Prince Wilhelm's 8th Brigade (west bank) and Warburg's 2nd Brigade (east bank); a French sortie retook Lorry on 23 January. Yorck's corps was sent west on 25 January and the blockade passed to Russian and later Kurhessian troops.
borderline: Mostly a blockade; the Prussians were the investing force only in its first two weeks, and the later fighting (Durutte's sorties of 24 March-4 April) was against Hessians.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Mostly a blockade; the Prussians were the investing force only in its first two weeks, and the later fighting (Durutte's sorties of 24 March-4 April) was against Hessians. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Metz (1814); en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Sixth Coalition
note: Start date 13 January in the infobox, 17 January in the text and the list. Ended by negotiation on 10 April after Napoleon's fall; Wikipedia calls it a French victory (the fortress was never taken). Role set to contingent because the Prussian share of the whole operation was small and brief.

name: Merxem
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Merxem (now Merksem, part of Antwerp) and Wijnegem, north-east of Antwerp
commanders A: Thomas Graham, Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow
commanders B: Nicolas Joseph Maison (I Corps), François Roguet
Prussian force: Part of Bülow's III Corps, attacking toward Wijnegem while Graham's British attacked Merxem.
borderline: Named 'Battle of Merxem' in Bülow's conflict list (no article); en.wikipedia's Siege of Antwerp only describes Bülow's attack toward Wijnegem on 13 January.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Named 'Battle of Merxem' in Bülow's conflict list (no article); en.wikipedia's Siege of Antwerp only describes Bülow's attack toward Wijnegem on 13 January.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Antwerp (1814); en.wikipedia Friedrich Wilhelm Freiherr von Bülow (conflict list: 'Battle of Merxem')
note: Outcome mixed: the British drove the French out of Merxem, but en.wikipedia says Bülow's attack toward Wijnegem was repulsed, and the Allies did not press on to Antwerp. The second Allied attack on Merxem (31 January-6 February) is folded into the siege entry.

name: Antwerp (siege, 1814)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Antwerp (Antwerpen) and its northern suburbs (Merksem, Deurne)
commanders A: Thomas Graham, Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow (to early February), Duke Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar (from February)
commanders B: Lazare Carnot (governor from February), Nicolas Joseph Maison (field army)
Prussian force: Bülow's III Corps in the January operations against Antwerp, with Graham's British; Bülow then marched into France and handed command in Belgium to the Duke of Saxe-Weimar.
losses A: about 1,500 in the 31 January-6 February attack
losses B: about 500 in the 31 January-6 February attack
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Antwerp (1814); en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Sixth Coalition
note: Result inconclusive (en.wikipedia; the list calls it a Coalition victory): the British bombardment of 2-5 February failed and the Allies fell back to a blockade; Carnot held Antwerp until an armistice after Napoleon's abdication and handed it over on 4 May. en.wikipedia credits the February bombardment to the British; Prussian support for that attack is uncertain.

name: Jülich (siege)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Jülich fortress on the Roer, with the besiegers at Schloss Hambach, Broich, Kirchberg, Bourheim and Aldenhoven
commanders A: Coalition commanders varied (de.wikipedia names none for the Lützow Free Corps); Cossacks under Alexei Ilovaisky at first
Prussian force: The Lützow Free Corps (a Prussian volunteer corps, about 2,900 infantry, 600 cavalry and 120 artillery in 1814) arrived on 17 February, began the siege proper from Schloss Hambach and repulsed the sorties towards Karthaus on 24 and 26 February; it was soon relieved by Swedish troops.
strength A: various (150 Cossacks at first, then the Lützow Free Corps, Swedish, Danish and Mecklenburg troops; about 4,000 Saxons took over the fortress)
losses A: Lützow Free Corps: 12 wounded on 24 February, 2 killed in the following sortie
losses B: about 100 killed on 24 February; 2,500 marched out at the capitulation; typhus killed up to 2,000 people in the town (including 300 citizens)
borderline: Essentially a blockade with six sorties and brief bombardments; the Prussian Lützowers besieged only for part of it (from 17 February until relieved by Swedes) and the place was handed over after Napoleon's abdication, not taken.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Essentially a blockade with six sorties and brief bombardments; the Prussian Lützowers besieged only for part of it (from 17 February until relieved by Swedes) and the place was handed over after Napoleon's abdication, not taken.
sources: de.wikipedia Belagerung von Jülich (1814); de.wikipedia Lützowsches Freikorps
note: News of the fall of Paris and the abdication arrived on 28 April; the garrison raised a white flag on 29 April and marched out with arms and nine guns on 4 May, when Saxon troops (three line and two Landwehr battalions) entered. Outcome given to the besiegers because the place was handed over (as for Magdeburg 1813–1814). The Danes served as allies of the Coalition after the Treaty of Kiel.

name: Brienne
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Brienne-le-Château, Aube
commanders A: Napoleon I, Michel Ney, Claude-Victor Perrin, Auguste de Marmont
commanders B: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, Fabian von Osten-Sacken, Zakhar Olsufiev
Prussian force: Blücher and his chief of staff Gneisenau commanded the Army of Silesia's troops on the field and were nearly captured at the château; all the units named in the fighting were Russian (Olsufiev, Sacken, Pahlen's cavalry).
borderline: Prussian command (Blücher) but no Prussian units engaged; listed because standard works and Wikipedia give Prussia as a belligerent.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian command (Blücher) but no Prussian units engaged; listed because standard works and Wikipedia give Prussia as a belligerent. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Brienne; en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Sixth Coalition
note: Napoleon took Brienne and the château, but Blücher withdrew in order to Trannes; en.wikipedia discusses the result at length, the list calls it a French victory.

name: La Rothière
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: La Rothière, north of Bar-sur-Aube, Aube
commanders A: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher (tactical command), Karl Philipp zu Schwarzenberg (overall), Fabian von Osten-Sacken, Ignác Gyulai, Crown Prince William of Württemberg, Karl Philipp von Wrede
Prussian force: Blücher had tactical command of the Allied army; the only Prussian unit named on the field is Prince Biron of Courland's Prussian cavalry brigade in Sacken's command, covering the gap between Sacken and the Crown Prince of Württemberg.
borderline: Prussian command (Blücher) but only one Prussian cavalry brigade present; Yorck's and Kleist's corps were elsewhere.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian command (Blücher) but only one Prussian cavalry brigade present; Yorck's and Kleist's corps were elsewhere. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of La Rothière; en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Sixth Coalition
note: Fought mainly by Sacken's Russians, Gyulai's Austrians, the Württemberg IV Corps and Wrede's Austro-Bavarian V Corps. The infobox does not label strength and loss figures by side; assigned by order.

name: La Chaussée
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: La Chaussée-sur-Marne, south-east of Châlons-sur-Marne (now Châlons-en-Champagne), Marne
commanders A: Ludwig Yorck von Wartenburg
Prussian force: Yorck's I Corps (its advance guard and cavalry) pursuing Macdonald's XI Corps down the Marne toward Châlons.
borderline: Minor named action ('combat de La Chaussée') from standard narratives; could not be verified online; no figures.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Minor named action ('combat de La Chaussée') from standard narratives; could not be verified online; no figures.
sources: Petre, Napoleon at Bay, 1814 (1914); Leggiere, Blücher: Scourge of Napoleon (2014) (from knowledge, not verified online)
note: Macdonald's rearguard was pushed back on Châlons, which he evacuated two days later.

name: Châlons-sur-Marne
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Châlons-sur-Marne (now Châlons-en-Champagne), Marne
commanders A: Ludwig Yorck von Wartenburg
Prussian force: Yorck's I Corps attacked and bombarded Châlons and forced Macdonald to evacuate the town on 5 February.
borderline: Listed as an engagement ('Châlons, 5 Feb') by napoleon-empire.org; fighting limited to an attack on the suburbs and a bombardment before Macdonald withdrew.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Listed as an engagement ('Châlons, 5 Feb') by napoleon-empire.org; fighting limited to an attack on the suburbs and a bombardment before Macdonald withdrew.
sources: napoleon-empire.org, Campaign of France 1814: military operations; Petre, Napoleon at Bay, 1814 (1914) (from knowledge)
note: Date 5 February in napoleon-empire.org (the evacuation); the Prussian attack and bombardment were on 4 February.

name: Montmirail
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: east of Montmirail (Marchais-en-Brie, L'Épine-aux-Bois, Fontenelle), Marne
commanders A: Napoleon I
commanders B: Fabian von Osten-Sacken, Ludwig Yorck von Wartenburg
Prussian force: Part of Yorck's I Corps, about 9,000 men and 16 guns: Pirch's 1st and Horn's 7th Brigades and the reserve cavalry, arriving at Fontenelle about 3 p.m. to help Sacken.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Montmirail; Petre, Napoleon at Bay (1914) and Nafziger as cited there
note: Nafziger gives 877 losses for the Prussian 1st Brigade alone.

name: Château-Thierry
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Château-Thierry and the heights to the south (Les Caquerets, Viffort, Montfaucon), Aisne
commanders A: Napoleon I
commanders B: Ludwig Yorck von Wartenburg, Fabian von Osten-Sacken
Prussian force: Yorck's I Corps, about 17,000, formed the main rearguard line: Katzler's advance guard, Horn's 7th Brigade, Prince Wilhelm's brigade and Jürgass's reserve cavalry; Stockhausen's 400 East Prussians were cut off when the Marne bridge was destroyed.
losses B: 2,751-3,000 and 9 guns (Prussians 1,251 and 6 guns, Russians 1,500 and 3 guns)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Château-Thierry (1814); en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Sixth Coalition
note: A rearguard battle fought jointly by Yorck's Prussians and Sacken's Russians; role set to principal because Yorck's corps held the main line and took the brunt, but it could be scored as major ally.

name: Vauchamps
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Vauchamps, Janvilliers and the road to Champaubert and Étoges, east of Montmirail, Marne
commanders A: Napoleon I, Auguste de Marmont, Emmanuel de Grouchy
commanders B: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, Friedrich von Kleist, Pyotr Kaptsevich
Prussian force: Blücher in command with Kleist's II Corps, about 13,500 men, beside Kaptsevich's Russian X Corps (6,500) and the remnant of the IX Corps (1,500); the army retreated in squares under repeated cavalry attack.
losses B: 9,000-10,000 (Kleist's corps 1,250-3,500 killed, wounded and missing plus 2,000 prisoners)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Vauchamps (citing Mir and Pigeard)
note: Includes the night action at Étoges, where Doumerc's cuirassiers captured Prince Urusov and about 600 Russians. Loss figures vary widely between Mir and Pigeard.

name: Méry-sur-Seine
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Méry-sur-Seine, north-west of Troyes, Aube
commanders A: Fabian von Osten-Sacken (Shcherbatov's VI Corps), detachment of Yorck's I Corps; Blücher commanding the Army of Silesia
commanders B: Nicolas Oudinot, Pierre François Joseph Boyer
Prussian force: 1,200 Prussians from Yorck's I Corps beside 5,000 Russians of Shcherbatov's VI Corps.
borderline: No article of its own in English or German Wikipedia; named as the Battle of Méry-sur-Seine in the campaign article.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No article of its own in English or German Wikipedia; named as the Battle of Méry-sur-Seine in the campaign article. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Laubressel (background section); en.wikipedia Campaign in north-east France (1814)
note: The French cleared Méry and gained the far bank but were thrown back; Schwarzenberg then withdrew behind the Seine. The campaign article dates it 21 February. Prussians about a fifth of the Allied force: borderline between contingent and major ally.

name: Gué-à-Tresmes
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Gué-à-Tresmes (Congis-sur-Thérouanne) and Lizy-sur-Ourcq, north-east of Meaux, Seine-et-Marne
commanders A: Auguste de Marmont, Édouard Mortier
Prussian force: Kleist's II Corps fought the main action, with Katzler's advance guard at Lizy and Zieten's reconnaissance toward May-en-Multien on 2 March; Kaptsevich's Russian corps supported. Yorck's I Corps did not engage.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Gué-à-Tresmes; en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Sixth Coalition
note: Includes the fights at Lizy, Neufchelles, May-en-Multien and Mareuil (28 February-2 March).

name: Soissons (siege, 1814)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Soissons, Aisne
commanders A: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow, Ferdinand von Wintzingerode
Prussian force: Bülow's III Corps (16,900 a week later at Laon) attacked from the north bank while Wintzingerode's Russian corps closed in from the south.
borderline: Short siege: a bombardment and attacks on the outskirts on 2 March, then capitulation on 3 March.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Short siege: a bombardment and attacks on the outskirts on 2 March, then capitulation on 3 March.
sources: historyofwar.org, Bülow von Dennewitz; napoleon-series.org, Prussian generals (Bülow); napoleon-empire.org, Campaign of France 1814; de.wikipedia Belagerung von Soissons (listed in the Winterfeldzug navigation box; page not readable here)
note: Moreau's garrison (largely Poles of the Vistula Legion) capitulated on 3 March and marched out with honours, giving Blücher the Aisne bridge. Strengths and losses not found in a source available here. The Russian capture of 14 February (Chernyshev) and the French attack of 5 March on Rudzevich's Russian garrison had no Prussians and are excluded.

name: Craonne
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: plateau of Craonne (Chemin des Dames), Aisne
commanders A: Napoleon I, Michel Ney, Étienne de Nansouty
commanders B: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, Ferdinand von Wintzingerode, Mikhail Vorontsov (on the field), Fabian von Osten-Sacken
Prussian force: No Prussian unit fought: Vorontsov's Russians held the plateau with Sacken's guns; Kleist's II Corps and Yorck's reserve cavalry were on the failed flank march with Wintzingerode, and Blücher left the field about 10 a.m. to find that column.
borderline: Prussian command (Blücher) and Prussian corps on the flank march, but no Prussian units engaged; listed because Wikipedia gives Prussia as a belligerent.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian command (Blücher) and Prussian corps on the flank march, but no Prussian units engaged; listed because Wikipedia gives Prussia as a belligerent. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Craonne; en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Sixth Coalition
note: French victory at heavy cost (called Pyrrhic by two historians); the Allies fell back on Laon.

name: Laon
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Laon, with Athies-sous-Laon, Ardon, Semilly and Clacy, Aisne
commanders A: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, August von Gneisenau, Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow, Ludwig Yorck von Wartenburg, Friedrich von Kleist, Ferdinand von Wintzingerode, Alexandre de Langeron, Fabian von Osten-Sacken
commanders B: Napoleon I, Auguste de Marmont, Michel Ney
Prussian force: Three Prussian corps, about 41,000 of Blücher's 103,800: Bülow's III Corps (16,900) held Laon and Semilly and retook Ardon; Yorck's I (13,500) and Kleist's II Corps (10,600) at Athies routed Marmont's corps in the night bayonet attack of 9/10 March.
losses B: 6,000-7,500, and 45 guns and 120 caissons lost by Marmont
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Laon; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Laon
note: Blücher fell ill on 9 March and Gneisenau carried the command. Includes the night attack at Athies (not a separate entry).

name: Reims
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Reims and the villages to the west (Rosnay, Gueux, Ormes), Marne
commanders A: Napoleon I, Auguste de Marmont, Michel Ney (13 March); Jean Lacoste-Duvivier (12 March, captured)
commanders B: Emmanuel de Saint-Priest (mortally wounded), Georgi Emmanuel, Friedrich von Jagow
Prussian force: Jagow's Prussian brigade (Landwehr infantry and cavalry, two batteries), 4,000-5,600 men in Saint-Priest's corps; it shared the surprise capture of Reims on 12 March and lost about 1,300 men and 10 guns on 13 March.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Reims (1814) (citing Digby Smith and Nafziger); de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Reims (title)
note: Two days: on 12 March the Allies took Reims by surprise from 3,000-4,000 National Guards; on 13 March Napoleon retook it. Outcome given for the battle of 13 March. Nafziger's returns put Jagow's brigade at about half Smith's 5,600.

name: Fère-Champenoise
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Fère-Champenoise, Soudé, Connantray, Bannes and Morains, Marne
commanders A: Alexander I, Karl Philipp zu Schwarzenberg, Grand Duke Constantine, Frederick William III, Crown Prince William of Württemberg, Michael Barclay de Tolly, Illarion Vasilchikov
commanders B: Auguste de Marmont, Édouard Mortier, Michel-Marie Pacthod
Prussian force: Frederick William III present with the Tsar; Nafziger's order of battle lists 800 Prussian Guards with 8 guns and Alexander ordered the Prussian Guard cavalry in; Zieten's Prussian reserve cavalry arrived only after the fighting.
doubts and flags: Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Fère-Champenoise; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Fère-Champenoise
note: Fought mainly by Russian, Württemberg and Austrian cavalry and, against Pacthod's and Amey's divisions, by the Russian cavalry of the Army of Silesia (Vasilchikov, Korff); de.wikipedia names no Prussian unit in the fighting.

name: Claye
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Claye (now Claye-Souilly), between Meaux and Paris, Seine-et-Marne
commanders A: Friedrich von Katzler (advance guard of Yorck's and Kleist's corps)
commanders B: Jean Dominique Compans, François Ledru des Essarts
Prussian force: The advance guard of the Army of Silesia (Yorck's and Kleist's corps) under Katzler, 2,600 infantry, 1,900 cavalry and 16 guns (infobox); Zieten's cavalry threatened the flank and Kleist's reinforcements came up near Souilly.
strength A: 2,600 infantry, 1,900 cavalry, 16 guns (the text says 4,500 infantry and artillery, 1,900 cavalry)
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Claye
note: de.wikipedia gives the result as an orderly French withdrawal: Compans's rearguard repulsed the Prussian infantry with a cavalry counterattack, then fell back on Villeparisis and Bondy; the Prussians took the ground but lost more. The infobox loss columns are unlabelled; assigned by order.

name: Paris (1814)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: north-east of Paris: Pantin, Romainville, Belleville, La Villette, La Chapelle and Montmartre
commanders A: Alexander I, Karl Philipp zu Schwarzenberg, Frederick William III, Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher (Ludwig Yorck von Wartenburg, Friedrich von Kleist), Michael Barclay de Tolly
commanders B: Joseph Bonaparte, Auguste de Marmont, Édouard Mortier, Bon-Adrien Jeannot de Moncey
Prussian force: Yorck's I Corps (10,000-15,500) and Kleist's II Corps (8,000-14,000) of the Army of Silesia took La Villette and assaulted La Chapelle; the Prussian Guard advanced from Pantin and with the Russian Guards took a French battery and Les Maisonettes.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Paris (1814) (citing Nafziger, von Damitz, Digby Smith, Bodart)
note: Prussian strength by Nafziger (higher) and von Damitz (lower); Prussian losses by Smith 1,353 and Bodart 2,100 (Nafziger 87 officers and 1,753 men). The city capitulated on 31 March.

name: Courtrai
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Courtrai (now Kortrijk) and Zwevegem, West Flanders
commanders A: Nicolas Joseph Maison
commanders B: Johann Adolf von Thielmann, Friedrich von Hellwig
Prussian force: 'A few Prussians' with Thielmann's Saxons of the III German Corps, including Major Friedrich von Hellwig's Prussian free corps (Streifkorps); numbers not given.
doubts and flags: Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Courtrai (1814); en.wikipedia List of battles of the War of the Sixth Coalition
note: Mainly a Saxon battle (Saxony had changed sides after Leipzig). Hellwig's corps is not explicitly called Prussian in the article.

name: Compiègne (1814)
war: War of the Sixth Coalition (War of Liberation)
place: Compiègne, Oise
commanders A: Major Othenin
Prussian force: A detachment of Bülow's III Corps; commander and strength not verified.
borderline: Date, commanders and details not verified: a Prussian attack on Compiègne held by Major Othenin's garrison, repulsed, around 1 April 1814; no Wikipedia article found.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Date, commanders and details not verified: a Prussian attack on Compiègne held by Major Othenin's garrison, repulsed, around 1 April 1814; no Wikipedia article found.
sources: French local history (V. Reig, 'A la chute de l'Empire: Compiègne en 1814', Annales historiques compiégnoises 29, 2006; only the title could be seen); otherwise from knowledge
note: Remembered in French tradition as the defence of Compiègne; the garrison held until the general armistice.

name: Gilly
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Gilly, east of Charleroi (Hainaut)
commanders A: Napoleon; Grouchy, Vandamme, Exelmans, Pajol; Letort (mortally wounded)
commanders B: Pirch II (2nd Brigade of Zieten's I Corps)
Prussian force: Pirch II's 2nd Brigade of Zieten's I Corps (6th and 28th Infantry, 2nd Westphalian Landwehr, with corps cavalry and a battery), about 6,500 men; Jagow's 3rd Brigade covered Lambusart.
losses A: Letort killed; Vincent's dragoon brigade 7 killed, 2 officers and 20 men wounded
losses B: fusilier battalion of the 28th: 13 officers and 614 men; fusilier battalion of the 6th: 216
sources: warhistory.org, Combat at Gilly; en.wikipedia Battle of Ligny and Waterloo campaign; en.wikipedia Louis-Michel Letort de Lorville
note: The evening rearguard fight that ended the first day of the campaign. The day's earlier actions, as Zieten's outposts were driven in at Thuin, Marchienne-au-Pont, Charleroi (150-200 Prussians taken) and Gosselies, are folded in here and not listed separately. Pirch II broke off and fell back on Fleurus; one square was broken by Letort's Guard dragoons.

name: Ligny
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Ligny, Saint-Amand, Brye and Sombreffe, north-east of Fleurus (Namur province)
commanders A: Napoleon; Soult, Grouchy, Vandamme, Gérard, Drouot
commanders B: Blücher (unhorsed and ridden over), Gneisenau; Zieten (I Corps), Pirch I (II Corps), Thielmann (III Corps)
Prussian force: Blücher's Army of the Lower Rhine with three corps, about 83,000 men and 224 guns: Zieten's I Corps held Ligny, Saint-Amand and Brye with Pirch I's II Corps in support, Thielmann's III Corps held Sombreffe and the left; Bülow's IV Corps did not arrive.
losses B: 16,000 killed and wounded, 8,000 deserted or missing; 21 guns
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ligny; de.wikipedia Sommerfeldzug von 1815
note: Napoleon's last victory. The Guard broke the Prussian centre at Ligny at dusk, but Gneisenau withdrew the army north towards Wavre in good order rather than east, which made the intervention at Waterloo possible.

name: Waterloo
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Mont-Saint-Jean, La Belle Alliance and Plancenoit, south of Waterloo (Walloon Brabant)
allies A: Great Britain; Netherlands; Hanover; Brunswick; Nassau
commanders A: Blücher, Gneisenau; Bülow (IV Corps), Zieten (I Corps), Pirch I (II Corps); Wellington (Anglo-allied army)
commanders B: Napoleon; Ney, Soult, d'Erlon, Reille, Lobau, Kellermann, Milhaud
Prussian force: Blücher's army, about 48,000-50,000 men and 126 guns engaged: Bülow's IV Corps attacked Lobau about 16:30 and, with parts of Pirch I's II Corps, stormed Plancenoit against the Young and Old Guard; Zieten's I Corps joined Wellington's left about 19:00.
losses B: 25,000 killed and wounded, 8,000 captured, 15,000 deserted; 220 guns
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Waterloo; en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (18-24 June)
note: The fight for Plancenoit is part of this battle, as is the Prussian night pursuit under Gneisenau through Genappe that broke up the French army. Prussia is counted as a major ally: Blücher's army fought beside Wellington's, which bore the main French attacks.

name: Wavre
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Wavre, Bierges and Limal, on the Dyle (Walloon Brabant)
commanders A: Grouchy; Vandamme, Gérard (wounded), Pajol
commanders B: Thielmann (chief of staff Clausewitz); Stengel at Limal
Prussian force: Thielmann's III Corps, weakened when Borcke's 9th Brigade marched off towards Waterloo; the Kurmark Landwehr held the town of Wavre and the 31st Infantry the Bierges bridge, while Stengel's small detachment lost the Limal bridge.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Wavre; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Wavre (via Sommerfeldzug von 1815)
note: A French tactical victory: Pajol forced Limal on the night of 18/19 June and Thielmann retreated on the morning of the 19th. A Prussian strategic success, since it kept Grouchy's 33,000 away from Waterloo.

name: Namur (1815)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Namur, at the confluence of the Sambre and Meuse, with Temploux and Flawinne to the west
commanders A: Pirch I (II Corps); Krafft (6th Brigade), Brause (7th Brigade); Sohr
Prussian force: Pirch I's II Corps: Krafft's 6th Brigade made the assaults on the gates (Colonels Zastrow and Bismarck killed, Reuss wounded) and Brause's 7th Brigade took the town; Sohr's cavalry and Thielmann's III Corps cavalry fought at Temploux and Flawinne.
losses A: about 1,500 (the 6th Brigade alone 44 officers and 1,274 men)
losses B: about the same as the Prussians, by the Prussian account
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (18-24 June); de.wikipedia Sommerfeldzug von 1815
note: Teste's division held the walls to cover Grouchy's retreat, repulsed the Prussian assaults with heavy loss and slipped away to Dinant in the evening. Scored as Prussian because they took the town, but often described as a successful French rearguard action.

name: Avesnes (siege)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Avesnes (now Avesnes-sur-Helpe), Nord
commanders A: Zieten (I Corps); Jagow (vanguard)
Prussian force: Zieten's I Corps; the vanguard under Jagow (3rd Brigade and 1st Silesian Hussars) invested the fortress and the corps artillery bombarded it overnight.
strength B: three National Guard battalions and some veterans
losses A: light (the Silesian Rifles lost 10 men in a sortie)
losses B: about 400 killed in the magazine explosion; the rest captured; 47 guns taken
borderline: A one-night bombardment with a sortie; the commandant surrendered at discretion after a magazine exploded.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A one-night bombardment with a sortie; the commandant surrendered at discretion after a magazine exploded.
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (18-24 June); en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign
note: The National Guards were sent home and the veterans marched to Cologne as prisoners.

name: Sedan (siege, 1815)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Sedan, on the Meuse (Ardennes)
commanders A: Engelhardt (Hesse-Kassel), acting for the sick Kleist
Prussian force: The North German Federal Corps (Hessian division under Engelhardt and the Thuringian brigade), about 25,000-26,200 men in all, attached to Blücher's army under the Prussian general Kleist; no Prussian units identified at Sedan.
borderline: North German Federal Corps (Hessian and Thuringian troops) under Prussian command, no Prussian units identified; Sedan capitulated after a few days' bombardment.
doubts and flags: Borderline: North German Federal Corps (Hessian and Thuringian troops) under Prussian command, no Prussian units identified; Sedan capitulated after a few days' bombardment. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Minor campaigns of 1815; en.wikipedia Reduction of the French fortresses in 1815
note: Capitulated on 25 June.

name: Bouillon
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Bouillon castle, on the Semois (Luxembourg province)
commanders B: Engelhardt, later Hake (North German Federal Corps)
Prussian force: Troops of the North German Federal Corps (Hessians and Thuringians) under Prussian command; no Prussian units identified.
borderline: A failed coup de main followed by a blockade, by North German Federal Corps troops only; not taken while the corps was there.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A failed coup de main followed by a blockade, by North German Federal Corps troops only; not taken while the corps was there. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Minor campaigns of 1815
note: The garrison was too strong for a coup de main and the place was only blockaded from 25 June until a Netherlands Reserve battalion under Tindal relieved the German troops on 21 August. Scored as a French success (the attempt failed).

name: Compiègne (1815)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Compiègne, on the Oise (Oise)
commanders A: Jagow (3rd Brigade of Zieten's I Corps)
Prussian force: Jagow's 3rd Brigade of Zieten's I Corps with the 1st Silesian Hussars and half a horse battery, which had occupied the town just before the French arrived.
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (25 June - 1 July); de.wikipedia Sommerfeldzug von 1815
note: d'Erlon's corps, coming from Soissons, attacked about 05:00 to secure the Oise bridge; after about 90 minutes of cannonade and skirmishing it withdrew.

name: Senlis
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Senlis (Oise)
commanders A: Sydow (vanguard of Bülow's IV Corps); Major Blankenburg
Prussian force: Sydow's detachment of Bülow's IV Corps: the 8th Hussars, 3rd Battalion of the 3rd Neumark Landwehr and Blankenburg's 1st Pomeranian Landwehr Cavalry.
borderline: A small night action.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A small night action.
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (25 June - 1 July)
note: About 21:00 Kellermann's cuirassiers drove the Pomeranian Landwehr cavalry out of Senlis; at 22:00 Sydow retook the town and infantry fire from the houses drove off the French cavalry, forcing d'Erlon's column onto another road. Date not re-verified: the sequence of the advance places it on the evening of 27 June, after Compiègne.

name: Mézières (siege, 1815)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Mézières and Charleville (now Charleville-Mézières), on the Meuse (Ardennes)
commanders A: Hake (North German Federal Corps)
Prussian force: The North German Federal Corps (Hessian division and Thuringian brigade) under the Prussian Lieutenant-General von Hake; no Prussian units identified.
borderline: North German Federal Corps troops under Prussian command; no Prussian units identified.
doubts and flags: Borderline: North German Federal Corps troops under Prussian command; no Prussian units identified. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Minor campaigns of 1815
note: Bombardment from 27 June; on 28 June Hessian battalions stormed Charleville under the guns of Mézières (folded in here). Trenches opened 2 August; the town surrendered 13 August and the citadel 1 September.

name: Villers-Cotterêts
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Villers-Cotterêts (Aisne)
commanders A: Pirch II (2nd Brigade of Zieten's I Corps)
Prussian force: Pirch II's 2nd Brigade of Zieten's I Corps; the fusilier battalion of the 6th Infantry and the Brandenburg Dragoons made the surprise attack about 01:00.
strength B: about 9,000 rallied by Grouchy, plus Vandamme's corps
losses B: a horse battery of 14 guns, 20 ammunition wagons and an escort of 150 captured
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (25 June - 1 July); en.wikipedia Villers-Cotterêts (disambiguation); de.wikipedia Sommerfeldzug von 1815
note: The Prussians surprised the town and nearly took Grouchy, but Vandamme's corps drove the 6th Infantry back and Pirch II withdrew towards Crépy-en-Valois and Nanteuil, while the French continued their retreat. Set as a draw; German accounts present it as a Prussian success (the town and 14 guns taken).

name: Nanteuil
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Lévignen and Nanteuil-le-Haudouin (Oise)
commanders A: Zieten (I Corps), Jagow (3rd Brigade); Prince William of Prussia (IV Corps vanguard cavalry)
Prussian force: Jagow's 3rd Brigade and the reserve cavalry of Zieten's I Corps (2nd West Prussian Dragoons, 1st Silesian Hussars), joined at Nanteuil by Prince William of Prussia with the IV Corps vanguard cavalry.
losses B: two guns at Lévignen; more than 2,000 prisoners at Nanteuil
borderline: No article of its own; named in German accounts as the action at Lévignen (Levigneux) and Nanteuil.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No article of its own; named in German accounts as the action at Lévignen (Levigneux) and Nanteuil.
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (25 June - 1 July); de.wikipedia Sommerfeldzug von 1815 (as Levigneux)
note: Reille's corps retreating on Paris was caught at Lévignen; the West Prussian Dragoons were repulsed, then the Silesian Hussars took two guns, and the pursuit ran on beyond Nanteuil. The Prussians claimed 16 guns and 4,000 prisoners for the whole day of 28 June.

name: Rocquencourt
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Rocquencourt, Vélizy and Le Chesnay, near Versailles (Yvelines)
commanders A: Exelmans, Piré (under Davout)
Prussian force: Sohr's cavalry brigade, the Brandenburg and Pomeranian Hussars, 600-700 men, sent ahead of the army to cut the Orléans road.
strength A: about 3,000 cavalry plus three battalions of the 33rd Line
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Rocquencourt
note: Exelmans ambushed the hussars, Piré's lancers struck them at Vélizy, and the remnant was cut off at Le Chesnay trying to break out to Saint-Germain. Thielmann's vanguard (Borcke's brigade) reoccupied Rocquencourt that evening. Often called the last French victory of the Napoleonic Wars.

name: Sèvres
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Sèvres, Meudon heights, Moulineaux and Issy, south-west of Paris (Hauts-de-Seine)
commanders A: Zieten (I Corps); Steinmetz (1st Brigade), Pirch II (2nd Brigade), Henckel von Donnersmarck (4th Brigade)
Prussian force: Zieten's I Corps: Steinmetz's 1st Brigade leading, supported by Pirch II's 2nd and Donnersmarck's 4th Brigades, with Jagow's 3rd Brigade on the Meudon heights.
borderline: en.wikipedia treats this as the first day of the Battle of Issy (2-3 July); listed separately because German accounts name the action at Sèvres. Drop it if Issy is taken as 2-3 July.
doubts and flags: Borderline: en.wikipedia treats this as the first day of the Battle of Issy (2-3 July); listed separately because German accounts name the action at Sèvres. Drop it if Issy is taken as 2-3 July.
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (2-7 July); en.wikipedia Battle of Issy; de.wikipedia Sommerfeldzug von 1815
note: The Prussians reached Sèvres about 15:00, forced the French back to Moulineaux, beat off a counter-attack there and took Issy in a night attack about 22:30.

name: Issy
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Issy (now Issy-les-Moulineaux), south-west of Paris (Hauts-de-Seine)
commanders A: Zieten (I Corps)
Prussian force: Zieten's I Corps; Issy was held behind barricades by the 12th and 24th Infantry and the 2nd Westphalian Landwehr with half a battery of 12-pounders.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Issy; en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (2-7 July)
note: Vandamme attacked from Vaugirard at 03:00 in two columns with 20 guns; after about four hours of failed attacks the French fell back and ceased fire at 07:00, asking for an armistice. This led to the Convention of Saint-Cloud and the surrender of Paris. en.wikipedia dates the battle 2-3 July and gives French losses of 3,000+ for both days, most of them on 2 July (see Sèvres). The last field action of the Hundred Days.

name: Maubeuge (siege)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Maubeuge, on the Sambre (Nord)
commanders A: Prince August of Prussia
Prussian force: Prince August of Prussia's siege corps, drawn from the Prussian II Army Corps; the 5th and 7th Brigades of II Corps with cavalry had blockaded the place since 21-22 June.
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (18-24 June) and (2-7 July); en.wikipedia Reduction of the French fortresses in 1815; Blesson, Beitrag zur Geschichte des Festungskrieges in Frankreich im Jahre 1815 (contents page)
note: First of Prince August's formal sieges, described in Blesson's engineer diary. Dates from the en.wikipedia capitulation table, whose fortress names did not come through: the five date pairs were matched to Maubeuge, Landrecies, Marienbourg, Philippeville and Rocroi in Blesson's order. French commandant and losses not found.

name: Landrecies (siege, 1815)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Landrecies, on the Sambre (Nord)
commanders A: Prince August of Prussia
Prussian force: Prince August of Prussia's siege corps from the II Army Corps; the place had been blockaded since 22 June by Sydow's vanguard of Bülow's IV Corps and then Krafft's 6th Brigade of II Corps.
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (18-24 June) and (2-7 July); Blesson (1818, contents page)
note: Capitulated 21 July. Dates matched from the en.wikipedia capitulation table (see Maubeuge). The year is in the name because a Prussian corps may have served at the siege of 1712.

name: Marienbourg (siege)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Marienbourg (now Mariembourg, part of Couvin), Namur province; French until the Second Peace of Paris
commanders A: Prince August of Prussia
Prussian force: Prince August of Prussia's siege corps from the II Army Corps.
borderline: A siege of one or two days: the small fortress capitulated after a short bombardment.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A siege of one or two days: the small fortress capitulated after a short bombardment.
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (2-7 July); Blesson (1818, contents page)
note: Capitulated 28 July. Dates matched from the en.wikipedia capitulation table (see Maubeuge).

name: Philippeville (siege)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Philippeville, Namur province; French until the Second Peace of Paris
commanders A: Prince August of Prussia
Prussian force: Prince August of Prussia's siege corps from the II Army Corps.
borderline: A short formal siege: capitulated after about a day of bombardment.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A short formal siege: capitulated after about a day of bombardment.
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (2-7 July); Blesson (1818, contents page)
note: Capitulated 8 August. Dates matched from the en.wikipedia capitulation table (see Maubeuge).

name: Rocroi (siege, 1815)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Rocroi (Ardennes)
commanders A: Prince August of Prussia
Prussian force: Prince August of Prussia's siege corps from the II Army Corps.
borderline: A short formal siege: capitulated after about a day of bombardment.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A short formal siege: capitulated after about a day of bombardment.
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (2-7 July); en.wikipedia Siege of Rocroi ("captured by the Prussian army in 1815"); Blesson (1818, contents page)
note: Capitulated 16 August. Dates matched from the en.wikipedia capitulation table (see Maubeuge).

name: Longwy (siege, 1815)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Longwy (Meurthe-et-Moselle)
commanders A: Prince Louis of Hesse-Homburg
Prussian force: Troops of the Prussian garrison of Luxembourg under Prince Louis of Hesse-Homburg, part of Prince August's command between the Sambre and the Moselle; strength not found.
borderline: Not verified in detail: the besieging force is inferred from the Catillon allotment (the Luxembourg garrison was to reduce the fortresses between the Sambre and the Moselle), and the amount of fighting is unknown.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Not verified in detail: the besieging force is inferred from the Catillon allotment (the Luxembourg garrison was to reduce the fortresses between the Sambre and the Moselle), and the amount of fighting is unknown.
sources: en.wikipedia Hundred Days; en.wikipedia Reduction of the French fortresses in 1815
note: en.wikipedia (Hundred Days) gives the capitulation as 13 September 1815. The start date of the siege was not found, so month is the month of capitulation.

name: Givet and Charlemont (siege)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Givet, Mont d'Haurs and the fort of Charlemont, on the Meuse (Ardennes)
commanders A: Prince August of Prussia
Prussian force: Prince August of Prussia with the Prussian II Army Corps and the British battering train.
borderline: Barely begun: Givet and Mont d'Haurs were given up without an assault and Charlemont was never bombarded.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Barely begun: Givet and Mont d'Haurs were given up without an assault and Charlemont was never bombarded.
sources: en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign: Waterloo to Paris (2-7 July); en.wikipedia Reduction of the French fortresses in 1815; en.wikipedia Waterloo campaign; Blesson (1818, contents page: 'Recognoscirung von Charlemont')
note: The siege was to begin on 8 September; Burke gave up Givet and Mont d'Haurs on 10 September and withdrew into Charlemont. The bombardment was set for 23 September, but on 20 September Prince August learned that hostilities were to cease throughout France. Sources differ on whether and when Charlemont capitulated (8 or 20 September); set as a draw.

name: Montmédy (siege, 1815)
war: War of the Seventh Coalition (Hundred Days)
place: Montmédy, with the lower town of Médy-Bas, on the Chiers (Meuse)
commanders A: Hake (North German Federal Corps)
Prussian force: The North German Federal Corps under the Prussian Lieutenant-General von Hake, with Prussian troops: 400 men of the Prussian 21st Infantry (II Corps) and 100 Saxe-Weimar troops stormed Médy-Bas on 15 September.
losses A: several Prussians wounded in the storm of Médy-Bas
sources: en.wikipedia Minor campaigns of 1815; steve-noon.co.uk, The storming of Medy-Bas, 15 September 1815 (after Prussian Regular Infantry 1809-15)
note: Twelve batteries were in position by 13 September; the lower town was stormed in the early hours of 15 September (folded in here). On 20 September the garrison agreed to march out with arms and baggage behind the Loire. Among the last shots of the Napoleonic Wars.

name: Rogalinek
place: Rogalinek and Rogalin, near Mosina, south of Posen
Prussian force: Prussian troops from the Posen area (units not verified).
borderline: Date and details unverified: en.wikipedia lists only 'Prussian victories at Mosina, Rogalin, Stęszew, Kórnik, Buk and Oborniki'.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Date and details unverified: en.wikipedia lists only 'Prussian victories at Mosina, Rogalin, Stęszew, Kórnik, Buk and Oborniki'.
sources: en.wikipedia Greater Poland uprising (1848)
note: Entered as Rogalinek; the en.wikipedia text says Rogalin (the two villages face each other across the Warta).

name: Oborniki
place: Oborniki (Obornik), north of Posen
Prussian force: Prussian troops (units not verified).
borderline: A skirmish ('potyczka') with its own pl.wikipedia article, which could not be read; date and details unverified.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A skirmish ('potyczka') with its own pl.wikipedia article, which could not be read; date and details unverified.
sources: pl.wikipedia Potyczka pod Obornikami (title only; the page could not be read); en.wikipedia Greater Poland uprising (1848)
note: en.wikipedia lists Oborniki among the Prussian victories of the rising.

name: Berlin (March Revolution)
place: Berlin, the barricades of the old city centre (Königstraße, Breite Straße, Friedrichstraße, Alexanderplatz)
factions B: Prussian Army (royal troops, mainly Guard units)
commanders B: Lieutenant-General Karl von Prittwitz (from 18 March, replacing Ernst von Pfuel)
Prussian force: About 14,000 soldiers with 36 guns of the Berlin and Potsdam garrisons (nearly all Guard formations) under Karl von Prittwitz.
losses A: over 200 civilians killed (the 'Märzgefallene'); over 600 insurgents wounded or captured
borderline: Street and barricade fighting rather than a field battle.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Street and barricade fighting rather than a field battle.
sources: de.wikipedia Märzrevolution 1848 in Berlin; de.wikipedia Karl von Prittwitz
note: A 12-hour fight on 18 March into the night; the troops took many barricades, but on 19 March (10:30) King Frederick William IV yielded to a deputation and withdrew the troops from the city, so the insurgents held Berlin. Press rumours at the time gave 400 to 1,800 military dead.

name: Trzemeszno
place: Trzemeszno (Tremessen), between Gniezno and Mogilno, Grand Duchy of Posen
Prussian force: Prussian troops of the Posen garrison (units not verified).
borderline: Day, forces and losses unverified: en.wikipedia's town article gives only the year and the Polish victory; pl.wikipedia 'Bitwa w Trzemesznie' could not be read.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Day, forces and losses unverified: en.wikipedia's town article gives only the year and the Polish victory; pl.wikipedia 'Bitwa w Trzemesznie' could not be read.
sources: en.wikipedia Trzemeszno (the town 'was the site of a battle, won by the Poles'); pl.wikipedia Bitwa w Trzemesznie (title only; the page could not be read); Great Russian Encyclopedia, Poznan rising of 1848 (Trzemeszno among the towns that joined the rising)
note: Usually dated 10 April 1848 (not verified here).

name: Grodzisk
place: Grodzisk Wielkopolski (Grätz), south-west of Posen
commanders A: Marcus Mosse (led the townspeople)
Prussian force: About 600 Prussian troops.
borderline: A local defence of the town, not a named battle article; exact date not given.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A local defence of the town, not a named battle article; exact date not given.
sources: en.wikipedia Greater Poland uprising (1848); pl.wikipedia Wojsko wielkopolskie 1848 roku
note: en.wikipedia: the population, led by the Jewish doctor Marcus Mosse, 'defended the town against encroaching 600 Prussian troops'. pl.wikipedia lists Grodzisk among the first clashes at the end of April (with Gostyń, Raszków and Koźmin).

name: Odolanów
place: Odolanów (Adelnau), south Greater Poland
Prussian force: Prussian troops (units not named in the source).
borderline: A minor skirmish ('potyczka'), named only in pl.wikipedia's survey of the 1848 Polish forces.

sources: pl.wikipedia Wojsko wielkopolskie 1848 roku
note: '22 kwietnia Prusacy wyparli Polaków z Odolanowa' (the Prussians drove the Poles out of Odolanów).

name: Schleswig
place: Schleswig town, Busdorf and the Danevirke, Duchy of Schleswig
commanders A: Friedrich von Wrangel
commanders B: Frederik Læssøe (chief of staff to Hans Hedemann)
Prussian force: Wrangel's army: the Prussian contingent of almost 12,000 men with Schleswig-Holstein troops; en.wikipedia says the troops of the German Confederation (Reich) did not take part.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Schleswig; en.wikipedia First Schleswig War; de.wikipedia Schleswig-Holsteinische Erhebung
note: Also called the Easter battle. Strengths as given by en.wikipedia's infobox.

name: Oeversee
place: Oeversee (Oversø), south of Flensburg, Duchy of Schleswig
commanders A: Friedrich von Wrangel (army commander)
Prussian force: The pursuit by Wrangel's German army of the Danish rearguard the day after Schleswig; the units engaged are disputed (see note).
borderline: Prussian participation uncertain: en.wikipedia calls it a 'Hanoverian victory in the Skirmish of Oversø' (troops of Halkett's 10th Federal Corps), de.wikipedia and the Fandom list a Prussian victory.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian participation uncertain: en.wikipedia calls it a 'Hanoverian victory in the Skirmish of Oversø' (troops of Halkett's 10th Federal Corps), de.wikipedia and the Fandom list a Prussian victory.

note: Not the better-known Austrian fight at Oeversee of 6 February 1864 (no Prussians; excluded).

name: Książ
place: Książ Wielkopolski (Xions), south of Śrem
commanders A: Colonel Brandt (promoted general for it); the column belonged to General von Blumen's force
Prussian force: Over 6,000 Prussians with 7 guns under Colonel Brandt.
losses B: about 300 killed and as many captured
sources: pl.wikipedia Wojsko wielkopolskie 1848 roku; pl.wikipedia Bitwa pod Miłosławiem; en.wikipedia Greater Poland uprising (1848)
note: The town was burned; en.wikipedia says Prussian troops murdered 600 prisoners there (pl.wikipedia: about 300 killed and as many captured).

name: Miłosław
place: Miłosław, south-east of Środa, Grand Duchy of Posen
commanders A: Ludwik Mierosławski (with Józef Garczyński and Feliks Białoskórski)
Prussian force: General von Blumen's column of about 2,100 infantry, 360 cavalry and 4 guns (2,500 in all), advancing in two columns from Środa and Września after its victory at Książ.
strength A: about 3,400 with the reinforcements (over 700 riflemen, 1,300 scythemen, about 370 cavalry), 4 guns
losses A: up to 200 killed, wounded and missing
losses B: 225 (50 killed, 156 wounded, 19 missing, by Prussian admission)
sources: pl.wikipedia Bitwa pod Miłosławiem; pl.wikipedia Wojsko wielkopolskie 1848 roku; en.wikipedia Battle of Miłosław
note: Polish victory, but the exhausted Poles could not pursue and the Prussians withdrew with most of their men and guns. Mierosławski held the town at first with only about 1,200 men until Garczyński (about 1,000) and Białoskórski (about 1,200) arrived.

name: Sokołowo
place: Sokołowo, near Września, Grand Duchy of Posen
commanders A: Ludwik Mierosławski
Prussian force: A Prussian column of 4 battalions, 2 squadrons and 6 guns under General Hirschfeld.
sources: pl.wikipedia Wojsko wielkopolskie 1848 roku; en.wikipedia Greater Poland uprising (1848)
note: The scythemen (kosynierzy) defeated a Prussian column; pl.wikipedia: 'Ceną było 300 zabitych i tyluż rannych' (300 killed and as many wounded, apparently Polish losses; the side is not stated). The last Polish victory of the rising, which capitulated at Bardo on 9 May.

name: Dybbøl (1848)
place: Dybbøl (Düppel) and Nybøl, Sundeved, opposite Sønderborg
commanders A: Hans Hedemann, Friderich Adolph Schleppegrell
commanders B: Friedrich von Wrangel, Eduard von Bonin, Hugh Halkett
Prussian force: Wrangel attacked with three German brigades (11,500 men) assembled at Kværs, about 20,000 with the reserves, including a Prussian line brigade and Halkett's 10th Federal Corps troops.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Dybbøl (1848); en.wikipedia First Schleswig War
note: The Germans took Nybøl, Stenderup and Bøffelkobbel and pushed the Danes back to Dybbøl, but the assault failed when Danish reserves came over from Als; a Danish counter-attack drove them back toward Nybøl. The 10th Federal Corps contingents (Hanover with Brunswick, Oldenburg, Mecklenburg and Hanseatic troops) are not itemised by the source.

name: Dybbøl (1849)
place: Dybbøl (Düppel), Sundeved, opposite Sønderborg
commanders B: Karl von Prittwitz (Prussian commander-in-chief of the federal army)
Prussian force: The attack was made by Saxon and Bavarian troops of the federal (Reich) army; its commander-in-chief, the Prussian general Karl von Prittwitz, took part. No Prussian units confirmed.
borderline: Fought by Saxon and Bavarian federal troops under a Prussian commander-in-chief; Prussian troops not confirmed.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Fought by Saxon and Bavarian federal troops under a Prussian commander-in-chief; Prussian troops not confirmed. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia First Schleswig War (timeline); de.wikipedia Karl von Prittwitz; military-history.fandom First Schleswig War
note: en.wikipedia and the Fandom list it as a Danish victory over Saxon forces; German regimental tradition remembers the storming of the Dybbøl outworks, so the result deserves checking.

name: Kolding
place: Kolding, south-east Jutland
commanders A: Eduard von Bonin (with Friedrich von Beckedorff and Eduard von Fransecky)
commanders B: Frederik Rubeck Bülow, Olaf Rye, C. F. Moltke
Prussian force: The army of Schleswig-Holstein (about 14,000, 40 guns) under the seconded Prussian general Eduard von Bonin, with Prussian officers such as Fransecky on its staff.
borderline: en.wikipedia calls it 'a Prussian army under Eduard von Bonin', but the troops were the Schleswig-Holstein army led by Prussian officers on secondment.
doubts and flags: Borderline: en.wikipedia calls it 'a Prussian army under Eduard von Bonin', but the troops were the Schleswig-Holstein army led by Prussian officers on secondment. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kolding (1849); de.wikipedia Schleswig-Holsteinische Erhebung
note: The Schleswig-Holsteiners took Kolding on 20 April and repulsed the Danish counter-attack of 23 April; the Danes retreated toward Vejle and Fredericia.

name: Dresden (May Uprising)
war: Revolutions of 1848–49 (Campaign for the Imperial Constitution)
place: Dresden, Kingdom of Saxony (barricades of the old town, the arsenal and the Landtag building)
commanders A: Colonel Friedrich von Waldersee (Prussian troops)
commanders B: Alexander Clarus Heinze (Bürgerwehr commander), Mikhail Bakunin; provisional government of Samuel Tzschirner, Otto Leonhard Heubner and Karl Todt
Prussian force: The 1st and Fusilier battalions of the Kaiser Alexander Guard Grenadier Regiment No. 1 and the Fusilier battalion of Infantry Regiment No. 24 under Colonel von Waldersee, beside a Saxon garrison of about 1,800; Holleben's larger Prussian detachment arrived on 10 May, after the fighting.
strength A: Saxon garrison about 1,800 with 6 guns, plus three Prussian battalions
losses B: 343 dead and wounded (99 identified and 98 unidentified dead, 114 wounded); Schuster estimates about 250 dead and 400–500 wounded
borderline: Street and barricade fighting.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Street and barricade fighting.
sources: de.wikipedia Dresdner Maiaufstand; de.wikipedia Reichsverfassungskampagne
note: The Prussian battalions fought in the last days (7–9 May per de.wikipedia). The revolutionaries fled the city; Bakunin was captured, Richard Wagner and Gottfried Semper escaped.

name: Elberfeld
war: Revolutions of 1848–49 (Campaign for the Imperial Constitution)
place: Elberfeld (now part of Wuppertal), Rhine Province
Prussian force: Regular Prussian troops sent into the town against the mayor's wishes (units not named in the source).
borderline: A barricade clash with 'several' dead, not a battle in the usual sense.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A barricade clash with 'several' dead, not a battle in the usual sense.
sources: de.wikipedia Elberfelder Aufstand; de.wikipedia Reichsverfassungskampagne
note: The troops failed to take the barricades on the evening of 9 May and left the town on 10 May; a security committee ruled until the insurgents under Otto von Mirbach left on 17 May, and Prussian troops occupied Elberfeld on 19 May.

name: Iserlohn
war: Revolutions of 1848–49 (Campaign for the Imperial Constitution)
place: Iserlohn, County of Mark, Province of Westphalia
factions B: Iserlohn and Hagen insurgents (Landwehr men and townspeople)
commanders A: Lieutenant-Colonel Schrötter (fusilier battalion, killed)
commanders B: Karl Schuchart (chairman of the security committee)
Prussian force: Infantry Regiment No. 24 with other units (strength not given).
strength B: about 400 Landwehr men and insurgents from Hagen, with local supporters
losses B: at least 34 dead in all, insurgents, civilians and soldiers (the article also gives 40 civilian deaths)
sources: de.wikipedia Iserlohner Aufstand von 1849
note: The rising began on 10 May with the mutiny at Hagen and the storming of the Iserlohn arsenal; the troops retook the town on 17 May. Blank calls it 'das Ende der Revolution in Westfalen'.

name: Århus
place: Vejlby and the Riis Forest, about 2 km north of Aarhus (Århus)
commanders A: Olaf Rye, Gotthold Møller
Prussian force: Infantry and cavalry of the Prussian division advancing through Jutland for the German Confederation (whole force about 16,000).
sources: en.wikipedia Skirmish of Århus; en.wikipedia First Schleswig War
note: Also called the cavalry fight at Vejlby. The strengths in en.wikipedia's infobox are whole-army figures, far more than were engaged. The Prussians, who had taken Aarhus on 30 May, fell back into the town and did not retake it until 20 June.

name: Kirchheimbolanden
place: Kirchheimbolanden, Bavarian Palatinate
commanders A: Colonel Gustav von Schleinitz (vanguard), under Woldemar von Hanneken and Moritz von Hirschfeld (I Corps); Prince William of Prussia in overall command
commanders B: Major Rouppert, Franz Zitz, Ludwig Bamberger
Prussian force: The vanguard of Hirschfeld's I Corps: the Berlin battalion of the 2nd Guard Landwehr Regiment, the fusilier battalion of the 24th Infantry, two squadrons of the 7th Uhlans and two guns.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Kirchheimbolanden; de.wikipedia Pfälzischer Aufstand
note: The first action of the Palatinate campaign, against the Rhenish-Hessian Freikorps; Mainz riflemen held out in the palace garden. The assignment of the loss figures to sides is inferred from the de.wikipedia text.

name: Ludwigshafen
place: Ludwigshafen am Rhein, opposite Mannheim
commanders A: Major Künzel (assault), under Moritz von Hirschfeld (I Corps)
commanders B: Ludwik Mierosławski (overall); Arnold Steck and Otto von Corvin-Wiersbitzki (artillery at Mannheim)
Prussian force: From the 1st Division of Hirschfeld's I Corps: the 1st Battalion of the 28th Infantry, a squadron of the 9th Hussars, a Jäger detachment and two guns under Major Künzel.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht von Ludwigshafen
note: The Prussians stormed the cotton-bale barricades and took the town by about 13:30 on 15 June; Baden revolutionary heavy guns at Mannheim then shelled it until 18 June (about 1,000 shells), burning the harbour. de.wikipedia's infobox gives strengths of 800 and 600 and losses of 17 dead, 9 wounded and 2 dead, 6 wounded without a clear side for each.

name: Rinnthal
place: Rinnthal, in the Queich valley between Wilgartswiesen and Annweiler
commanders A: Major Mutius (advance guard of the 2nd Division, I Corps)
Prussian force: The advance guard of the 2nd Division of Hirschfeld's I Corps under Major Mutius: the fusilier battalion of the 25th Infantry, a Jäger company and two guns, with a battalion sent round the flank via Spirkelbach.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Rinnthal; de.wikipedia Pfälzischer Aufstand
note: The hardest fight of the Palatinate campaign; Friedrich Engels served in Willich's Freischar. de.wikipedia's infobox gives strengths of 1,600 and 1,300 and losses of 20 dead, 20 wounded, 20 captured and 9 wounded without a clear side for each (probably the latter Prussian). The retreat turned into flight at Sarnstall.

name: Waghäusel
place: Waghäusel and Wiesental, between Mannheim and Karlsruhe, Grand Duchy of Baden
commanders A: Moritz von Hirschfeld (I Corps; chief of staff Albrecht von Roon); Prince William of Prussia in overall command
Prussian force: Hirschfeld's I Corps, which had crossed the Rhine at Germersheim on 20 June; its left-wing vanguard bore the first attack.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Waghäusel; de.wikipedia Badische Revolution; de.wikipedia Gefechte an der Murglinie
note: The decisive battle of the Baden campaign ('Gefechte bei Waghäusel und Wiesental'): the revolutionaries first drove back the Prussian vanguard near the sugar factory but broke off the pursuit; as more Prussians crossed the Rhine and threatened encirclement they fell back in disorder. de.wikipedia's infobox gives 11,000 and losses of 20 dead and 110 wounded without clear sides.

name: Ubstadt
place: Ubstadt, north of Bruchsal, Grand Duchy of Baden
Prussian force: Prussian troops of the Prince of Prussia's army advancing on Bruchsal after Waghäusel (corps and units not verified).
borderline: No article (red link in de.wikipedia); the date is not given there and comes from standard accounts, unverified.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No article (red link in de.wikipedia); the date is not given there and comes from standard accounts, unverified.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefechte an der Murglinie; de.wikipedia Badische Revolution (list of actions, red link 'Gefecht bei Ubstadt')
note: A rearguard action: revolutionary units briefly opposed the Prussians to cover the main army's withdrawal to the Murg.

name: Durlach
place: Durlach (now part of Karlsruhe), at the Pfinz bridges by the Obermühle
commanders A: Woldemar von Hanneken (1st Division), Colonel Karl August von Brandenstein (detachment), under Moritz von Hirschfeld
Prussian force: Hanneken's 1st Division of I Corps, about 5,000 (battalions of the 28th and 30th Infantry, the 2nd Battalion of the 16th Landwehr, artillery), with the 3rd and 4th Divisions outflanking.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Durlach; de.wikipedia Badische Revolution
