note: Brandenstein's frontal attack on the barricades failed with heavy losses to the Landwehr (including the Iserlohn battalion); flanking moves forced Becker out at about 15:30. His stand let Mierosławski move his stores to Rastatt and reach the Murg; Karlsruhe was occupied.

name: Brüsterort
place: Off Brüsterort (now Cape Taran, Mayak), Samland coast of East Prussia
commanders A: Commodore Jan Schröder; Leutnant 1. Klasse Barandon (captain of the ship)
Prussian force: The paddle aviso Preußischer Adler under Lieutenant Barandon, with Commodore Jan Schröder aboard in command.
strength B: 1 brig (St. Croix); the corvette Galathea nearby
borderline: No article of its own; described in de.wikipedia's article on the ship.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No article of its own; described in de.wikipedia's article on the ship.
sources: de.wikipedia Preußischer Adler (Schiff)
note: Counted as the baptism of fire of the Prussian navy. In a calm the steamer engaged the sailing brig for several hours without result; when the wind rose and the Danish corvette Galathea came in sight, Schröder broke off toward Danzig. Date as implied by the ship article (it reached Danzig Bay on the morning of 27 June).

name: Murg line
place: The Murg from Steinmauern via Rastatt, Kuppenheim and Bischweier to Gernsbach, Grand Duchy of Baden
commanders A: Prince William of Prussia; Moritz von Hirschfeld (I Corps), Karl von der Groeben (II Corps), Eduard von Peucker (federal Neckar Corps)
commanders B: Ludwik Mierosławski; Johann Philipp Becker, Mersy, Oborski
Prussian force: The two improvised Prussian corps of the Prince of Prussia (Hirschfeld's I and Groeben's II) with Peucker's federal Neckar Corps, about 60,000 men and 100 guns in all.
losses A: 295 Prussians killed or wounded (28 June – 1 July); 6 Neckar Corps soldiers killed at Gernsbach
losses B: not recorded; probably several times the Prussian losses
borderline: A series of actions treated by de.wikipedia as one ('Gefechte an der Murglinie'); Gernsbach is also entered separately.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A series of actions treated by de.wikipedia as one ('Gefechte an der Murglinie'); Gernsbach is also entered separately.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefechte an der Murglinie; de.wikipedia Badische Revolution; de.wikipedia Gefecht in Gernsbach
note: Actions at Waldprechtsweier, Ötigheim and Michelbach (28 June), on the Federbach and at Rauental, Bischweier, Oberweier and Muggensturm (29 June; artillery fire hit a shrine near the Prince of Prussia), Kuppenheim, Rotenfels, Niederbühl and Oos (30 June). About 6,500 revolutionaries were shut up in Rastatt and the rest fled south. The federal contingents are those listed by de.wikipedia ('Hessian' taken as Hesse-Darmstadt).

name: Gernsbach
place: Gernsbach, in the Murg valley, Grand Duchy of Baden
commanders A: Eduard von Peucker (Prussian general commanding the federal Neckar Corps)
Prussian force: Peucker's federal Neckar Corps (about 12,000 infantry, 600 cavalry and 16 guns), advancing from Württemberg under the overall command of the Prince of Prussia; no Prussian units named.
borderline: Non-Prussian federal troops only, under a Prussian commander; part of the Murg line fighting (entered separately because it has its own article).
doubts and flags: Borderline: Non-Prussian federal troops only, under a Prussian commander; part of the Murg line fighting (entered separately because it has its own article). Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht in Gernsbach; de.wikipedia Gefechte an der Murglinie
note: After about four hours of street fighting the town fell in the evening, breaking the southern end of the Murg line.

name: Rastatt (siege, 1849)
place: Federal fortress of Rastatt, Grand Duchy of Baden
commanders A: Karl von der Groeben (II Corps)
commanders B: Colonel Gustav Tiedemann (governor); Gustav von Biedenfeld and Otto von Corvin signed the surrender
Prussian force: Groeben's Prussian II Corps with some federal troops: about 12,500 men, about 30 field guns and heavy siege artillery.
strength A: about 12,500, about 30 field guns and siege artillery
strength B: about 6,500 men and 180 officers, 16 field guns, about 550 fortress guns
losses B: unknown (80 dead found after the sortie of 8 July); about 5,600 captured
sources: de.wikipedia Belagerung der Festung Rastatt; de.wikipedia Gefechte an der Murglinie; de.wikipedia Badische Revolution
note: A loose blockade with bombardment; the main sortie, against Niederbühl and Rauental on 8 July, failed. The garrison surrendered unconditionally on 23 July, ending the revolution; 27 of 51 death sentences were carried out (Tiedemann, Biedenfeld, Böhning, Heilig, Elsenhans among them).

name: Fredericia (1849)
place: Fredericia, on the Little Belt, Jutland
commanders A: Christian Julius de Meza, Olaf Rye (killed), Colonel Niels Christian Lunding (garrison)
Prussian force: The besieging Schleswig-Holstein army (16,000) under the seconded Prussian general Eduard von Bonin, ordered to the siege by the Prussian commander-in-chief Karl von Prittwitz; no Prussian regular units engaged.
borderline: Fought by the Schleswig-Holstein army under Prussian officers on secondment; Prussian regulars not engaged.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Fought by the Schleswig-Holstein army under Prussian officers on secondment; Prussian regulars not engaged. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Fredericia; hhogman.se The First Schleswig War
note: A night sortie at 01:00 broke the siege begun on 9 May; an armistice followed (Prussia's of 10 July 1849) and all German troops had left Denmark by 25 August. en.wikipedia's figures are inconsistent with its own remark that the Danes were outnumbered.

name: Bronnzell
place: Bronnzell, south of Fulda, Electorate of Hesse (Hesse-Kassel)
Prussian force: Prussian outposts, including Hussar Regiment No. 10, facing the federal execution army of Bavarians and Austrians.
losses A: a trumpeter's horse (Heloise, the 'Schimmel von Bronnzell'), later put down; two officers' coats pierced
borderline: A limited outpost exchange of fire ('begrenztes Vorpostengefecht') stopped by officers.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A limited outpost exchange of fire ('begrenztes Vorpostengefecht') stopped by officers.
sources: de.wikipedia Schimmel von Bronnzell; de.wikipedia Herbstkrise 1850
note: The only shots fired between Prussia and the Austro-Bavarian federal army in the crisis over Hesse-Kassel; Frederick William IV shrank from war, the Prussians were pulled back to their supply roads and Prussia gave way at Olmütz (29 November 1850).

name: Tres Forcas
war: Prussian punitive expedition against the Rif pirates
place: Cape Tres Forcas (Three Forks), Rif coast, Morocco
Prussian force: A landing party of 68 from the corvette Danzig led by Prince Adalbert in person: 13 naval officers, a marine officer, 30 sailors and ship's boys and 23 marines.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht von Tres Forcas; en.wikipedia Battle of Tres Forcas
note: A landing, so typed 'land', though made by the navy. The opponents were Rif Berbers (Amazigh; en.wikipedia: 'Morocco'), punished for piracy against Prussian shipping. The party drove them onto a plateau but withdrew as reinforcements gathered; Adalbert was shot in the thigh, his adjutant Niesemann was killed and the 16-year-old Eduard von Knorr wounded.

name: Missunde
place: Missunde (Mysunde), on the south shore of the Schlei near Kosel, Duchy of Schleswig
commanders A: Georg Daniel Gerlach (with C. A. Vogt's 2nd Brigade and H. C. Hertel's fortress artillery)
Prussian force: Prince Frederick Charles's I Corps, about 10,000 men and 64 guns; the vanguard under Major von Krohn (fusiliers of the 24th, companies of the 15th, 7th Jäger, 3rd Hussars) and the 2nd Battalion of the 60th did the fighting.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht von Missunde; en.wikipedia Second Schleswig War
note: The first action of the war: after a long artillery duel in fog the Prussian command broke off the attempt to force the Schlei. The Danes evacuated the Danevirke, Missunde included, on the night of 5–6 February, and the Prussians crossed unopposed at Arnis on 6 February.

name: Jasmund
place: Off Rügen, east of the Jasmund peninsula, Bay of Pomerania
commanders A: Rear-Admiral Edvard van Dockum
Prussian force: Jachmann's squadron: the screw frigate Arcona, the corvette Nymphe and the paddle steamer Loreley, with six gunboats.
strength A: 1 ship of the line, 1 steam frigate, 2 steam corvettes
strength B: 2 steam corvettes (Arcona, Nymphe), 1 paddle steamer, 6 gunboats
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Jasmund (1864); en.wikipedia Second Schleswig War
note: A tactical Danish victory: after about two hours the Prussians were driven back to Swinemünde and the blockade held. en.wikipedia's infobox classes Arcona as a corvette.

name: Dybbøl (17 March 1864)
place: Dybbøl (Düppel) village and Rackebüll (Ragebøl), before the Dybbøl redoubts
commanders A: Prince Frederick Charles (I Corps)
Prussian force: Troops of Prince Frederick Charles's corps before Dybbøl (units not verified).
borderline: Named in German accounts as the 'Gefecht bei Düppel' (or Rackebüll) but verified here only from en.wikipedia's timeline; no article found.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Named in German accounts as the 'Gefecht bei Düppel' (or Rackebüll) but verified here only from en.wikipedia's timeline; no article found.
sources: en.wikipedia Second Schleswig War (timeline)
note: en.wikipedia: 'The Prussian army drives back the Danish outposts in front of Dybbøl.' Other pre-siege attacks (22 February, 28 March, 4 April) are not entered.

name: Fredericia (siege, 1864)
place: Fortress of Fredericia, on the Little Belt, Jutland
commanders A: Ludwig von Gablenz (Austrian corps); Field Marshal Friedrich von Wrangel (allied commander-in-chief)
Prussian force: Mainly Gablenz's Austrian corps (divisions of Gablenz and Neipperg); Prussian forces under Wrangel also took part (units not specified).
borderline: Austrian-led investment; bombardment from 20 March and a repelled sortie, no assault; the Prussian share is not quantified.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Austrian-led investment; bombardment from 20 March and a repelled sortie, no assault; the Prussian share is not quantified. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: de.wikipedia Evakuierung der Festung Fredericia; en.wikipedia Second Schleswig War
note: Wrangel's surrender demand was refused on 21 March; on 29 March the Danes surprised Austrian Guard Hussars at Assendrup. The garrison left for Funen on the nights of 27–29 April and the allies entered on 29 April. de.wikipedia's introduction wrongly dates the evacuation to 28 March.

name: Dybbøl (1864)
place: Dybbøl (Düppel) redoubts, opposite Sønderborg
commanders A: Prince Frederick Charles
Prussian force: Prince Frederick Charles's army: 11,000 men in the storming columns, 26,000 in reserve and 126 guns; about 65,000 shells were fired in the bombardment.
strength A: 11,000 in the first wave, 26,000 in reserve, 126 guns
strength B: 5,000 at the defences, 6,000 in reserve, 66 guns, 11 mortars, 1 ironclad
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Dybbøl; en.wikipedia Second Schleswig War; de.wikipedia Deutsch-Dänischer Krieg
note: Siege and bombardment from 2 April (en.wikipedia's infobox: 7–18 April). On 18 April the first line of redoubts fell within 13 minutes of the 10:00 assault; the Danish 8th Brigade's counter-attack (1,399 of about 3,000 lost) covered the retreat to Als. de.wikipedia gives about 4,800 Danish and 1,200 Prussian losses.

name: Heligoland
place: Off Heligoland, German Bight
commanders A: Edouard Suenson
commanders B: Wilhelm von Tegetthoff (Austria); Korvettenkapitän Gustav Klatt (Prussian flotilla)
Prussian force: A small Prussian flotilla under Gustav Klatt: the aviso Preussischer Adler and the gunboats Blitz and Basilisk, which lagged behind and fired with little effect.
strength A: 2 screw frigates (Niels Juel, Jylland), 1 screw corvette (Hejmdal)
strength B: 2 Austrian screw frigates (Schwarzenberg, Radetzky), 1 Prussian aviso, 2 Prussian gunboats
losses B: 36 killed, 108 wounded (Austrian); no Prussian losses reported
doubts and flags: Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Heligoland (1864); de.wikipedia Preußischer Adler (Schiff); de.wikipedia Deutsch-Dänischer Krieg
note: en.wikipedia calls the result disputed: a Danish tactical victory (the burning Schwarzenberg withdrew to neutral Heligoland waters), but the Danish blockade of the German North Sea ports ended.

name: Als
place: Island of Als (Alsen), crossing of the Alssund from Sottrup Skov/Øster Snogbæk to Arnkil
commanders A: Herwarth von Bittenfeld (Prince Frederick Charles as allied commander-in-chief)
Prussian force: Herwarth von Bittenfeld's corps of about 23,000, led by the Manstein and Wintzingerode divisions, crossing by boat at night and then by pontoon bridge.
strength B: about 10,000 and the monitor Rolf Krake
losses B: 3,092 (216 killed, 462 wounded, 1,878 captured, 536 missing); 30 guns captured
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Als; de.wikipedia Deutsch-Dänischer Krieg; en.wikipedia Second Schleswig War
note: en.wikipedia's infobox dates the operation 29 June – 1 July 1864; the crossing and battle were on 29 June. The Danes withdrew to Funen.

name: Lundby
place: Lundby, south of Aalborg, north Jutland
commanders A: Captain von Schlutterbach
Prussian force: One Prussian infantry company of 124 men under Captain von Schlutterbach, firing from behind an earth bank.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lundby; en.wikipedia Second Schleswig War; de.wikipedia Deutsch-Dänischer Krieg
note: The last battle of the war: a Danish company charging uphill was stopped about 20 metres short of the Prussian line. (A summary of de.wikipedia gave 11 July; en.wikipedia and the Danish tradition give 3 July.)

name: North Frisian Islands
place: Wyk harbour on Föhr and the Wadden Sea off the North Frisian Islands
commanders A: Bernhard von Wüllerstorf-Urbair, Wilhelm von Tegetthoff, Fregattenkapitän Karl Kronowetter (Austria); Kapitänleutnant Archibald MacLean (Prussian gunboat Blitz)
Prussian force: The Prussian gunboats Basilisk and Blitz alongside the Austrian ships (Juan d'Austria, Kaiser, Elisabeth, gunboats Seehund and Wall); Blitz caught Hammer, who surrendered on 19 July.
strength A: Austrian ironclad, ship of the line, steamer and 2 gunboats, 2 Prussian gunboats, about 200 Austrian Feldjäger
strength B: 2 steamers, 8 gun launches, 12 customs cutters and 10 other craft, about 250 men
losses B: 9 officers and 185 sailors captured (the text: 7 officers, 2 officials and 185 men); flotilla taken
borderline: Mainly an Austrian operation with little fighting (the bombardment of the Danish flotilla at Wyk and its surrender), fought as the armistice was being concluded.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Mainly an Austrian operation with little fighting (the bombardment of the Danish flotilla at Wyk and its surrender), fought as the armistice was being concluded. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: de.wikipedia Einnahme der nordfriesischen Inseln
note: de.wikipedia 'Einnahme der nordfriesischen Inseln': landings on Sylt (12–13 July) were Austrian; the bombardment at Wyk began on 18 July and fighting resumed on 19 July because the armistice took effect only on 20 July. The captured craft were taken to Cuxhaven as Prussian prizes.

name: Langenbruck
place: Langenbruck (now Dlouhý Most) and Münkendorf (now Minkovice), on the road south-west of Reichenberg (Liberec), Bohemia
commanders A: advance guard of the 8th Division, Prince Frederick Charles's First Army (commander at the action not named)
Prussian force: A squadron of the 6th Uhlan Regiment leading the 8th Division on the Reichenberg road, supported by the division's infantry, whose rifle fire stopped the Austrian hussars' counter-charge.
strength A: 1 squadron of the 6th Uhlans (with infantry in support)
strength B: 2.5 squadrons of Liechtenstein Hussars (infobox); the text names three Liechtenstein squadrons and the Radetzky Hussars
losses B: not given (losses from the Prussian infantry fire)
borderline: A small cavalry clash (one Prussian squadron), named as a Gefecht by de.wikipedia.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A small cavalry clash (one Prussian squadron), named as a Gefecht by de.wikipedia.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Langenbruck
note: The uhlans drove an Austrian half-squadron out of Münkendorf, were thrown back by two squadrons onto their infantry, and the hussars withdrew to Langenbruck under heavy rifle fire. The First Army had crossed into Bohemia on 23 June.

name: Hühnerwasser
place: Hühnerwasser (now Kuřívody, part of Ralsko), south of Böhmisch Leipa (Česká Lípa)
commanders A: Karl Eberhard Herwarth von Bittenfeld (Elbe Army), Alexander von Schoeler
Prussian force: The advance guard of Herwarth von Bittenfeld's Elbe Army: von Schoeler's brigade, one brigade engaged.
losses B: 277 killed, wounded and captured (13 officers and 264 men)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Hühnerwasser; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Hühnerwasser
note: The first engagement of the war in Bohemia; Gondrecourt broke off his attack and fell back on Münchengrätz.

name: Liebenau
place: Liebenau (now Hodkovice nad Mohelkou), south-east of Reichenberg (Liberec), towards Sichrow (Sychrov)
commanders A: Heinrich von Horn (8th Division, advance of Prince Frederick Charles's First Army)
Prussian force: The advance guard of the First Army (8th Division with cavalry and artillery) pushing south from Reichenberg towards the Iser.
borderline: Minor advance-guard and cavalry action; no Wikipedia article with details found, commanders and outcome from the course of the advance rather than a verified account.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Minor advance-guard and cavalry action; no Wikipedia article with details found, commanders and outcome from the course of the advance rather than a verified account.
sources: de.wikipedia Deutscher Krieg (mentions the Gefecht bei Liebenau); Prussian General Staff, Der Feldzug von 1866 in Deutschland (from knowledge, not verified online)
note: de.wikipedia Deutscher Krieg dates it 25 June; the Prussian General Staff account places it on 26 June, the morning before Podol. The Austrian light cavalry fell back from Liebenau and Sichrow towards Turnau; the Prussians then occupied Turnau without a fight.

name: Podol
place: Podol (now part of Svijany), at the Iser (Jizera) bridges south of Turnau (Turnov)
commanders A: Julius von Bose (15th Brigade, 8th Division)
Prussian force: The advance guard of the 8th Division (five companies under Major Flotow), then Bose's 15th Brigade of the First Army; a night fight for the village and the Iser bridges.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Podol; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Hühnerwasser (context)
note: Fought from about 8.30 pm to 1 am; the Prussian breech-loader's first big effect on Austrian shock tactics.

name: Oświęcim
place: Oświęcim (Auschwitz) railway station and Brzezinka, western Galicia
commanders A: Johann von Trentinaglia (brigade), Friedrich von Ziegler (garrison)
Prussian force: Count Stolberg-Wernigerode's Upper Silesian detachment, about 3,000-4,000: two fusilier companies of the 62nd Regiment, four Landwehr battalions, the Landwehr Uhlan Regiment and two guns.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Oświęcim (1866)
note: A raid to cut the Kraków-Olmütz railway; the Prussians took Brzezinka but failed to clear the station and withdrew towards Nikolai. One of the few Austrian successes of the war. (en.wikipedia's infobox wrongly says Bohemia.)

name: Náchod
place: Náchod and the Wysokow (Vysokov) plateau, Bohemia
commanders A: Karl Friedrich von Steinmetz
Prussian force: Steinmetz's V Corps of the Crown Prince's Second Army, with Kirchbach's 10th Division arriving to secure the Wysokow heights.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Náchod; de.wikipedia 2. Armee (Deutscher Krieg)

name: Trautenau
place: Trautenau (now Trutnov), Bohemia
commanders A: Ludwig von Gablenz (X Corps)
Prussian force: Bonin's I Corps and the cavalry reserve of the Second Army; driven back through the pass to Goldenöls.
losses A: 4,787 killed, wounded and captured (191 officers and 4,596 men); en.wikipedia 5,000
losses B: 1,338 killed and wounded (56 officers and 1,282 men); en.wikipedia 1,400
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Trautenau; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Trautenau
note: The only Austrian victory over a Prussian army corps in Bohemia, bought at more than three times the Prussian loss.

name: Langensalza (1866)
place: Langensalza (now Bad Langensalza), on the Unstrut by Merxleben
commanders A: George V of Hanover, Alexander von Arentschildt
commanders B: Eduard von Flies (Eduard Vogel von Falckenstein in overall command)
Prussian force: Flies's detachment of about 9,000 (Prussian line and Landwehr troops with the Saxe-Coburg and Gotha regiment), attacking the Hanoverian army without orders.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Langensalza (1866); de.wikipedia Deutscher Krieg
note: Allies of Prussia: Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. A Hanoverian tactical victory, but the encircled Hanoverian army capitulated on 29 June.

name: Münchengrätz
place: Münchengrätz (now Mnichovo Hradiště), on the Iser (Jizera)
commanders A: Prince Frederick Charles, Karl Eberhard Herwarth von Bittenfeld
Prussian force: The Elbe Army (31st Brigade) with the 7th and 8th Divisions of the First Army; about 14,000 and 18 guns engaged.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Münchengrätz
note: Clam-Gallas's Iser Army (Leiningen's, Piret's and Abele's brigades) fell back towards Gitschin; the Saxons of the Iser Army were not seriously engaged.

name: Skalitz
place: Skalitz (now Česká Skalice), on the Aupa (Úpa)
commanders A: Karl Friedrich von Steinmetz
Prussian force: Steinmetz's V Corps (9th and 10th Divisions) of the Second Army.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Skalitz; de.wikipedia 2. Armee (Deutscher Krieg)

name: Burkersdorf (1866)
place: Burkersdorf (now Střítež, part of Trutnov), Soor (Žďár) and Rudersdorf (Rubínovice), south of Trautenau (Trutnov)
commanders A: Crown Prince Frederick William, Prince August of Württemberg (Guard Corps)
Prussian force: Prince August of Württemberg's Guard Corps: Hiller von Gärtringen's 1st Guard Division at Burkersdorf and Plonski's 2nd Guard Division, which cut off and nearly destroyed Grivičić's brigade at Rudersdorf.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Burkersdorf (1866); de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Trautenau, Gefecht bei Königinhof, 2. Armee (Deutscher Krieg)
note: German works call it the Gefecht bei Soor (Burkersdorf); the fight with Grivičić's brigade at Rudersdorf/Neu-Rognitz is treated here as part of it, not as a separate entry. It reversed Trautenau and forced Gablenz to retreat.

name: Gitschin
place: Gitschin (now Jičín), Bohemia
commanders A: August von Werder (3rd Division), Wilhelm von Tümpling (5th Division)
commanders B: Eduard Clam-Gallas, Crown Prince Albert of Saxony
Prussian force: The 3rd and 5th Divisions of the First Army, about 26,000 (24 battalions, 36 guns) under Werder and Tümpling.
losses A: 1,553 killed and wounded (71 officers and 1,482 men; en.wikipedia: 329 killed, 1,212 wounded)
losses B: 5,295 (Austrians 4,704, Saxons 591); de.wikipedia: 183 officers and 5,111 men, at least 217 captured
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Gitschin; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Gitschin
note: The Prussians stormed Gitschin and took 20 guns; the Iser Army fell back to the upper Elbe.

name: Königinhof
place: Königinhof (now Dvůr Králové nad Labem), on the Elbe
commanders A: Prince August of Württemberg, Colonel Bernhard von Kessel
commanders B: Colonel von Stocklin (Infantry Regiment Coronini No. 6)
Prussian force: The advance guard of the Guard Corps (1st Foot Guards) under Colonel von Kessel, about 5,000 committed.
strength B: 800 (de.wikipedia); en.wikipedia gives 15,000-20,000 for the Austrian forces nearby
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Königinhof; en.wikipedia Battle of Königinhof
note: Stocklin surrendered with much of the Coronini regiment, which lost a colour.

name: Schweinschädel
place: Schweinschädel (now Svinišťany), on the Aupa (Úpa) near Jaroměř
commanders A: Karl Friedrich von Steinmetz, Hugo von Kirchbach
Prussian force: Steinmetz's V Corps, two divisions, about 24,000.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Schweinschädel; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Schweinschädel

name: Königgrätz
place: Sadowa (Sadová) and Chlum, north-west of Königgrätz (Hradec Králové)
commanders A: Wilhelm I, Helmuth von Moltke, Prince Frederick Charles, Crown Prince Frederick William, Karl Eberhard Herwarth von Bittenfeld
commanders B: Ludwig von Benedek, Crown Prince Albert of Saxony
Prussian force: The whole Prussian field army in Bohemia under Wilhelm I and Moltke: Frederick Charles's First Army, Herwarth's Elbe Army and the Crown Prince's Second Army, whose arrival on the Austrian right at Chlum decided it; about 221,000.
losses B: Austrians 42,812 (5,658 killed, 7,574 wounded, 7,410 missing, 22,170 captured); Saxons 1,501
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Königgrätz; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Königgrätz; Wawro, The Austro-Prussian War (1996)
note: Also called Sadowa. de.wikipedia gives Prussian losses of 359 officers and 8,794 men (1,929 killed, 6,948 wounded, 276 missing) and Saxon losses of 135 killed, 940 wounded, 426 missing.

name: Dermbach
place: Dermbach, Zella and Wiesenthal, Rhön (Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach)
commanders A: August von Goeben (13th Division); Eduard Vogel von Falckenstein (Main Army)
commanders B: Prince Karl of Bavaria; Friedrich von Zoller, Jakob von Hartmann
Prussian force: Goeben's 13th Division of the Main Army, attacking Zella (Kummer) and Wiesenthal (Wrangel) with about 5,000 men in each thrust.
strength A: about 5,000 in each of the two attacks
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Dermbach; en.wikipedia Battle of Dermbach; historyofwar.org Battle of Dermbach
note: en.wikipedia and historyofwar.org call it a Prussian victory; de.wikipedia finds no clear winner: Goeben took Zella, Wiesenthal and the Nebelberg and then withdrew as planned, and the Bavarians claimed success. The Bavarians concentrated at Kaltennordheim on 5 July and then left Thuringia. Bavarian losses from de.wikipedia (en.wikipedia's figure is not usable).

name: Hünfeld
place: Hünfeld, north-east of Fulda (Electorate of Hesse)
commanders A: Gustav von Beyer
commanders B: Prince of Thurn und Taxis (Bavarian Reserve Cavalry)
Prussian force: The leading troops of Beyer's division of the Main Army, marching from Geisa.
borderline: Small encounter; the Bavarian cavalry fled after brief firing.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Small encounter; the Bavarian cavalry fled after brief firing.
sources: en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main; historyofwar.org Battle of Dermbach; Frankenland (Würzburg) journal article on 1866
note: The Bavarian Reserve Cavalry broke and scattered towards Gersfeld, Bischofsheim, Brückenau and Hammelburg, ending any junction of the Bavarians with the VIII Federal Corps at Fulda.

name: Kissingen
place: Kissingen (now Bad Kissingen), on the Franconian Saale, with Friedrichshall, Aschach and Nüdlingen
commanders A: Eduard Vogel von Falckenstein, August von Goeben, Edwin von Manteuffel
commanders B: Prince Karl of Bavaria, Oskar von Zoller (killed), Johann Baptist Stephan
Prussian force: The Main Army under Vogel von Falckenstein: Goeben's 13th Division stormed Kissingen and Manteuffel's division fought at Friedrichshall and Nüdlingen; about 18,000 (16 battalions, 9 squadrons, 31 guns).
sources: de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Kissingen; en.wikipedia Battle of Kissingen; en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main
note: Losses as de.wikipedia gives them, for the day's fighting on the Saale with no breakdown by action; en.wikipedia's infobox figures are inconsistent. Hammelburg the same day is a separate entry.

name: Hammelburg
place: Hammelburg, on the Franconian Saale
commanders A: Gustav von Beyer
Prussian force: Beyer's division of the Main Army; its artillery forced the Bavarians from the Thulba line and the town.
borderline: de.wikipedia treats it inside the Kissingen article; en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main names it separately.
doubts and flags: Borderline: de.wikipedia treats it inside the Kissingen article; en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main names it separately.
sources: de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Kissingen (Gefechte bei Kissingen und Hammelburg); en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main; en.wikipedia Battle of Kissingen
note: The Bavarians retreated over the Saale towards Arnstein.

name: Laufach
place: Laufach and Frohnhofen, in the Spessart east of Aschaffenburg
commanders A: August von Goeben, Karl von Wrangel
Prussian force: Part of Goeben's 13th Division (Wrangel's 26th Brigade): 7 battalions, 2 squadrons, 2 batteries.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Frohnhofen; en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main
note: de.wikipedia: Gefecht bei Frohnhofen. The Hessian (3rd) Division of the VIII Federal Corps attacked and was repulsed; the text gives 124 Hessian prisoners, the infobox 115.

name: Aschaffenburg
place: Aschaffenburg, on the Main (the Fasanerie, the Herstall gate and the Main bridge)
commanders A: August von Goeben, Ferdinand von Kummer
commanders B: Erwin von Neipperg, Major-General von Hahn
Prussian force: Goeben's 13th Division of the Main Army, about 16,600.
losses A: 171 (27 killed, 144 wounded); regimental histories: 17 officers and 163 men killed and wounded
losses B: 710 killed and wounded (226 killed, 484 wounded), and the Austrians alone about 1,986 captured (22 officers and 1,964 men)
sources: de.wikipedia Gefechte bei Aschaffenburg; en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main
note: The Federal troops were mainly Hahn's Austrian brigade of Neipperg's 4th Division of the VIII Federal Corps, with Hessian (Darmstadt) and Kurhessian units; many were cut off at the Main bridge. Frankfurt was occupied without a fight on 16 July.

name: Tobitschau
place: Tobitschau (now Tovačov) and Dub (Dub nad Moravou), on the March (Morava) south of Olmütz (Olomouc)
commanders A: Adolf von Bonin (I Corps), Major-General von Malotki, Julius von Hartmann
commanders B: Ludwig von Benedek; Rothkirch's brigade of VIII Corps
Prussian force: Malotki's brigade (4th and 44th Regiments) of Bonin's I Corps from Prossnitz, with Prussian cuirassiers who captured 18 guns, and Hartmann's cavalry division of the Second Army.
losses B: over 2,000 including many prisoners (historyofwar.org); VIII Corps and Saxons 1,584: 265 killed, 399 wounded, 181 missing, 739 captured (armedconflicts.com)
sources: historyofwar.org Battle of Tobitschau; armedconflicts.com (Infantry Regiment Reischach); de.wikipedia Egbert von Frankenberg und Proschlitz (Gefecht bei Tobitschau)
note: Cut the Austrian Northern Army's retreat from Olmütz along the March, nearly capturing Benedek, and forced it east over the Little Carpathians; the Prussians drew back at the end of the day. historyofwar.org heads its page 16 July but describes the fighting on 15 July.

name: Rokytnice
place: Rokeinitz (now Rokytnice), Dluhonice and Předmostí, south of Prerau (Přerov)
commanders A: Julius von Hartmann
Prussian force: Hartmann's cavalry division, about 8 1/2 squadrons (some 1,200 riders), one horse battery and an infantry company, crossing the March and Bečva.
strength B: two brigades of I Corps engaged (about 15,000 in the area)
borderline: Often counted as part of Tobitschau (same day, same pursuit); listed separately because the Austrian and Prussian staff histories name a Rokeinitz action, but not verified in an encyclopaedia article.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Often counted as part of Tobitschau (same day, same pursuit); listed separately because the Austrian and Prussian staff histories name a Rokeinitz action, but not verified in an encyclopaedia article.
sources: Czech local-history account of the 1866 fighting at Rokytnice and Přerov (geocaching.com GC6ZCC9); historyofwar.org Battle of Tobitschau (Hartmann's crossing of the Bečva)
note: Hartmann's charges drove two Austrian brigades from Rokytnice and Dluhonice and raided a supply train at Předmostí; an Austrian hussar counterattack (12th Hussars) freed prisoners and Hartmann withdrew to Tobitschau about 5 pm. The Prussians entered Přerov on 16 July.

name: Blumenau
place: Blumenau (now Lamač, part of Bratislava), north of Pressburg (Bratislava)
commanders A: Eduard von Fransecky, Julius von Bose
commanders B: Archduke Albrecht (at Pressburg); Count Thun-Hohenstein (II Corps), Friedrich von Mondel
Prussian force: Fransecky's force (7th and 8th Divisions), 18 1/2 battalions, 24 squadrons and 78 guns, with Bose's brigade turning the Austrian flank through the hills.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lamacs; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Blumenau
note: en.wikipedia's article is titled 'Battle of Lamacs' but calls it Blumenau. Broken off at noon by the armistice with Bose's brigade behind the Austrian flank; the Austrians withdrew into Pressburg, which stayed in their hands. en.wikipedia: Prussian victory; de.wikipedia gives no verdict. Loss figures are unlabelled in both infoboxes and assigned by their order (de.wikipedia: 207 Prussian, 489 Austrian). The last Prussian-Austrian fight of the war.

name: Hundheim
place: Hundheim (now part of Külsheim), west of the Tauber
commanders A: Colonel Hermann von Fabeck; Eduard Moritz von Flies (division)
commanders B: Major-General von La Roche (1st Baden Brigade); Prince Wilhelm of Baden (division)
Prussian force: The Saxe-Coburg and Gotha Infantry Regiment of Flies's Prussian division, with a squadron of the Magdeburg Dragoons No. 6 and two guns, about 1,300 under Colonel von Fabeck.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Hundheim; de.wikipedia Mainfeldzug; en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main
note: Allies of Prussia: Saxe-Coburg and Gotha (its regiment served in the Prussian army under the 1861 military convention). Fabeck fell back to the Tiefentaler Hof and the Badeners did not follow, then withdrew behind the Tauber that night; de.wikipedia names no winner, en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main counts it a Prussian success.

name: Tauberbischofsheim
place: Tauberbischofsheim, on the Tauber (Grand Duchy of Baden)
commanders A: August von Goeben (13th Division); Edwin von Manteuffel (Main Army)
commanders B: Oskar von Hardegg (Württemberg division); Prince Alexander of Hesse (VIII Federal Corps)
Prussian force: Goeben's 13th Division of Manteuffel's Main Army (the Main Army then about 60,000).
strength B: 42,000 (whole VIII Federal Corps; the Württemberg division engaged)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Tauberbischofsheim; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Tauberbischofsheim
note: The Württemberg (1st) Division of the VIII Federal Corps was thrown back over the Tauber; en.wikipedia also lists Baden, Hesse-Darmstadt, Austria and Nassau as belligerents for the corps as a whole.

name: Werbach
place: Werbach and Hochhausen, on the Tauber (Grand Duchy of Baden)
commanders A: August von Goeben, Ludwig von Weltzien
Prussian force: Weltzien's Oldenburg-Hanseatic Brigade of Goeben's 13th Division, about 5,000.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Werbach; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Werbach
note: Allies of Prussia: Oldenburg and the Hanseatic cities (Bremen, Hamburg, Lübeck). The Badeners gave up Werbach after Hochhausen fell.

name: Gerchsheim
place: Gerchsheim (now part of Großrinderfeld), between the Tauber and Würzburg
commanders A: Edwin von Manteuffel, August von Goeben
Prussian force: Goeben's 13th Division (25th and 26th Brigades, with the Oldenburg-Hanseatic troops), about 16,000.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Gerchsheim; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Gerchsheim
note: Allies of Prussia: Oldenburg. The VIII Federal Corps (Württemberg, Baden, Hesse-Darmstadt and Austro-Nassau divisions) was driven back towards Würzburg; fighting ended at dark.

name: Helmstadt
place: Helmstadt, Uettingen and Neubrunn, west of Würzburg
commanders A: Edwin von Manteuffel, Gustav von Beyer
commanders B: Prince Karl of Bavaria, Johann Baptist Stephan, Prince Luitpold
Prussian force: Beyer's division of the Main Army, about 15,000.
losses A: 353 killed, wounded and missing (13 officers and 340 men)
losses B: 730 killed, wounded and missing (36 officers and 694 men)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Helmstadt; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Helmstadt; de.wikipedia Mainfeldzug
note: Against the Bavarian 1st (Stephan) and 3rd (Luitpold) Divisions; the 3rd ran out of ammunition. Prince Ludwig (later Ludwig III) was wounded. The fighting at Uettingen and Neubrunn on 25 July is counted here.

name: Rossbrunn
place: Roßbrunn, Uettingen and Hettstadt, west of Würzburg
commanders A: Eduard von Flies, Ludwig von Korth, Thassilo Krug von Nidda, Hugo von Thile
commanders B: Jakob von Hartmann (4th Division), Maximilian von Feder (2nd Division)
Prussian force: Flies's division of the Main Army (Korth's 2nd combined brigade, the 59th and 36th Regiments, and Krug von Nidda's cavalry).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Roßbrunn; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Roßbrunn and Gefechte bei Uettingen; en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main; de.wikipedia Deutscher Krieg
note: Also called Uettingen (de.wikipedia's navbox: 'Uettingen/Roßbrunn'); one entry for the 26 July fighting. Verdicts differ: en.wikipedia Battle of Roßbrunn 'Bavarian victory', de.wikipedia 'unentschieden', en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main and de.wikipedia Deutscher Krieg a Prussian win. Scored here on the field: the Prussians repulsed the dawn attack on Uettingen and took the Kirchberg, Osnert and Heiligenberg heights, the Bavarian cavalry won the cavalry fight at Hettstadt, and the Bavarians withdrew behind the Main to Würzburg. Losses as en.wikipedia assigns them.

name: Würzburg (bombardment)
place: Marienberg Fortress, Würzburg
commanders A: Edwin von Manteuffel
commanders B: Prince Karl of Bavaria (army behind the Main)
Prussian force: The artillery of Manteuffel's Main Army, firing on the Marienberg from the left bank of the Main.
borderline: An artillery bombardment and counter-battery exchange, not an infantry engagement; may fall under the rule that leaves out bombardments without an engagement.
doubts and flags: Borderline: An artillery bombardment and counter-battery exchange, not an infantry engagement; may fall under the rule that leaves out bombardments without an engagement.
sources: en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main; en.wikipedia Marienberg Fortress; de.wikipedia Mainfeldzug
note: The arsenal (Zeughaus) burned; the shelling stopped with a local truce once news of the Nikolsburg armistice arrived, and the Prussians later occupied Würzburg. en.wikipedia Campaign of the Main and de.wikipedia Mainfeldzug put the start on 26 July; 27 July is the usual date in German accounts.

name: Seybothenreuth
place: Seybothenreuth, south-east of Bayreuth
commanders A: Grand Duke Friedrich Franz II of Mecklenburg-Schwerin (II Reserve Corps)
Prussian force: The advance of the Prussian II Reserve Corps (Prussian and Mecklenburg troops, about 25,000 in all) under the Grand Duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, advancing from Hof on Bayreuth and Nuremberg.
strength B: about 8,000 (whole Bavarian eastern corps); the IV Battalion of the Infantry Leib Regiment engaged
borderline: Small action against a single Bavarian battalion.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Small action against a single Bavarian battalion.
sources: de.wikipedia Mainfeldzug; de.wikipedia Königlich Bayerisches Infanterie-Leib-Regiment; de.wikipedia Deutscher Krieg
note: The last fight of the war: the Bavarian battalion was scattered. Nuremberg was occupied without a fight on 31 July.

name: Schirlenhof
place: Schirlenhof inn near Gundershoffen, south-west of Niederbronn-les-Bains (Bas-Rhin)
commanders B: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin (Württemberg General Staff)
Prussian force: No Prussian troops: a mounted reconnaissance patrol of Baden dragoons led by the Württemberg staff officer Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, surprised at the Schirlenhof inn by French chasseurs à cheval.
losses A: Maréchal des logis Claude Férréol Pagnier killed
losses B: Lieutenant Winsloe (Baden dragoons) killed; most of the patrol captured, Zeppelin escaped
borderline: South German troops only; a patrol fight, the first clash of the war, named in German works (Gefecht/Patrouillengefecht am Schirlenhof)
doubts and flags: Borderline: South German troops only; a patrol fight, the first clash of the war, named in German works (Gefecht/Patrouillengefecht am Schirlenhof). Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: Alsace Verte, 'Graves of the first victims of the war of 1870' (Niederbronn); Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961); de.wikipedia Gefecht am Schirlenhof (title only, page not reached)
note: The German side is entered as 'Prussia' (the federal command) with Baden and Württemberg as allies, but only South German riders fought. The French dead and the Baden officer are buried at Niederbronn.

name: Saarbrücken
place: Saarbrücken and St. Johann, the heights south of the town (Rhine Province of Prussia; now Saarland)
commanders A: Charles Frossard (II Corps), with Napoleon III and the Prince Imperial present; Bazaine nominally in charge
Prussian force: Pestel's outpost detachment at Saarbrücken, elements of the 40th (Hohenzollern) Fusilier Regiment of the 16th Division with uhlans, about 1,400 infantry, which fell back across the Saar in good order.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Saarbrücken; Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961); Wawro, The Franco-Prussian War (2003)
note: The only French offensive of the war's opening: three French divisions pushed back a single Prussian outpost; Napoleon III's 'baptism of fire' for the Prince Imperial. The French did not exploit it.

name: Wissembourg (1870)
place: Wissembourg (Weißenburg) and the Geisberg heights, on the Lauter (Bas-Rhin)
commanders A: Crown Prince Frederick William (Third Army); Hugo von Kirchbach (V Corps), Julius von Bose (XI Corps), Jakob von Hartmann (II Bavarian Corps)
Prussian force: The advance of the Crown Prince's Third Army: Kirchbach's V Corps and Bose's XI Corps with Bothmer's 4th Bavarian Division, about 25,000 men and 144 guns engaged; the Prussian King's Grenadiers stormed the Geisberg.
losses B: 1,600 killed and wounded, 700 captured (en.wikipedia infobox; its text gives about 1,000 killed and wounded and 1,000 prisoners)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Wissembourg (1870); de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Weißenburg (1870) (listed in Kategorie:Konflikt 1870); Howard (1961)
note: First German victory of the war; Douay's division of MacMahon's I Corps was overwhelmed and Douay killed. en.wikipedia also lists Baden and Württemberg on the German side, but their troops were not engaged.

name: Wörth
place: Wœrth (Wörth) and Frœschwiller on the Sauer, north of Haguenau (Bas-Rhin)
commanders A: Crown Prince Frederick William (Third Army), Leonhard von Blumenthal (chief of staff); Hugo von Kirchbach (V Corps), Julius von Bose (XI Corps), Jakob von Hartmann (II Bavarian Corps)
Prussian force: The Crown Prince's Third Army; Kirchbach's V Corps and Bose's XI Corps carried the battle at Wörth, Elsasshausen and Frœschwiller, with Hartmann's II Bavarian Corps on the right and the Württemberg Division in support.
losses B: 15,096 (5,884 killed and wounded, 9,212 missing or captured), 28 guns
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Wœrth/Frœschwiller; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Wörth; Howard (1961); Wawro (2003)
note: Also called Frœschwiller or Reichshoffen (the French name, after the charge of the cuirassiers). MacMahon's army abandoned Alsace and retreated to Châlons.

name: Spicheren
place: The Spicheren heights (Rotherberg) and Stiring-Wendel, between Saarbrücken and Forbach (Moselle)
commanders A: Karl Friedrich von Steinmetz (First Army); on the field Georg von Kameke (14th Division), then August von Goeben, Heinrich von Zastrow and Constantin von Alvensleben
Prussian force: Kameke's 14th Division (VII Corps) attacked on its own initiative, with François's 27th Brigade in the lead (François killed); reinforced piecemeal from VII and VIII Corps of the First Army and Alvensleben's III Corps of the Second Army.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Spicheren; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Spichern; Howard (1961)
note: Also called Forbach or Spichern. Fought the same day as Wörth; Frossard withdrew towards Metz and the French Army of the Rhine fell back on the Moselle.

name: Bitche (siege, 1870–71)
place: Citadel of Bitche (Bitsch), northern Vosges (Moselle)
commanders A: Commandant Louis-Casimir Teyssier
Prussian force: Not a Prussian siege: the blockade and bombardment were carried out by Bavarian troops (Kohlermann's detachment from Germersheim, later more Bavarian battalions); the Prussian IV Corps only passed the fortress on 8–9 August.
losses B: 23 killed, 62 wounded (infobox; the text gives 19 killed and 62 wounded Bavarians)
borderline: South German troops only (Bavarians; a Württemberg regiment shelled it in August per the Stuttgarter Zeitung); no Prussian unit is recorded fighting at the fortress
doubts and flags: Borderline: South German troops only (Bavarians; a Württemberg regiment shelled it in August per the Stuttgarter Zeitung); no Prussian unit is recorded fighting at the fortress. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Bitche; Stuttgarter Zeitung, 'Die Zitadelle Bitsch im Deutsch-Französischen Krieg: eingeschlossen, aber unbesiegt'
note: Bombardments 23 August and 11–21 September, then blockade. The citadel never surrendered: Teyssier's garrison marched out under arms on 25/26 March 1871 after the peace preliminaries and the keys were handed over on 26 March. en.wikipedia's infobox says 'German victory'; here the defender is counted the victor because the place was never taken. End date varies (25–27 March) in the sources.

name: Lichtenberg (siege, 1870)
place: Lichtenberg Castle, northern Vosges (Bas-Rhin)
commanders A: Hugo von Obernitz (Württemberg Field Division), Hermann von Hügel (attack column)
Prussian force: No Prussian units: a Württemberg column under Generalmajor von Hügel (1st and 3rd Jäger Battalions, two infantry companies, three batteries, a pioneer detachment) of the Württemberg Division commanded by the Prussian general von Obernitz.
strength A: two Jäger battalions, two companies, three batteries
losses A: 2 officers and 36 men killed and wounded (12 killed, 24 wounded)
losses B: 10 killed, 27 wounded, the rest of the garrison captured; 4 guns, 3 howitzers and 204 Chassepots taken
borderline: South German troops only (Württembergers under a Prussian divisional commander)
doubts and flags: Borderline: South German troops only (Württembergers under a Prussian divisional commander). Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Lichtenberg
note: The castle was bombarded and set on fire on 9 August; the garrison raised the white flag that night and the castle was occupied on 10 August. en.wikipedia's strength line '30 officers and 280 soldiers' is ambiguous (possibly the garrison) and is not used.

name: Phalsbourg (siege, 1870)
place: Phalsbourg (Pfalzburg), at the Saverne pass of the Vosges (Moselle)
commanders A: Wilhelm von Tümpling (VI Corps); Major von Giese (siege)
Prussian force: The 12th Division of Tümpling's VI Corps blockaded and shelled the fortress from 13 August; from 18–19 August Silesian Landwehr with a battery under Major von Giese kept up the blockade.
strength B: a battalion of the 63rd Line, 100 gunners, a Garde Mobile battalion and about 500 Algerian troops and Zouaves
losses A: 1 officer and 1 man wounded (en.wikipedia; evidently incomplete)
losses B: 52 officers and about 1,837 men captured, 65 guns
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Phalsbourg; Howard (1961)
note: Start date 10 August per en.wikipedia (first summons and shelling); the blockade proper began 13 August. A French sortie at Unter-Eichen-Baracken on 24 August was repulsed. The garrison capitulated from hunger and smallpox on 12 December; Germans entered on 14 December.

name: Marsal (siege, 1870)
place: Marsal, on the Seille, south of Château-Salins (Moselle)
commanders A: Jakob von Hartmann (II Bavarian Corps), Friedrich von Bothmer (4th Bavarian Division)
Prussian force: The Prussian 4th Cavalry Division summoned Marsal on 13 August without result; on 14 August the II Bavarian Corps (Bothmer's 4th Division, 7th Infantry Brigade and corps artillery) bombarded it into surrender.
strength A: 7th Bavarian Infantry Brigade, a cavalry brigade and the corps artillery reserve
losses B: 16 officers and several hundred men captured, 61 guns, about 8,000 rifles
borderline: South German troops only (the Prussian cavalry only summoned it); a short bombardment and surrender with little fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: South German troops only (the Prussian cavalry only summoned it); a short bombardment and surrender with little fighting. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Marsal; de.wikipedia Belagerung von Toul (guns taken at Marsal used against Toul)
note: The fall of Marsal opened the road from Dieuze to Nancy.

name: Borny–Colombey
place: Between Colombey, Borny and Noisseville, east of Metz (Moselle)
commanders A: Karl Friedrich von Steinmetz (First Army); Heinrich von Zastrow (VII Corps), Edwin von Manteuffel (I Corps)
commanders B: Marshal François Achille Bazaine; Claude Decaen (III Corps, mortally wounded), Paul de Ladmirault (IV Corps)
Prussian force: Von der Goltz's 26th Brigade (VII Corps) attacked the French rearguard on its own initiative and drew in Zastrow's VII Corps and Manteuffel's I Corps of Steinmetz's First Army.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Borny–Colombey; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Colombey (listed in Kategorie:Konflikt 1870); Howard (1961)
note: Also Colombey-Nouilly or Borny. Tactically indecisive (en.wikipedia: 'inconclusive'); the French held their line and withdrew into Metz at night as planned, but the fight delayed Bazaine's retreat across the Moselle by a day, which German works count as a success.

name: Strasbourg (siege, 1870)
place: Strasbourg (Straßburg), Bas-Rhin
commanders A: August von Werder
Prussian force: Werder's siege corps: the Baden Division with the Prussian Guard Landwehr Division, the 1st Reserve Division and Landwehr battalions (Schneidemühl, Konitz, Deutsch-Krone), Prussian and Württemberg siege artillery and engineers, about 40,000 men.
losses A: 936 (177 killed or died of wounds, 715 wounded, 44 missing)
losses B: about 2,500 killed and wounded (German General Staff estimate; 861 deaths from all causes), 17,562 captured; 1,277 guns taken; 341 civilians killed
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Strasbourg; de.wikipedia Belagerung von Toul (campaign navbox); Howard (1961)
note: The Baden Division observed the city from 11 August; the siege corps arrived and opened fire on 14 August and the bombardment of the city began on 23 August. Sorties on 16, 28 and 29 August were repulsed. Capitulated 28 September.

name: Toul (siege, 1870)
place: Toul on the Moselle, west of Nancy (Meurthe-et-Moselle)
commanders A: Gustav von Alvensleben (IV Corps; Zychlinski led the assault of 16 August); later Grand Duke Frederick Francis II of Mecklenburg-Schwerin (XIII Corps)
Prussian force: On 16 August Zychlinski's reinforced 14th Infantry Brigade (27th and 93rd Regiments) of the IV Corps failed in a coup de main; the siege was finished by the Grand Duke of Mecklenburg's XIII Corps (17th Division, 2nd Landwehr Division) with siege artillery.
losses A: 232 (54 killed or died of wounds, 169 wounded, 9 missing)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Toul; de.wikipedia Belagerung von Toul
note: Elements of the II Bavarian Corps (5th Bavarian Infantry Regiment, using guns taken at Marsal) also took part in the first attempt (de.wikipedia). After the failed assault Toul was only blockaded; the formal siege opened on 12 September and the place capitulated on 23 September after a bombardment, freeing the railway to Paris.

name: Mars-la-Tour
place: Mars-la-Tour, Vionville and Rezonville, west of Metz on the Verdun road (Meurthe-et-Moselle and Moselle)
commanders A: Prince Frederick Charles (Second Army); Constantin von Alvensleben (III Corps), Konstantin von Voigts-Rhetz (X Corps)
commanders B: Marshal François Achille Bazaine; Canrobert, Frossard, Le Bœuf, Ladmirault
Prussian force: Alvensleben's III Corps (Brandenburgers) attacked what it took for a rearguard and held the whole French army all day, joined in the afternoon by Voigts-Rhetz's X Corps and the 5th and 6th Cavalry Divisions; von Bredow's 'death ride' (7th Cuirassiers, 16th Uhlans) silenced Canrobert's guns.
strength A: 30,000 at first, 80,000 by evening, over 210 guns
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Mars-la-Tour; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Mars-la-Tour; Howard (1961); Wawro (2003)
note: Also Vionville or Rezonville. Tactically indecisive (en.wikipedia 'inconclusive'; de.wikipedia 'taktisches Unentschieden') but a major strategic German success: the Germans cut the road to Verdun and Bazaine fell back towards Metz on 17 August. de.wikipedia gives German losses as 15,780.

name: Hiddensee (1870)
place: At sea off Hiddensee, west of Rügen (Pomerania; now Mecklenburg-Vorpommern)
commanders A: Kapitän zur See Count Franz von Waldersee
Prussian force: The aviso Grille with three gunboats of the Stralsund flotilla under Count Franz von Waldersee, which attacked ships of the French Baltic squadron and withdrew into shallow water.
strength A: the aviso Grille and three gunboats
borderline: Date not verified: en.wikipedia SMS Grille gives '17 July' (before Grille was recommissioned on 24 July, so evidently an error) and links the French ships to their Køge Bay base; 17 August is taken from the German naval histories; a long-range exchange without damage
doubts and flags: Borderline: Date not verified: en.wikipedia SMS Grille gives '17 July' (before Grille was recommissioned on 24 July, so evidently an error) and links the French ships to their Køge Bay base; 17 August is taken from the German naval histories; a long-range exchange without damage.
sources: de.wikipedia Seegefecht vor Hiddensee (listed in Kategorie:Konflikt 1870; page not reached); en.wikipedia SMS Grille
note: Inconclusive: neither side was hit. en.wikipedia says the sortie disrupted French plans to attack Swinemünde; Waldersee received the Iron Cross.

name: Gravelotte
place: Gravelotte, Amanvillers and Saint-Privat-la-Montagne, west of Metz (Moselle)
commanders A: King Wilhelm I, Helmuth von Moltke; Karl Friedrich von Steinmetz (First Army), Prince Frederick Charles (Second Army)
commanders B: Marshal François Achille Bazaine; Marshal François Certain de Canrobert (VI Corps at St Privat)
Prussian force: Moltke directed the First Army (VII and VIII Corps, 1st Cavalry Division) against the Mance ravine and the Second Army (Guard Corps, IX Corps with the Hessian 25th Division, XII Saxon Corps, with III, X and II Corps) against the French right; the Guard was cut down before St Privat, which fell at dusk to the Guard and the Saxons.
losses B: 12,275 (1,146 killed, 6,709 wounded, 4,420 captured or missing; records incomplete)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Gravelotte; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Gravelotte; Howard (1961); Wawro (2003)
note: Also Gravelotte–St Privat. The largest battle of the war; Bazaine withdrew into Metz, where his army was besieged.

name: Metz (siege, 1870)
place: Metz (Moselle)
commanders A: Prince Frederick Charles; Steinmetz (First Army, later Manteuffel); Frederick Francis II of Mecklenburg-Schwerin
Prussian force: Prince Frederick Charles invested Metz with the First and Second Armies (I, II, III, VII, VIII, IX, X Corps, the Hessian 25th Division and Kummer's reserve division), 168,435 men and 642 field guns at first, 197,326 by September.
losses A: 5,740 killed and wounded (240 officers, 5,500 men); 40,000 sick
losses B: 12,481 killed and wounded; about 173,000 captured at the surrender (6,000 officers and 167,000 men) and 20,000 sick; 622 field guns, 2,876 fortress guns, 72 mitrailleuses
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Metz (1870); de.wikipedia Belagerung von Toul (campaign navbox); Howard (1961)
note: One entry for the siege; its named sortie battles are separate entries (Noisseville 31 August – 1 September here; Peltre, Bellevue/Ladonchamps and others in the next period). Bazaine's Army of the Rhine capitulated on 27 October and the Germans entered Metz on 29 October. Start date given as 19 or 20 August.

name: Danzig Bay (1870)
place: Off Neufahrwasser in the Bay of Danzig (now Nowy Port, Gdańsk Bay), towards the Putziger Wiek (Puck Bay)
commanders A: Korvettenkapitän Weickhmann (SMS Nymphe)
Prussian force: The screw corvette Nymphe under Korvettenkapitän Weickhmann made a night sortie from Neufahrwasser and fired two broadsides at the anchored French squadron before escaping behind the coastal batteries.
strength B: 3 ironclads (including Surveillante and Thétis) and an aviso
borderline: A single-ship night attack with no standalone Wikipedia article; named in German naval histories as Nymphe's attack on the French squadron off Danzig
doubts and flags: Borderline: A single-ship night attack with no standalone Wikipedia article; named in German naval histories as Nymphe's attack on the French squadron off Danzig.
sources: en.wikipedia SMS Nymphe (1863) (after Hildebrand, Röhr and Steinmetz; Stenzel)
note: No damage on either side; accounts differ on the target (Thétis or the flagship Surveillante). Bouët-Willaumez concluded that his ironclads could not operate close inshore and left Danzig, which the Germans counted as a success.

name: Buzancy
place: Buzancy, south of Sedan (Ardennes)
commanders A: Friedrich Senfft von Pilsach (24th Saxon Cavalry Brigade)
commanders B: Pierre Louis Charles de Failly (V Corps); Major de la Porte (captured)
Prussian force: Saxon cavalry of the XII Corps (federal army): the 3rd Saxon Reiter Regiment with a squadron of the 18th Uhlans and a horse battery, under Senfft von Pilsach.
strength A: the 3rd Saxon Reiter Regiment, a squadron of the 18th Uhlans and a horse battery
losses A: 2 captains and 32 men wounded, 27 horses; killed not given
losses B: killed and wounded not given; Major de la Porte and 12 troopers captured
borderline: A cavalry action, named in en.wikipedia and German regimental histories
doubts and flags: Borderline: A cavalry action, named in en.wikipedia and German regimental histories.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Buzancy
note: The first contact between the Army of the Meuse and MacMahon's Army of Châlons on its march to relieve Metz.

name: Nouart
place: Nouart and the Wiseppe valley, south of Beaumont-en-Argonne (Ardennes)
commanders A: Prince George of Saxony (XII Corps)
commanders B: Pierre Louis Charles de Failly (V Corps)
Prussian force: The Saxon XII Corps of the federal army under Prince George, with the 46th Infantry Brigade most engaged.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Nouart
note: Total losses of both sides about 600. De Failly withdrew through the woods to Beaumont, where he was surprised the next day.

name: Beaumont
place: Beaumont-en-Argonne, pursuit to Mouzon on the Meuse (Ardennes)
commanders A: Crown Prince Albert of Saxony (Army of the Meuse); Gustav von Alvensleben (IV Corps), Prince George of Saxony (XII Corps), Ludwig von der Tann (I Bavarian Corps)
commanders B: Pierre Louis Charles de Failly (V Corps)
Prussian force: Alvensleben's Prussian IV Corps surprised de Failly's V Corps in its camps, supported by the Saxon XII Corps and von der Tann's I Bavarian Corps, and drove it back on Mouzon.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Beaumont; de.wikipedia Belagerung von Toul (campaign navbox lists Beaumont); Howard (1961)
note: en.wikipedia's text calls the IV Corps commander 'Constantin von Alvensleben' in error; it was Gustav von Alvensleben. The defeat drove MacMahon's army back across the Meuse to Sedan.

name: Noisseville
place: Noisseville and Servigny, east of Metz (Moselle)
commanders A: Prince Frederick Charles; Edwin von Manteuffel (I Corps)
Prussian force: Manteuffel's East Prussian I Corps with Kummer's reserve division bore the French break-out attempt on the east bank of the Moselle and retook Noisseville on 1 September, reinforced from the investing army (Hessian troops also engaged).
losses B: 146 officers and 3,401 men (the article's text: 145 officers and 3,379 men)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Noisseville; de.wikipedia Schlacht von Noisseville (listed in Kategorie:Konflikt 1870); Howard (1961)
note: A sortie battle of the siege of Metz. Bazaine's army gained ground on 31 August (Noisseville, Servigny) but was driven back into Metz on 1 September, the day of Sedan.

name: Sedan
place: Sedan, Ardennes (with Bazeilles, Floing, Illy and Givonne)
commanders A: Wilhelm I, Helmuth von Moltke, Crown Prince Frederick William (Third Army), Crown Prince Albert of Saxony (Army of the Meuse)
commanders B: Napoleon III (captured), Patrice de MacMahon (wounded), Auguste Ducrot, Emmanuel de Wimpffen
Prussian force: The Third Army (V and XI Prussian Corps, I and II Bavarian Corps, Württemberg Division) and the Army of the Meuse (Guard, IV Corps and the Saxon XII Corps), about 200,000 men; V and XI Corps closed the ring from the west at Floing and Illy, the Guard and XII Corps from the east.
losses B: 3,220 killed, 14,811 wounded; about 104,000 captured (with the capitulation) and 558 guns
sources: Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961); Wawro, The Franco-Prussian War (2003); en.wikipedia Battle of Sedan; fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande de 1870-1871
note: Bazeilles (I Bavarian Corps against French marine infantry; fighting there began on 31 August) is treated as part of the battle, as in en.wikipedia. The Army of Châlons capitulated on 2 September and Napoleon III was taken prisoner.

name: Soissons (siege, 1870)
place: Soissons, Aisne
commanders A: Grand Duke Frederick Francis II of Mecklenburg-Schwerin; Lieutenant-General von Selchow (siege from 1 October)
Prussian force: First troops of the Grand Duke of Mecklenburg's XIII Corps, then a siege corps under von Selchow of Landwehr battalions, cavalry, pioneers and field and fortress artillery (9 battalions, about 7,200 infantry).
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Soissons; fr.wikipedia Siège de Soissons (1870) and Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande
note: en.wikipedia: town surrounded 11 September; fr.wikipedia chronology dates the start of the defence to 24 September. Bombardment 12-15 October; capitulation signed late on 15 October, effective 16 October. About 600 prisoners escaped in transit. Sources differ on the prisoner count.

name: Mont-Mesly
place: Mont-Mesly near Créteil and Villeneuve-Saint-Georges, south-east of Paris (Val-de-Marne)
Prussian force: The advance guard of the Third Army (17th Brigade, V Corps) crossing the Seine at Villeneuve-Saint-Georges on the march to encircle Paris.
borderline: Small action at the start of the investment; German unit identification from the French chronology only
doubts and flags: Borderline: Small action at the start of the investment; German unit identification from the French chronology only.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Paris (1870-1871) (Villeneuve-Saint-Georges, 17 September); fr.wikipedia Chronologie du siège de Paris (1870-1871)
note: Vinoy's attempt to cover the depot at Villeneuve-Saint-Georges; the French were driven back by artillery and the Germans continued the investment. Vinoy claimed about 400 German losses (58 killed), unverified. Not to be confused with the Mont-Mesly fighting of 30 November, included under Villiers.

name: Paris (siege, 1870–1871)
place: Paris, Seine (now Paris and the surrounding departments)
commanders A: Wilhelm I, Helmuth von Moltke, Crown Prince Frederick William (Third Army), Crown Prince Albert of Saxony (Army of the Meuse)
commanders B: Louis Jules Trochu, Joseph Vinoy, Auguste Ducrot
Prussian force: The Third Army and the Army of the Meuse: the Guard, IV, V, VI, XI and Saxon XII Corps, later II Corps and Landwehr, with the II Bavarian Corps and the Württemberg Division; about 240,000 regulars.
strength B: about 200,000 regulars, Garde Mobile and sailors, and about 200,000 National Guards
losses B: about 24,000 killed and wounded; the garrison capitulated (en.wikipedia also gives about 47,000 civilian casualties)
sources: Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961); en.wikipedia Siege of Paris (1870-1871); fr.wikipedia Chronologie du siège de Paris
note: One entry for the siege; its named battles (Châtillon, Chevilly, Bagneux, Buzenval 1870, the two Le Bourget fights, Villiers/Champigny, and Buzenval 1871) are listed separately. The siege ended with the armistice of 28 January 1871; the German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles on 18 January.

name: Châtillon (1870)
place: Plateau of Châtillon and Petit-Bicêtre (Clamart, Vélizy), south-west of Paris (Hauts-de-Seine)
commanders A: Hugo von Kirchbach (V Corps), Jakob von Hartmann (II Bavarian Corps)
Prussian force: The Prussian V Corps (Kirchbach), with the II Bavarian Corps beside it, marching round the south of Paris towards Versailles.
sources: Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961); de.wikipedia navbox (Gefecht bei Sceaux); fr.wikipedia Chronologie du siège de Paris (première bataille de Châtillon)
note: German name Gefecht bei Sceaux (or Petit-Bicêtre and Châtillon); French first battle of Châtillon. Ducrot's corps gave way under artillery fire (some Zouave units fled into Paris) and he abandoned the Châtillon redoubt, spiking eight guns. Strengths and losses not verified.

name: Peltre
place: Peltre and Mercy-le-Haut, south-east of Metz, Moselle
commanders A: General Lapasset (Army of the Rhine, under Bazaine)
Prussian force: Prussian outpost troops of the Metz investment holding Peltre, which was overrun.
borderline: Foraging sortie: the French took the village and brought back supplies and prisoners, then withdrew into Metz
doubts and flags: Borderline: Foraging sortie: the French took the village and brought back supplies and prisoners, then withdrew into Metz.
sources: fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande (combat de Peltre, 27 September); Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: Part of a day of sorties from Metz (also Colombey-Mercy and La Maxe). The outcome is given as a French tactical success; the Germans reoccupied Peltre.

name: Chevilly
place: Chevilly, L'Haÿ, Thiais and Choisy-le-Roi, south of Paris (now Chevilly-Larue, Val-de-Marne)
commanders A: Wilhelm von Tümpling (VI Corps)
Prussian force: The Prussian VI Corps (Tümpling) of the Third Army, holding the southern sector of the investment.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Paris (1870-1871) (Battle of Chevilly); de.wikipedia Deutsch-Französischer Krieg; Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: The first French sortie in force from Paris, repulsed. Loss figures are approximate.

name: Toury
place: Toury, Eure-et-Loir, north of Orléans
commanders A: General Reyau (cavalry of the forming XV Corps)
commanders B: Prince Albrecht of Prussia (4th Cavalry Division)
Prussian force: Prince Albrecht's 4th Cavalry Division, screening the Paris investment towards the Loire, was surprised and fell back.
borderline: Small action; French commander identification not verified
doubts and flags: Borderline: Small action; French commander identification not verified.
sources: fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande (combat de Toury); Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: The French advance prompted Moltke to send von der Tann's I Bavarian Corps and the 22nd Division south, leading to Artenay and Orléans.

name: Nompatelize
place: Nompatelize, La Bourgonce and Saint-Rémy, near Saint-Dié, Vosges
commanders A: Alfred von Degenfeld (Baden brigade of Werder's XIV Corps)
Prussian force: No Prussian units engaged: the advance guard of Werder's XIV Corps was Degenfeld's Baden brigade (3rd and 6th Infantry Regiments, Leib-Grenadiers, dragoons and two batteries); the corps commander August von Werder was Prussian.
borderline: South German troops only
doubts and flags: Borderline: South German troops only. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: fr.wikipedia Bataille de Nompatelize; fr.wikipedia Guerre franco-allemande de 1870 (navbox)
note: Also called La Bourgonce or Étival. The Germans burned houses in the villages; Cambriels then evacuated the Vosges. Strength figures vary widely between sources.

name: Bellevue
place: Bellevue, Ladonchamps, Saint-Rémy and the Tapes farms, Woippy, north of Metz, Moselle
commanders A: Prince Frederick Charles; Ferdinand von Kummer (Landwehr division)
Prussian force: Kummer's Landwehr division north of Metz on the left bank of the Moselle, supported by troops of X Corps; about 40,000 (en.wikipedia).
losses A: about 1,800 (en.wikipedia text; its infobox gives 1,300 killed and wounded and 500 captured)
losses B: about 1,300 (en.wikipedia text; its infobox gives 1,200 killed and wounded and 100 captured)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bellevue; de.wikipedia navbox (Schlacht bei Bellevue); fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande
note: Also Ladonchamps or les Tapes. The last major sortie from Metz, a foraging attack; preceded by fighting for Ladonchamps chateau on 1-4 October. Metz capitulated on 27 October. The en.wikipedia infobox and text disagree on losses.

name: Ablis
place: Ablis, Seine-et-Oise (now Yvelines), between Rambouillet and Chartres
Prussian force: Prussian hussars quartered in the village, surprised at night.
borderline: Francs-tireurs night raid; small and not verified online
doubts and flags: Borderline: Francs-tireurs night raid; small and not verified online.
sources: Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961) (francs-tireurs and reprisals)
note: French irregulars surprised the cavalry quartered in Ablis; the Germans burned the village in reprisal. Details (units, losses) not verified.

name: Saint-Quentin (1870)
place: Saint-Quentin, Aisne
commanders A: Anatole de La Forge (prefect of the Aisne)
Prussian force: A small German column with cavalry and guns, sent to occupy the town, withdrew after a fight at the barricades.
borderline: Small action: defence by the National Guard and townspeople
doubts and flags: Borderline: Small action: defence by the National Guard and townspeople.
sources: fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande (8 October: National Guard repels a Prussian attack)
note: The Germans returned and occupied the town later in October. Distinct from the battle of Saint-Quentin of 19 January 1871.

name: Artenay
place: Artenay, Loiret, north of Orléans
commanders A: Ludwig von der Tann (I Bavarian Corps); Count Wilhelm zu Stolberg (2nd Cavalry Division), Prince Albrecht of Prussia (4th Cavalry Division)
Prussian force: The Prussian 2nd and 4th Cavalry Divisions on the flanks of von der Tann's I Bavarian Corps (Dragoon Regiment No. 5 and Uhlan Regiment No. 2 led the pursuit); Wittich's 22nd Division followed in support.
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Artenay; de.wikipedia Deutsch-Französischer Krieg
note: The Bavarians did the infantry fighting; the Prussian cavalry divisions were engaged on the wings.

name: Orléans (first, 1870)
place: Northern suburbs of Orléans (Les Aydes, Saran, Ormes) and the city, Loiret
commanders A: Ludwig von der Tann (I Bavarian Corps); Ludwig von Wittich (22nd Division)
Prussian force: Wittich's Prussian 22nd Division fought beside the I Bavarian Corps in the attack on the northern suburbs, with the 2nd and 4th Cavalry Divisions.
losses B: about 3,000 captured, besides killed and wounded
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Artenay; de.wikipedia Schlacht von Orléans
note: The first battle of Orléans; the city was occupied the same day. The French retook it after Coulmiers (9 November); the December battle is listed as Orléans (second, 1870).

name: Bagneux
place: Bagneux and Châtillon, south of Paris (Hauts-de-Seine)
commanders A: Jakob von Hartmann (II Bavarian Corps)
commanders B: Louis Jules Trochu; Generals Blanchard and Susbielle (XIII Corps)
Prussian force: Mainly the II Bavarian Corps (Hartmann), which held Bagneux and Châtillon; parts of the Prussian V Corps and its artillery took part.
borderline: Prussian share small (mainly Bavarians)
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian share small (mainly Bavarians).
sources: de.wikipedia Gefecht von Châtillon; fr.wikipedia Deuxième bataille de Châtillon (1870); en.wikipedia Siege of Paris (1870-1871)
note: German name Gefecht von Châtillon; French second battle of Châtillon or combat de Bagneux. A reconnaissance in force: the French took Bagneux, then withdrew on Trochu's order, and Hartmann's counterattack restored the line; Commandant de Dampierre was mortally wounded. French claims of over 4,200 German casualties are not credible.

name: Verdun (siege, 1870)
place: Verdun, Meuse
commanders A: General von Gayl
Prussian force: Prussian Landwehr and Saxon troops with siege artillery, about 15,000 infantry and 140 guns (en.wikipedia).
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Verdun (1870); fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande
note: The Saxon XII Corps tried to take Verdun by a coup de main on 24 August (repulsed); a blockade followed from late September and the formal siege from 13 October (en.wikipedia dates are inconsistent). The garrison made several sorties and capitulated on 8 November.

name: Neu-Breisach (siege)
place: Neuf-Brisach (German Neu-Breisach) and Fort Mortier, Haut-Rhin
commanders A: Hermann von Schmeling (4th Reserve Division)
Prussian force: Schmeling's 4th Reserve Division (Prussian Landwehr, with some Baden and Bavarian units) and siege artillery.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Neu-Breisach
note: Blockade from 9 October, investment completed 13 October, bombardment from 2 November; Fort Mortier surrendered on 7 November and the town on 10 November.

name: Châteaudun
place: Châteaudun, Eure-et-Loir
commanders A: Ludwig von Wittich (22nd Division)
Prussian force: Wittich's Prussian 22nd Division, about 12,000 men with 24 guns, with cavalry of Prince Albrecht's 4th Cavalry Division.
strength B: about 1,200 (francs-tireurs de Paris, Châteaudun National Guard and other volunteers)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Châteaudun; fr.wikipedia Bataille de Châteaudun
note: The town was stormed after a defence lasting into the night and about 263 houses were burned in reprisal; Châteaudun received the Légion d'honneur. German losses are not reliably given (a French eyewitness claim of 2,500 is not credible).

date: 20–24 October 1870 (bombardment from the night of 19 October)
name: Sélestat (siege)
place: Sélestat (German Schlettstadt), Bas-Rhin
commanders A: Hermann von Schmeling (4th Reserve Division)
Prussian force: Schmeling's 4th Reserve Division: Landwehr Regiments Nos. 1, 3, 4, 5, 43 and 45, Infantry Regiment No. 25 and siege artillery, with some Baden and Bavarian units.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Sélestat
note: Trenches opened on 21 October; after heavy shelling on 22 October the garrison raised the white flag on 24 October.

name: Buzenval (1870)
place: Rueil-Malmaison, Buzenval and La Malmaison, west of Paris (Hauts-de-Seine)
commanders A: Hugo von Kirchbach (V Corps)
Prussian force: The Prussian V Corps (9th and 10th Divisions; Infantry Regiment No. 46 at Malmaison, Grenadier Regiment No. 6 in the Bois Béranger), with detachments of IV Corps and the Guard.
strength B: about 6,000 infantry and 30 guns, with 4,600 infantry and 46 guns in reserve
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Buzenval (1870); fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande
note: Also called La Malmaison; the first battle of Buzenval (the second was 19 January 1871).

name: Ognon (Étuz and Cussey)
place: Étuz, Cussey-sur-l'Ognon, Voray and Châtillon-le-Duc on the Ognon, north of Besançon (Haute-Saône and Doubs)
commanders A: August von Werder (XIV Corps)
Prussian force: Werder's XIV Corps: the Baden division attacked the Ognon crossings at Étuz and Cussey; no Prussian units engaged (Werder was Prussian).
borderline: South German troops only; details not verified
doubts and flags: Borderline: South German troops only; details not verified. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande (combats of Cussey-sur-l'Ognon, Châtillon-le-Duc and Auxon-Dessus, 21-23 October)
note: German name Gefecht am Ognon. The Badeners crossed the river and Cambriels fell back to the entrenched camp of Besançon, but the French held before Besançon and claimed success at Châtillon-le-Duc; Werder then turned west to Gray and Dijon.

name: Gray
place: Essertenne and Talmay, on the Vingeanne south-west of Gray, near the Saône (Haute-Saône and Côte-d'Or)
commanders A: Prince Wilhelm of Baden, under August von Werder (XIV Corps)
Prussian force: Prince Wilhelm of Baden's Baden troops of Werder's XIV Corps (en.wikipedia names a battalion of the Baden Leib-Grenadiers and the 2nd Baden Grenadier Regiment); no Prussian units are named.
losses B: 15 officers and 430 men captured at Talmay (text; the infobox says 500), and 60 prisoners near Mornay and Saint-Seine-l'Église
borderline: South German troops only
doubts and flags: Borderline: South German troops only. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Gray; fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande de 1870-1871 (27 October: Saint-Seine-sur-Vingeanne and Talmay)
note: Also called the Battle of Talmay. The Badeners scattered Lavalle's Garde Mobile at Essertenne and surrounded a body of it at Talmay; the French left Gray, which Werder then used as his base before taking Dijon (30-31 October). The en.wikipedia article's casualty figures are internally inconsistent.

name: Le Bourget (first, 1870)
place: Le Bourget, north-east of Paris (Seine-Saint-Denis)
commanders A: Crown Prince Albert of Saxony (Army of the Meuse); Rudolph Otto von Budritzki (2nd Guard Infantry Division)
Prussian force: The 2nd Guard Infantry Division of the Prussian Guard Corps retook the village on 30 October, about 6,000 men (en.wikipedia).
losses B: about 1,400 killed and wounded and 1,200 captured (en.wikipedia)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Le Bourget; en.wikipedia Siege of Paris (1870-1871); de.wikipedia navbox (Schlacht von Le Bourget)
note: De Bellemare seized Le Bourget without orders in the night of 27-28 October (en.wikipedia dates the battle 27-30 October); the Guard stormed it back on 30 October.

name: Dijon (October 1870)
place: Dijon, Côte-d'Or
commanders A: Gustav Friedrich von Beyer (Baden division), under August von Werder
Prussian force: Two Baden brigades of Werder's XIV Corps under the Prussian general Beyer; no Prussian units engaged.
borderline: South German troops only
doubts and flags: Borderline: South German troops only. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Dijon (1870); fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande (first battle of Dijon)
