note: Garde Mobile and National Guards defended the suburbs; Dijon capitulated on 31 October. en.wikipedia counts this as the first battle of Dijon (29-30 October) and Nuits (18 December) as the second; it does not clearly assign the loss figures to each side.

name: Belfort (siege, 1870–1871)
place: Belfort, Haut-Rhin (now Territoire de Belfort)
commanders A: Udo von Tresckow; August von Werder (XIV Corps)
Prussian force: Tresckow's 1st Reserve Division (Prussian Landwehr) with siege artillery and pioneers, reinforced in 1871; about 26,000 at its height (en.wikipedia).
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Belfort; fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande
note: Investment 3 November 1870, bombardment from 3 December. The fortress was never taken: it was handed over with the honours of war on 18 February 1871 on the French government's orders, after the armistice, and Belfort stayed French in the peace (en.wikipedia: inconclusive). Of the named fights of 1871 around the siege, Les Perches and the Lisaine relief battle are separate entries; Danjoutin and Pérouse are not.

name: Coulmiers
place: Coulmiers, Loiret, west of Orléans
commanders A: Louis d'Aurelle de Paladines (Army of the Loire)
commanders B: Ludwig von der Tann (I Bavarian Corps)
Prussian force: Count Stolberg's Prussian 2nd Cavalry Division on the flank of von der Tann's I Bavarian Corps, which did nearly all the fighting.
losses B: 54 officers and 1,112 men, and about 1,000 prisoners (en.wikipedia infobox)
borderline: Prussian share limited to the 2nd Cavalry Division; en.wikipedia names only the Bavarians
doubts and flags: Borderline: Prussian share limited to the 2nd Cavalry Division; en.wikipedia names only the Bavarians.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Coulmiers; de.wikipedia Deutsch-Französischer Krieg; Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: The first French victory of the war; von der Tann evacuated Orléans. The en.wikipedia infobox does not state clearly which side each loss figure belongs to.

name: Havana (1870)
place: Off Havana, Cuba (then a Spanish colony)
commanders A: Eduard von Knorr (gunboat Meteor)
Prussian force: The North German Federal Navy gunboat Meteor under Eduard von Knorr.
sources: fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande (combat naval du Bouvet et du Meteor, 9 November); fr.wikipedia Guerre franco-allemande de 1870 (navbox)
note: Bouvet's fire brought down Meteor's masts, whose rigging fouled her propeller; a Prussian shell disabled Bouvet's boiler and she escaped under sail into Spanish waters, where the neutral authorities stopped the pursuit. Both sides claimed success; casualties were a few killed and wounded on each side (figures not verified).

name: Thionville (siege, 1870)
place: Thionville (German Diedenhofen), Moselle
commanders A: Georg von Kameke (14th Division); Heinrich von Zastrow (VII Corps)
Prussian force: Kameke's 14th Division of VII Corps with siege artillery, after a loose blockade since August.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Thionville (1870); fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande
note: Blockade from the summer; investment 13 November, bombardment 22-24 November, capitulation 24 November.

name: Montmédy (siege, 1870)
place: Montmédy, Meuse
commanders A: Georg von Kameke (14th Division); Prince Kraft zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen (siege artillery)
Prussian force: Kameke's 14th Division with siege artillery under Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen; Saxon troops had bombarded the fortress briefly on 5 September.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Montmédy; fr.wikipedia Siège de Montmédy (1870); fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande
note: First bombarded on 5 September (fr.wikipedia dates the defence from then); formal siege from mid-November; capitulation 14 December, freeing 24 officers and 237 men held prisoner in the fortress.

name: Dreux
place: Dreux and Tréon, Eure-et-Loir
commanders A: Grand Duke Frederick Francis II of Mecklenburg-Schwerin; Hermann von Tresckow (17th Division)
Prussian force: Tresckow's 17th Division of the Grand Duke of Mecklenburg's army detachment, clearing the forward troops of the French Army of the West.
borderline: Minor action; unit details not verified online
doubts and flags: Borderline: Minor action; unit details not verified online.
sources: fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande (combat de Tréon, 17 November); Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: French name combat de Tréon. Opens the Grand Duke's westward sweep (Torçay on 18 November, Bretoncelles on 21 November) before he turned back towards Orléans.

name: Châtillon-sur-Seine
place: Châtillon-sur-Seine, Côte-d'Or
commanders A: Ricciotti Garibaldi (4th Brigade, Army of the Vosges)
Prussian force: A Prussian Landwehr garrison of about 800 infantry and cavalry guarding the lines of communication, surprised in its quarters.
losses B: 167 captured (11 officers) and 82 horses; French accounts add 150-180 killed and about 200 wounded
sources: fr.wikipedia Combat de Châtillon-sur-Seine; en.wikipedia Battle of Dijon (1870) (about 200 prisoners)
note: A francs-tireurs surprise by Garibaldi's Army of the Vosges (French and foreign volunteers). The Germans retaliated with looting, arson and a contribution on the town. The French figures for German killed and wounded are probably inflated.

name: La Fère (siege, 1870)
place: La Fère, Aisne
commanders A: Karl von Zglinitzki (4th Infantry Brigade, I Corps); Colonel von Kahlden
Prussian force: Zglinitzki's brigade of the I Corps (Manteuffel's First Army), with six fortress artillery companies, a pioneer company and a siege park of 49 guns.
strength B: about 2,800 (Garde Mobile, mobile artillery, francs-tireurs), 80 guns (36 rifled)
losses B: about 30 killed and wounded; the garrison captured (about 400 escaped)
sources: fr.wikipedia Siège de La Fère (1870); fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande
note: Fully invested about 19 November (fr.wikipedia chronology dates the start to 5 November); bombardment from dawn on 25 November; capitulation on 26 or 27 November (sources differ). The brigade then joined Manteuffel before Amiens.

name: Bretoncelles
place: La Fourche, La Madeleine-Bouvet and Bretoncelles, Orne, near Nogent-le-Rotrou
commanders A: Grand Duke Frederick Francis II of Mecklenburg-Schwerin
Prussian force: Troops of the Grand Duke of Mecklenburg's army detachment (17th and 22nd Divisions) advancing on Nogent-le-Rotrou and Le Mans.
borderline: Minor action; details not verified online
doubts and flags: Borderline: Minor action; details not verified online.
sources: fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande (combat de La Fourche, de La Madeleine and Bretoncelles, 21 November); Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: German name Gefecht bei La Madeleine-Bouvet. The French fell back towards Le Mans; the Grand Duke was then recalled eastwards towards Orléans.

name: Ladon and Mézières
place: Ladon and Mézières-en-Gâtinais (Maizières), Loiret
commanders A: Prince Frederick Charles (Second Army); Generals Lehmann and Valentini
commanders B: Louis d'Aurelle de Paladines; Charles Crouzat (XX Corps)
Prussian force: Brigades of Voigts-Rhetz's X Corps (Second Army) under Lehmann and Valentini, about 12,000 infantry (en.wikipedia).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ladon and Mézières; fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande (24 November: Ladon, Boiscommun, Neuville-aux-Bois, Maizières)
note: en.wikipedia gives 17 November, but the fighting was on 24 November (fr.wikipedia chronology), with parallel actions at Neuville-aux-Bois and Boiscommun. The prelude to Beaune-la-Rolande. German name Gefecht bei Ladon und Maizières.

name: Dijon (November 1870)
place: Pasques, Prenois, Lantenay, Talant and Hauteville, north-west of Dijon, Côte-d'Or
commanders A: August von Werder (XIV Corps)
Prussian force: Baden troops of Werder's XIV Corps holding Dijon; no Prussian units engaged.
borderline: South German troops only; details not verified
doubts and flags: Borderline: South German troops only; details not verified. Only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others: listed, not scored.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Dijon (1870) (failed attempt to retake Dijon, 26 November); fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande (combats at Pasques, Prenois, Hauteville, Talant, Lantenay)
note: Garibaldi's night attack on Dijon was repulsed at Talant and Hauteville, and the Baden counterattack at Pasques and Lantenay drove the Army of the Vosges back towards Autun.

name: Amiens (1870)
place: Villers-Bretonneux, Dury, Boves and Gentelles, south and east of Amiens, Somme
commanders A: Edwin von Manteuffel (First Army), August von Goeben (VIII Corps)
Prussian force: Manteuffel's First Army: Goeben's VIII Corps (15th and 16th Divisions) and Bentheim's 2nd Division of I Corps, with a cavalry division.
strength B: about 25,500 (17,500 of the Army of the North and 8,000 Garde Mobile at Amiens)
losses A: 1,292 killed and wounded (76 officers, 1,216 men); en.wikipedia adds 300 missing
losses B: 1,383 killed and wounded and 800-1,000 captured or missing
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Amiens (1870); de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Amiens (1870); fr.wikipedia Bataille de Villers-Bretonneux (1870)
note: Also called Villers-Bretonneux (with the combats of Boves, Gentelles, Cachy and Dury, 26-27 November). Goeben entered Amiens on 28 November; the citadel surrendered on 29 November after its commandant Vogel was mortally wounded.

name: Beaune-la-Rolande
place: Beaune-la-Rolande, Loiret
commanders A: Konstantin von Voigts-Rhetz (X Corps), Constantin von Alvensleben (III Corps), Prince Frederick Charles (Second Army)
commanders B: Charles Crouzat (XX Corps), Jean-Baptiste Billot (XVIII Corps)
Prussian force: Voigts-Rhetz's X Corps (three brigades, including the 19th Division and Conta's 9th Brigade) held the town until Alvensleben's III Corps (5th Division) and the 1st Cavalry Division arrived; about 11,000 men and 70 guns at first.
losses B: estimates range from about 3,100 (1,300 killed and wounded, 1,800 captured) to 8,000-9,000
sources: de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Beaune-la-Rolande; en.wikipedia Battle of Beaune-la-Rolande
note: The Army of the Loire's right wing failed to break through towards Fontainebleau and Paris. The painter Frédéric Bazille was killed with the 3rd Zouaves.

date: 29 November – 3 December 1870 (main fighting 30 November and 2 December)
name: Villiers
place: Champigny-sur-Marne, Bry-sur-Marne and Villiers-sur-Marne, east of Paris (Val-de-Marne)
commanders A: Eduard von Fransecky (II Corps), Crown Prince Albert of Saxony (Army of the Meuse)
commanders B: Auguste Ducrot (Second Army of Paris), Louis Jules Trochu
Prussian force: The Württemberg Division and the Saxon XII Corps held Villiers, Coeuilly and Champigny on 30 November; Fransecky's Prussian II Corps took command of the sector and counterattacked on 2 December.
strength B: about 52,000 engaged (en.wikipedia); Ducrot's sortie army about 80,000
losses B: about 3,500 killed and wounded and 1,500 captured (en.wikipedia)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Villiers; de.wikipedia navbox (Schlacht bei Villiers); fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande; Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: Also called Champigny: the 'great sortie'. The diversions of 29-30 November at L'Haÿ, Choisy-le-Roi (Gare-aux-Boeufs), Mont-Mesly and Épinay-sur-Seine are included here. Other accounts give considerably higher totals than the en.wikipedia infobox.

name: Étrépagny
place: Étrépagny, Eure (Vexin), between Gisors and Les Andelys
Prussian force: A Saxon detachment (infantry and cavalry of the Army of the Meuse's flank guard in the Vexin) quartered in the town, surprised at night.
borderline: Night surprise by Garde Mobile and francs-tireurs; small; details not verified online
doubts and flags: Borderline: Night surprise by Garde Mobile and francs-tireurs; small; details not verified online.
sources: fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande (combat d'Étrépagny, night of 29-30 November)
note: The Germans burned Étrépagny in reprisal. Saxon troops count as North German (XII Corps).

name: Mézières (siege, 1870–1871)
place: Mézières (now part of Charleville-Mézières), Ardennes
commanders A: Georg von Kameke (14th Division)
Prussian force: Kameke's 14th Division, moved from Montmédy, with siege artillery.
borderline: Start date of the investment (December 1870) not verified

note: Fought all afternoon round the Château d'Ardenay and La Butte, with about fifty dead, mostly French (fr.wikipedia); en.wikipedia says the French checked the German centre until nightfall, but de.wikipedia has the Germans reaching Ardenay on 9 January, and it became Friedrich Karl's headquarters.

name: Duneau
place: Duneau, near Connerré, Sarthe
Prussian force: Troops of the XIII Corps advancing down the Huisne (sector); unit and strength not given.
borderline: Minor combat named only in French Wikipedia's chronology of the war (no en/de article); German unit and result not verified.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Minor combat named only in French Wikipedia's chronology of the war (no en/de article); German unit and result not verified.
sources: fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande de 1870-1871; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Le Mans
note: Result inferred: the XIII Corps fought beyond Duneau at Connerré and Montfort on 10–11 January. German unit inferred from the sector of the advance described in en.wikipedia Battle of Le Mans (XIII Corps on the right along the Huisne, III and IX Corps in the centre on the Vendôme–Saint-Calais–Le Mans road, X Corps on the left along the Loir).

name: Le Mans
place: Le Mans and the Huisne valley east of it (Changé, Parigné-l'Évêque, Champagné, the Auvours plateau, Le Tertre, Pontlieue), Sarthe
commanders A: Prince Friedrich Karl (Second Army); Grand Duke Friedrich Franz II of Mecklenburg (XIII Corps); Constantin von Alvensleben (III Corps); Albrecht von Manstein (IX Corps); Konstantin von Voigts-Rhetz (X Corps)
commanders B: Antoine Chanzy (Second Army of the Loire); Jauréguiberry (XVI Corps), de Colomb (XVII Corps), Jaurès (XXI Corps)
Prussian force: Prince Friedrich Karl's Second Army: III, IX, X and XIII Corps with the 1st, 2nd, 4th and 6th Cavalry Divisions, about 58,000 infantry, 15,000 cavalry and 324 guns (73,000).
losses A: about 3,400–3,500 killed and wounded (200 officers and 3,200 men for 6–12 January), about 500 captured
losses B: 6,000–7,000 killed and wounded, 20,000–22,000 captured, 17 guns and 2 colours; some 50,000 deserted
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Le Mans; de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Le Mans; fr.wikipedia Bataille du Mans (1871); fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande de 1870-1871; Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: Includes the combats of Parigné-l'Évêque, Changé and Champagné on 10 January, the storming of Yvré-l'Évêque and Pontlieue on 12 January and the capture of the Conlie camp in the night of 12/13 January. de.wikipedia's article on the Second Army dates the battle 6–12 January, counting the advance (the combats of 6–9 January are listed separately here).

name: Arcey
place: Arcey and Sainte-Marie, west of Montbéliard, Doubs
commanders A: Charles Denis Bourbaki (Army of the East)
Prussian force: Outposts of Werder's XIV Corps, among them the 1st Rhenish Infantry Regiment No. 25 of the 4th Reserve Division; strength not given.
borderline: Minor advance-guard combat before the Lisaine; no en/de article (named 'combat d'Arcey-Sainte-Marie' in the French chronology and in German regimental literature).
doubts and flags: Borderline: Minor advance-guard combat before the Lisaine; no en/de article (named 'combat d'Arcey-Sainte-Marie' in the French chronology and in German regimental literature).
sources: fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande de 1870-1871; de.wikipedia Gefecht bei Villersexel (bibliography); fr.wikipedia Bataille de la Lizaine
note: The French advance guard drove the German outposts from Arcey and Sainte-Marie back to the Lisaine line, where the main battle began on 15 January.

name: Chassillé
place: Chassillé, west of Le Mans on the Laval road, Sarthe
Prussian force: German pursuit troops on the Le Mans–Laval road (X Corps sector); unit and strength not given.
borderline: Minor combat named only in French Wikipedia's chronology of the war (no en/de article); German unit and result not verified.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Minor combat named only in French Wikipedia's chronology of the war (no en/de article); German unit and result not verified.
sources: fr.wikipedia Chronologie de la guerre franco-allemande de 1870-1871
note: Pursuit of Chanzy's army after Le Mans; result inferred from the German advance to Saint-Jean-sur-Erve on 15 January. The chronology also lists a combat at Yvré-l'Évêque on 13 January (counted here with Le Mans).

name: Saint-Jean-sur-Erve
place: Saint-Jean-sur-Erve, Mayenne
commanders A: Karl von Schmidt (detachment of X Corps)
Prussian force: A mixed detachment of X Corps under Karl von Schmidt: three battalions, nine squadrons and eight guns, pursuing Chanzy's army after Le Mans.
losses B: not recorded (about 300 killed, wounded and missing in French accounts; Rousset thought them about equal to the German)
borderline: Minor rearguard combat of the pursuit after Le Mans; French Wikipedia article only.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Minor rearguard combat of the pursuit after Le Mans; French Wikipedia article only.
sources: fr.wikipedia Combat de Saint-Jean-sur-Erve (Rousset, Histoire générale de la guerre franco-allemande)
note: French accounts call it a successful rearguard defence (Chanzy claimed 3,000 German losses, which Rousset rejects): the French held the Erve until evening and withdrew in good order, and the Germans took the village at nightfall.

name: Lisaine
place: The Lisaine (Lizaine) between Montbéliard, Héricourt and Chenebier, Haute-Saône and Doubs
commanders A: August von Werder (XIV Corps); Wilhelm von Schmeling, Adolf von Glümer, Alfred von Degenfeld, Adolf Keller, Kolmar von Debschitz
commanders B: Charles Denis Bourbaki (Army of the East); Crémer's division at Chenebier
Prussian force: Werder's XIV Corps: Schmeling's Prussian 4th Reserve Division at Héricourt, the Goltz Brigade, Zimmermann's East Prussian Landwehr Brigade and Debschitz's Landwehr detachment, with the Baden Division (Degenfeld's, Wechmar's and Keller's brigades) on the right at Chenebier and Frahier; about 40,000–45,000 men and 146 guns, with siege guns from Belfort.
losses A: 1,800 killed and wounded, 400 captured (en.wikipedia); 81 officers and 1,847 men (de.wikipedia)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of the Lisaine; de.wikipedia Schlacht an der Lisaine; fr.wikipedia Bataille d'Héricourt (1871); Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: Also called the battle of Héricourt. Bourbaki's attempt to relieve Belfort failed; Keller's Baden brigade retook Chenebier on 17 January and the French withdrew that evening.

name: Sillé-le-Guillaume
place: Sillé-le-Guillaume, Sarthe
Prussian force: German troops pursuing Chanzy's army north-west of Le Mans; unit and strength not given.
borderline: Named only as a place of fighting on 15 January in en.wikipedia's Armée de la Loire article; no details.
doubts and flags: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored. Borderline: Named only as a place of fighting on 15 January in en.wikipedia's Armée de la Loire article; no details.
sources: en.wikipedia Armée de la Loire; fr.wikipedia Sillé-le-Guillaume
note: The town hall briefly served as the prefecture of the Sarthe while the German troops advanced on the town.

name: Longwy (siege, 1871)
place: Longwy, Meurthe-et-Moselle
commanders A: Georg von Kameke (14th Division); Colonel von Cosel (siege corps)
Prussian force: A siege corps of the 14th Division under Colonel von Cosel, with siege artillery under Major Wolf; Kameke in overall command; a Landwehr detachment under Major Count Schmettau had blockaded the place before.
borderline: A loose Landwehr blockade from late November 1870; the siege proper and bombardment began on 16–19 January 1871.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A loose Landwehr blockade from late November 1870; the siege proper and bombardment began on 16–19 January 1871.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Longwy (1871)
note: Field batteries opened fire on 16 January and the siege artillery on 19 January; the garrison asked for terms on 24 January and surrendered on 25 January. en.wikipedia gives 9 killed and 20 wounded without saying for which side.

name: Avallon
place: Avallon, Yonne
Prussian force: The 4th Pomeranian Infantry Regiment No. 21 (Kettler's 8th Brigade, II Corps) marching from Paris to join Manteuffel's Army of the South; strength not given.
borderline: Minor combat named in a German regimental article; French defenders not identified.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Minor combat named in a German regimental article; French defenders not identified.
sources: de.wikipedia Infanterie-Regiment von Borcke (4. Pommersches) Nr. 21; fr.wikipedia Avallon
note: The Prussians bombarded Avallon and took it, then looted shops and some houses (fr.wikipedia).

name: Saint-Quentin
place: Saint-Quentin, Aisne
commanders A: August von Goeben (First Army)
commanders B: Louis Faidherbe (Army of the North; Lecointe's XXII and Paulze d'Ivoy's XXIII Corps)
Prussian force: Goeben's First Army: Kummer's 15th and Barnekow's 16th Divisions (VIII Corps), Prince Albrecht's 3rd Reserve Division, von Gayl's combined division of I Corps, the 12th (Saxon) Cavalry Division (Count zur Lippe) and Dohna's cavalry brigade, about 33,000 men.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of St. Quentin (1871); fr.wikipedia Bataille de Saint-Quentin (1871); Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: The last battle of the Army of the North; fought on the same day as the Paris sortie at Buzenval. Faidherbe withdrew on Cambrai. Preceded on 18 January by a combat round Vermand and Pœuilly as Goeben caught the French flank march (not entered separately).

name: Buzenval (1871)
place: Buzenval park, Montretout and Saint-Cloud, below Mont Valérien, west of Paris (now Rueil-Malmaison and Saint-Cloud, Hauts-de-Seine)
commanders A: Crown Prince Friedrich Wilhelm (Third Army); Hugo von Kirchbach (V Corps)
commanders B: Louis Jules Trochu; Auguste-Alexandre Ducrot, Joseph Vinoy and Bellemare (columns)
Prussian force: Kirchbach's V Corps (9th and 10th Divisions) with the 1st Guard Landwehr Regiment, about 12,000 men in 12 battalions in the front line (en.wikipedia: 23,000), with artillery of IV Corps firing across the Seine.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Buzenval (1871); de.wikipedia Schlacht bei Buzenval; Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: Also called the battle of Mont-Valérien or the second battle of Buzenval (the October 1870 sortie is Malmaison). The last great sortie of the siege of Paris; the siege itself is one entry. The French fell back into the forts on 20 January; Paris signed the armistice on 28 January.

name: Dijon (1871)
place: Dijon and its northern outskirts (Talant, Fontaine, Plombières, Pouilly), Côte-d'Or
commanders A: Giuseppe Garibaldi (Army of the Vosges)
commanders B: Major General von Kettler (8th Infantry Brigade)
Prussian force: Kettler's 8th Infantry Brigade (4th Pomeranian Infantry Regiment No. 21 and 8th Pomeranian Infantry Regiment No. 61, II Corps), about 4,000 men, detached from Manteuffel's Army of the South to pin Garibaldi.
losses B: about 700 killed and wounded (en.wikipedia); the colour of the 2nd Battalion, 61st Regiment, lost at Pouilly on 23 January
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Dijon (1870) (section on 21–23 January 1871); de.wikipedia Infanterie-Regiment von Borcke (4. Pommersches) Nr. 21; Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: Kettler's attacks on Talant and Fontaine (21 January), at Plombières (22 January) and at Pouilly (23 January) were repulsed, but his demonstration kept Garibaldi in Dijon while Manteuffel marched against Bourbaki's line of retreat. Garibaldi's army included Italian, Polish (Józef Hauke-Bosak, killed) and other volunteers. The only German colour lost in the war.

name: Les Perches
place: The Hautes-Perches and Basses-Perches redoubts south of Belfort, Territoire de Belfort
commanders A: Colonel Pierre Philippe Denfert-Rochereau (Belfort garrison)
Prussian force: Storming columns of Tresckow's siege corps (1st Reserve Division) before Belfort; strength not given.
borderline: A named assault inside the siege of Belfort (the siege itself is one entry).
doubts and flags: Borderline: A named assault inside the siege of Belfort (the siege itself is one entry).
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Belfort; fr.wikipedia Siège de Belfort (1870-1871)
note: Tresckow's premature assault on the Perches redoubts was repulsed; the Germans occupied the Perches only on 8 February, after the French withdrew under bombardment, and Belfort surrendered on 16 February (garrison out on 18 February). Earlier in January the besiegers had taken Danjoutin (8 January) and Pérouse (20–21 January) as part of the siege.

name: Pontarlier
place: Sombacourt, Chaffois, Frasne, Pontarlier and the Cluse gorge below the Fort de Joux, Doubs
commanders A: Edwin von Manteuffel (Army of the South); Eduard von Fransecky (II Corps); Heinrich von Zastrow (VII Corps)
Prussian force: Manteuffel's Army of the South (II and VII Corps): the 14th Division at Sombacourt and Chaffois, II Corps at Frasne, and du Trossel's brigade at Pontarlier and La Cluse.
losses B: 19 officers and 365 men killed; 15,000 captured including 2 generals; 10 guns and mitrailleuses (en.wikipedia)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Pontarlier; de.wikipedia Schlacht an der Lisaine (pursuit); Howard, The Franco-Prussian War (1961)
note: The pursuit of Bourbaki's (from 26 January Clinchant's) army, which the armistice of 28 January did not cover: combats of Sombacourt and Chaffois (29 January) and Frasne (29/30 January; en.wikipedia also lists Les Planches on 29 and Sainte-Marie on 31 January), the taking of Pontarlier and the combat at La Cluse (1 February), where the French rearguard and the Fort de Joux held off du Trossel's brigade while the army crossed into Switzerland at Les Verrières (convention of 1 February; about 87,000 interned).
